chunks.heading: 2027 HKDSE Geography Assessment Framework

chunks.text:
Candidates should be able to:

- (a–c) explain human–environment interaction, place characteristics, and geographical patterns/change over space and time
- (d–h) critically evaluate regional identity; understand sustainable development; recognise perceptions/values in decision-making; evaluate strategies for managing conflicting environmental demands; appreciate growing global interdependency
- (i–j) identify geographical questions and build a logical enquiry; select geographical/generic skills, present and interpret findings, draw evidence-based conclusions

Grading is standards-referenced; assessment should be both formative and summative.
chunks.heading: Assessment objectives (a–j)

chunks.text:
Paper 1 — 75%, 2¾ h (Compulsory Part)
- A MCQ — 20% (~30 min)
- B fieldwork-based, compulsory — 15% (~45 min)
- C data/skill-based structured — 30% (answer 2 of 4)
- D short essay — 10% (answer 1 of 3)

Paper 2 — 25%, 1¼ h (Elective Part)
- E structured — 15%
- F short essay — 10%
- One from each; both may come from the same elective.

Both papers may test skills, attitudes/values, and map work on local topographic maps (1:20,000 / 1:5,000) or simplified map extracts.

chunks.text:

- Changing Industrial Location

chunks.heading: 1. Three Types of Plate Boundaries

chunks.text:
- Found at: Destructive & Constructive boundaries
- Destructive: Magma rises from subduction
- Constructive: Magma rises to fill gap
chunks.heading: 🌋 Volcano

chunks.text:
- Found at: Destructive boundary (oceanic-oceanic)
- Examples: Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, Taiwan
chunks.heading: 🏝️ Volcanic Island Arc

chunks.text:
- Found at: Destructive boundary
- Examples: 
  - Mariana Trench: 11,022m (deepest)
  - Philippine Trench: 10,497m
  - Chile-Peru Trench: 8,050m
chunks.heading: 🌊 Ocean Trench

chunks.text:
- Found at: Constructive boundary
- Examples: Mid-Atlantic Ridge (Iceland)
chunks.heading: 🏔️ Mid-Oceanic Ridge

chunks.text:
Oceanic + Continental:
1. Oceanic plate moves towards continental plate
2. Oceanic plate subducts under continental
3. Magma rises → Volcanoes on land
4. Ocean trench forms

Oceanic + Oceanic:
1. Two oceanic plates move towards each other
2. One subducts
3. Volcanic island arc forms

Continental + Continental:
1. Two continental plates collide
2. Neither subducts (both light)
3. Fold mountains form (e.g., Himalayas: 8,848m)
chunks.heading: Destructive Boundary (Convergent)

chunks.text:
1. Plates move apart
2. Tensional force creates gap
3. Magma rises from mantle
4. Mid-ocean ridge forms
5. New crust created
chunks.heading: Constructive Boundary (Divergent)

chunks.text:
1. Plates slide horizontally past each other
2. Friction builds up pressure
3. Pressure releases → Earthquake
4. NO vertical movement → NO volcanoes

chunks.heading: 4. Key Data

chunks.text:
Question prompts:

1. "Is there a volcano?" 
   - Yes → Destructive or Constructive
   - No + Earthquake → Transform

2. "Is there a trench?"
   - Yes → Destructive

3. "Is there a mid-ocean ridge?"
   - Yes → Constructive

4. "Are plates moving towards or apart?"
   - Towards → Destructive
   - Apart → Constructive
   - Sideways → Transform
chunks.heading: 5. How to Identify

chunks.text:
| Boundary | Examples |
|----------|----------|
| Destructive | Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, Himalayas, Andes, Mariana Trench |
| Constructive | Iceland, Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East Pacific Rise |
| Transform | San Andreas Fault (USA), Alpine Fault (NZ) |
chunks.heading: 6. Examples

chunks.text:
❌ "Transform boundaries have volcanoes"
✅ Wrong! Transform = earthquakes ONLY

❌ "Constructive boundaries have trenches"
✅ Wrong! Trenches = destructive

❌ "All volcanoes are at plate boundaries"
✅ Wrong! Hot spots (e.g., Hawaii) are NOT at boundaries
chunks.heading: 7. Common Mistakes

chunks.text:
| Boundary | Memory Tip |
|----------|------------|
| Destructive | "D" for "Crash" → towards → subduction |
| Constructive | "C" for "Come apart" → diverge |
| Transform | "T" for "Rub past" → slide |
chunks.heading: 8. Mnemonics

chunks.text:
- Know the difference between features
- Be able to explain WHY features form
- Remember: Transform = lateral movement only
- Continental-continental = no subduction = fold mountains
- Oceanic-continental = oceanic subducts = trench + volcanoes

chunks.heading: Sub-layers:

chunks.text:
Plates move due to several driving mechanisms:

1. Convection Currents (Primary Force)
- Heat from Earth's core causes magma in the asthenosphere to rise
- As hot magma rises, it spreads and pushes plates away from ridge
- Cooler, denser material sinks back down
- Creates circular motion → drives plate movement

2. Slab Pull
- Older, colder oceanic plates are denser
- When subducting, the heavy slab "pulls" the rest of the plate behind it
- Considered the strongest driving force

3. Ridge Push
- At mid-ocean ridges, newly formed crust is higher
- Gravity causes the ridge to "push" the plate away
- Less significant than slab pull
chunks.heading: Why Do Plates Move?

chunks.text:
#platemovement

| Mechanism           | Description                         | Importance      |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- | --------------- |
| Convection Currents | Circular motion of magma            | Primary driver  |
| Slab Pull           | Pulling force from subducting plate | Strongest force |
| Ridge Push          | Gravity pushing from ridge          | Secondary       |

- Plates float on asthenosphere
- Move due to convection currents
- Rate: ~5-9cm per year
1996 Q1
chunks.heading: Plate Movement Summary

chunks.text:
When two plates move TOWARDS each other:

| Combination | Result |
|------------|--------|
| Oceanic + Continental | Ocean trench + Volcanic mountains |
| Oceanic + Oceanic | Volcanic island arc |
| Continental + Continental | Fold mountains (no subduction) |

Examples:
- Himalayas: 8,848m, 2,900km long
- Japan: 118 volcanoes
- Mariana Trench: 11,022m (deepest)
chunks.heading: A. DESTRUCTIVE (Convergent)

chunks.text:
When two plates move APART:

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Mid-Oceanic Ridge | Underwater mountain range |
| Ocean Trench | Deep elongated trough |

Examples:
- Mid-Atlantic Ridge (Iceland)
- East Pacific Rise
chunks.heading: B. CONSTRUCTIVE (Divergent)

chunks.text:
When plates slide PAST each other:

- No volcanic activity
- Major earthquake risk

Examples:
- San Andreas Fault (USA)
- Alpine Fault (NZ)

-RIFT VALLEY
When plates pull APART within continent:

1. Tensional force creates normal faults
2. Central block sinks
3. Valley formed

Example: East Africa Rift Valley

docs.title: 2. Internal forces and processes
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP1/Concepts/2. Internal forces and processes.md

chunks.text:
| Force | Description | Effect on Rocks | Resulting Landforms |
|-------|-------------|----------------|---------------------|
| Compressional | Squeezing/pushing together | Rocks shorten, fold, thicken | Fold mountains, reverse faults |
| Tensional | Pulling apart | Rocks stretch, thin, fracture | Normal faults, rift valleys |
| Shearing | Sliding past each other | Rocks grind horizontally | Transform faults, earthquakes |
chunks.heading: 2.1 Types of Internal Forces

chunks.text:
| Force | → | Process | → | Landform |
|-------|---|---------|---|----------|
| Compressional | → | Folding | → | Fold mountains (e.g., Himalayas) |
| Compressional | → | Faulting (Reverse) | → | Fault scarps |
| Tensional | → | Faulting (Normal) | → | Rift valleys (e.g., East Africa) |
| Shearing | → | Faulting (Transform) | → | Fault lines (e.g., San Andreas) |
chunks.heading: How Forces Relate to Processes:

chunks.text: Internal processes are geological forces that shape Earth's surface from within the Earth. Caused by energy from Earth's interior (mantle convection, radioactive decay).
chunks.heading: 2.2 What are Internal Processes?

chunks.text: Compressional forces squeeze rock layers, causing them to bend and wrinkle.
chunks.heading: Definition:

chunks.text:
1. Compressional force pushes plates together
2. Rock layers squeezed
3. Layers bend upward (anticline) or downward (syncline)
4. Fold mountains form
chunks.heading: Formation:

chunks.text:
| Type      | Description        |
| --------- | ------------------ |
| Anticline | Fold arches upward |
| Syncline  | Fold dips downward |
| Monocline | Single bend        |
chunks.heading: Types:

chunks.text: Tensional or compressional forces cause rock to break and displace.
chunks.heading: Definition:

chunks.text:
1. Force builds up
2. Rock cannot bend → breaks
3. One side moves relative to other
4. Fault line forms
chunks.heading: Formation:

chunks.text:
| Type      | Force         | Movement            |
| --------- | ------------- | ------------------- |
| Normal    | Tensional     | One block drops     |
| Reverse   | Compressional | One block pushed up |
| Transform | Lateral       | Slides past         |
chunks.heading: Types:

chunks.text:
- San Andreas Fault
- East Africa Rift Valley
chunks.heading: Examples:

chunks.text:
| Process | Force | Rock Behavior | Result |
|---------|--------|---------------|--------|
| Folding | Compression | Bends | Fold mountains |
| Faulting | Tension/Compression | Breaks | Fault lines |
| Volcanism | Various | Melts/Erupts | Volcanoes |

chunks.heading: 2.6 KEY TERMS

chunks.text: Eruption of molten rock (magma) onto Earth's surface.
chunks.heading: Definition:

chunks.text:
1. Magma rises through cracks
2. Reaches surface → becomes lava
3. Lava cools and solidifies
4. Volcanic landforms build up
chunks.heading: Formation:

chunks.text:
| Feature | Description | Example |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| Lava flow | Molten rock flowing on surface | Hawaiian volcanoes |
| Volcanic cone | Mountain from layered lava/ash | Mt. Fuji |
| Crater | Bowl-shaped depression at summit | Mt. Vesuvius |
| Caldera | Large collapsed crater | Yellowstone |
| Lava plateau | Extensive flat lava flows | Deccan Traps |
| Ash cloud | Volcanic ash ejected high | Mt. Pinatubo |
| Pyroclastic flow | Fast-moving hot gas & ash | Mt. St. Helens |

chunks.text:

| Batholith     | Large pluton, exposed by erosion              | Sierra Nevada     |

chunks.text:
| Landform              | Description                 | Example   |
| --------------------- | --------------------------- | --------- |
| Shield volcano    | Broad, gentle slopes (<10°) | Mauna Loa |

chunks.heading: Types of Extrusive Volcanoes:

chunks.text:
| Feature | Vent Eruption | Fissure Eruption |
|---------|----------------|-------------------|
| Definition | Magma erupts through a single opening (pipe) | Magma erupts through linear cracks/fissures |
| Type | Central eruption | Linear eruption |
| Lava type | Usually more viscous (andesite/rhyolite) | Usually fluid basaltic lava |
| Eruption style | Explosive or effusive | Generally effusive (quiet) |
| Result | Volcanic cone/cinder cone | Lava plateaus, shield volcanoes |
| Examples | Mt. Fuji, Mt. St. Helens | Hawaiian volcanoes, Deccan Traps |

Key Difference:
- Vent: Point source eruption (one central opening)
- Fissure: Line source eruption (long crack in crust)

chunks.heading: 2. Oceanic Crust – Oceanic Crust Divergence

chunks.text: Transform plate boundaries are where two plates slide horizontally past each other. No new crust is created or destroyed. These boundaries are also called conservative boundaries because crust is neither created nor destroyed.
chunks.heading: Definition

chunks.text:
1. Two plates move in opposite directions OR in the same direction but at different speeds
2. Plates are locked by friction
3. Stress builds up along the fault line
4. When stress exceeds rock strength → sudden release → earthquakes
5. No vertical movement, no volcanic activity
chunks.heading: Formation Process

chunks.text:
| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| Transform fault | Vertical fracture where plates slide past each other |
| Fault trace | Surface expression of the fault |
| Earthquakes | Frequent, often shallow focus |
| No volcanoes | No magma generation (no subduction) |
| No mountains | No vertical uplift |
chunks.heading: Key Features

chunks.text:
| Fault | Location | Plates |
|-------|----------|--------|
| San Andreas Fault | USA (California) | Pacific Plate ↔ North American Plate |
| North Anatolian Fault | Turkey | Anatolian Plate ↔ Eurasian Plate |
| Alpine Fault | New Zealand | Pacific Plate ↔ Australian Plate |
| Haiti Fault | Caribbean | Gonâve Plate ↔ Caribbean Plate |
chunks.heading: Examples

chunks.text:
- Plates are locked by friction
- Stress accumulates over time
- When stress > rock strength → snap → earthquake
- Focus is usually shallow (<30km) → strong shaking at surface
chunks.heading: Why Earthquakes Occur

chunks.text:
| Feature | Transform | Convergent | Divergent |
|---------|-----------|------------|-----------|
| Movement | Lateral sliding | Collision | Separation |
| Crust change | None (conservative) | Destroyed | Created |
| Volcanoes | ❌ No | ✅ Yes (usually) | ✅ Yes (sometimes) |
| Earthquakes | ✅ Shallow, frequent | ✅ Deep/shallow | ✅ Usually small |
| Landforms | Fault lines | Mountains, trenches | Ridges, valleys |
chunks.heading: Key Differences from Other Boundaries

chunks.text: "At a transform plate boundary, two plates slide horizontally past each other. Friction locks the plates, causing stress to build up. When the stress is released, earthquakes occur. No volcanic activity because there is no subduction or decompression melting."

docs.title: 3.4 Intraplate Volcanism- Hot Spot & Mantle Plume
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP1/Concepts/3.4 Intraplate Volcanism- Hot Spot & Mantle Plume.md

chunks.text:
- NOT formed at plate boundaries
- Caused by mantle plume (hot spot) rising from deep within the mantle
- Pacific Plate moves northwest over the stationary hot spot
- Creates chain of volcanic islands (age progression)

Process:
1. Mantle plume (hot rock) rises from deep mantle
2. Volcano forms on oceanic crust
3. Plate moves, volcano moves away from hot spot
4. Volcano becomes extinct, new volcano forms
5. Chain of islands/seamounts created

Key Terms:
- Mantle plume / Hot spot
- Intraplate volcanism
- Plate movement direction
- Age progression (older → younger)
- Shield volcano
- Seamount / Guyot
- Volcanic chain

Examples:
- Hawaiian Islands (Mauna Loa, Mauna Kea)
- Emperor Seamounts

Annotation Example:
"Hawaiian Islands were formed by a mantle plume (hot spot) beneath the Pacific Plate. As the plate moves northwest, a chain of volcanoes is created. The oldest islands are in the northwest (Emperor Seamounts), while the youngest (Big Island) is currently over the hot spot."

chunks.heading: 4.5: KEY EXAMPLES

chunks.text:
Key Terms:
- Partial melting: Only ~1-10% of mantle rock melts → produces magma
- Decompression melting: Pressure drops → rock can melt at lower temperature

| Type | Features | Explosivity | Examples |
|------|----------|-------------|----------|

chunks.heading: 4.2.2 Examples at Different Plate Boundaries

chunks.text:
2022 P1 Q6

1. Convergent Boundaries — MOST POWERFUL
- Two plates collide or subduct
- Massive strain accumulates over long time
- When it releases → HUGE energy
- Example: Japan 2011 (M9.1), Chile 1960 (M9.5)
- Also: Friction causes very high stress before release
- Depth factor: Often shallow (<70km) → most destructive at surface

2. Transform Boundaries — STRONG & FREQUENT
- Plates slide horizontally past each other
- Friction locks plates → stress builds → sudden release
- Many small/medium earthquakes
- Example: San Andreas (M7.9), Turkey (M7.6)
- Frequent because plates constantly grinding
- Depth factor: Usually shallow (<30km) → strong shaking at surface

3. Divergent Boundaries — SMALLER
- Plates move apart slowly
- Less stress accumulation
- Usually smaller earthquakes
- Example: Iceland (M6.3)
- But can still be significant if near population centers
- Depth factor: Can be shallow or intermediate → moderate shaking

	4.1 VOLCANIC ERUPTIONS

Explain why wave erosion and deposition occur simultaneously along the southeastern coast of Hong Kong.  Discuss whether hard coastal management strategies should be adopted to protect this part of the coast in Hong Kong.

The southeastern coast of Hong Kong shows both wave erosion and deposition at the same time because a single, connected wave system meets a coast whose physical conditions vary from place to place, so different segments of the same coast process energy differently under the same weather.

First, the atmospheric and marine factors supply the energy. The prevailing easterly wind blows over a long, open fetch across the Pacific, building high-energy waves that strike the south-east-facing coast. Water depth and the roughness of the seabed shape the waves as they travel in, but the deep offshore water lets the swell arrive with its energy largely intact — this is the common driver acting on the whole coast simultaneously.

Second, the type of breaker that each wave becomes depends on the offshore gradient, and this is what splits one wave system into two simultaneous behaviours. Off the steep-shelving rock headlands, the incoming energy is released as plunging breakers: the crest curls over and crashes down violently, a sudden, concentrated hammer-blow of water — a destructive wave whose swash is powerful and whose backwash drags debris back down the rock face. Hydraulic action and abrasion exploit the lines of weakness — the joints and faults in the volcanic rock — and erosion proceeds. Off the gently shelving floors of the adjacent sheltered bays, the same swell arrives as spilling breakers: foam spills down the front of the wave, energy dissipates gradually, and the wave arrives at the beach as a weak, constructive wave — its swash still carries sediment up the beach while its weak backwash cannot pull it back, so competence falls and sediment settles. Because headlands and bays lie side by side, plunging and spilling breakers — erosion and deposition — are produced by the _same_ wind and wave event at the _same_ moment.

Wave refraction reinforces the split: crests bend around the headlands so energy converges on the exposed heads, while it diverges into the bays; combined with geological resistance — more resistant rock on the heads, weaker or jointed rock — the high-energy segments are cut back while the low-energy segments accumulate the sediment delivered by longshore drift, much of it eroded from the headlands moments earlier.

Because the wind and wave supply is continuous while breaker regime, refraction and geology vary along the coast, erosion and deposition are not alternating stages but concurrent outcomes of the same wave event: the coast is re-shaped in both directions at once, with eroded material from one site becoming the supply of the next.

Whether hard strategies — seawalls, revetments, groynes and breakwaters — should be adopted depends on the needs of protection against their cost-effectiveness, impacts and conflicts, and these begin with the land use of the coast itself.

The south-eastern coast is dominated by conservation and recreation rather than urban development. Large stretches fall within country park and UNESCO Global Geopark territory: rocky headlands, sandy bays, country park facilities such as campsites, trails and picnic sites. Settlement is limited to a few small, dispersed villages — Shek O and scattered shore hamlets — with no industry, no port and a population density far below the urban core; most of the shoreline has essentially no permanent residents. The coast's value lies in geotourism, water recreation and natural amenity, not in dense property.

Against this background the need for protection is real but localised. Typhoon waves and storm surges threaten the coastal villages, the road links that are the area's only lifelines, the valued bathing and surfing beaches, and the country park facilities near the shore. Where these assets sit close to the waterline, hard structures give direct, engineered defence — a seawall or revetment absorbs wave energy before it reaches property, and is cost-effective where the value of what is protected clearly exceeds the construction and maintenance outlay.

However, the issues must be weighed. Hard structures are expensive to build and maintain, and with a low population and dispersed assets the cost per beneficiary is high — cost-effectiveness weakens quickly away from the few asset clusters. Their interaction with the natural coast creates secondary problems: groynes trap sediment and starve downdrift beaches, seawalls reflect energy and scour the foreshore at their toe, so erosion is transferred rather than solved. Above all there is conflict with land use: concrete works devalue the country park and geopark scenery — the very amenity that gives this coast its recreational and touristic worth — and fixed defences interrupt the natural coast–environment interaction of cliff retreat and beach fluctuation. A conflict arises between engineering the coast and conserving it.

Judgement: given the low population and conservation-led land use, hard strategies should not be adopted across the board. They are justified selectively, after cost–benefit analysis, at the defined hotspots — a village cluster, a road section, a valued beach. Along the open rocky shore and country-park coastline, soft and accommodative measures — beach nourishment where sand matters, zoning and building restrictions, monitoring and typhoon warning — fit the land use and protect the coast at lower financial and environmental cost. Hard engineering is a tool for the few protected points, not a policy for this coast as a whole.

(1) Constructive waves are high and powerful, and their backwash removes material from the beach.
(2) Wave energy increases with both the fetch and the wind speed.
(3) Destructive waves have a steep front and a powerful backwash, so they remove material from the beach.

A (1) only
B (1) and (2) only
C (2) and (3) only
D (1), (2) and (3)
chunks.heading: Question 1

chunks.text:
At the foot of a cliff, a wave throws pebbles against the rock face and scours a notch into it. Out at sea, two rock fragments collide with each other and break into smaller, rounded pieces. Which of the following identifies these two processes in the correct order?

A Abrasion; attrition
B Hydraulic action; abrasion
C Attrition; abrasion
D Abrasion; solution
chunks.heading: Question 2

chunks.text:
Which of the following statements about longshore drift are correct?

(1) The swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle to the shoreline.
(2) The backwash carries the sediment straight down the slope, at right angles to the shoreline.
(3) Longshore drift is produced by the wind blowing parallel to the coast.

A (1) only
B (1) and (2) only
C (2) and (3) only
D (1), (2) and (3)
chunks.heading: Question 3

chunks.text:
Photograph 1 shows a natural opening through a rocky headland, with a sheltered bay behind it.

Which of the following shows the coastal features formed by wave erosion at a headland, in the order in which they develop?

A Stack → cave → arch → stump
B Arch → cave → stack → stump
C Wave-cut platform → cave → arch → stack
D Cave → arch → stack → stump
chunks.heading: Question 4

chunks.text:
Photograph 2 shows a rocky coast at low tide.

Which of the following statements are correct?

(1) The isolated pillar of rock is a stack, which forms when the roof of an arch collapses.
(2) The flat rock surface at the base of the cliff is a wave-cut platform, formed by wave erosion as the cliff retreated landwards.
(3) The flat rock surface was formed mainly by the deposition of fine sediment brought down by rivers.

A (1) only
B (1) and (2) only
C (2) and (3) only
D (1), (2) and (3)
chunks.heading: Question 5

chunks.text:
Photograph 3 is an aerial view of a narrow ridge of sediment projecting from the coast into the sea, with a curved, hooked end.

Which of the following must be true of the coast where this landform developed?

A Bands of hard and soft rock run at right angles to the shoreline, so alternate headlands and bays formed.
B Waves reaching this coast are always destructive, so they removed material from the beach.
C Sediment is supplied to the coast and moved along it by longshore drift.
D A river deposited sediment across the mouth of the bay, building a barrier that later hardened.
chunks.heading: Question 6

chunks.text:
Photograph 4 shows a coastal defence structure and the beach beside it at low tide.

Which of the following statements are correct?

(1) The structure is a groyne, built at right angles to the shore to interrupt the movement of sediment along the coast; the beach is higher on one side because sediment is trapped against it.
(2) The structure is a breakwater, built parallel to the shore and some distance out to sea to absorb wave energy.
(3) The structure is a sea wall, built along the top of the beach to prevent the land behind it from flooding.

A (1) only
B (1) and (2) only
C (2) and (3) only
D (1), (2) and (3)
chunks.heading: Question 7

chunks.text:
In Hong Kong's coastal management framework, soft engineering measures are used alongside hard structures. Which of the following correctly pairs a soft engineering measure with its effect?

A Seawall — absorbs wave energy before it reaches the shore, so it is classed as soft engineering.
B Groyne — works with natural processes to stabilise sediment, so it is classed as soft engineering.
C Breakwater — a soft measure that rebuilds the sand dunes behind a beach.
D Beach nourishment — adds sand to the beach so that it absorbs more wave energy, but the added sand is temporary and must be replenished.
chunks.heading: Question 8

chunks.text:
[code block omitted]

Q1 — C ((2) and (3))
- (1) False — describes destructive waves. Constructive waves are low and gentle, with a swash stronger than the backwash, so they build the beach.
- (2) True — energy rises with fetch and wind speed.
- (3) True — steep front, powerful backwash, net removal.
- Distractor family: right phenomenon, wrong category — the two wave types are swapped, not replaced with nonsense.

Q2 — A (abrasion; attrition)
- Pebbles thrown at the cliff = abrasion (rock fragments used as tools). Two fragments colliding in transit = attrition.
- B confuses abrasion with hydraulic action (air compressed in cracks). C reverses the two definitions — the commonest slip. D offers solution (chemical) for a mechanical collision.

Q3 — B ((1) and (2))
- (3) False — the agent is waves approaching at an angle, not wind. Right idea, wrong justification: wind generates the waves, but the drift is produced by the wave angle and the gravity-driven backwash.

Q4 — D (cave → arch → stack → stump)
- A puts the stack first. B starts with the arch, so it cannot be followed by the cave it came from. C starts with the wave-cut platform — the trap for candidates who reason "it is at the base, so it forms first", when the platform grows only as the cliff retreats.
chunks.heading: Teacher key and rationale

chunks.text:
Q5 — B ((1) and (2))
- (3) False — a wave-cut platform is an erosional surface exposed at low tide, not a deposit. Right idea, wrong category: deposition does happen on coasts, just not here.
- Photo check: the stack and the flat platform are both plainly visible, with people on the platform for scale.

Q6 — C
- A spit needs a sediment supply and a transport agent along the shore. A states the condition for a discordant coastline — the neighbouring concept. B is false because a depositional landform cannot be built by erosion alone. D describes a barrier/delta, contradicting the ridge shown in the photograph.
- Avoids used stem M31 ("favourable factors for the formation of coastal deposition features") by asking what must be true of this coast rather than requesting a factor list.

Q7 — A ((1) only)
- B is the neighbouring facility trap: a breakwater is a real coastal structure but sits offshore and parallel to the shore. C names a third real structure in the wrong place.
- Photo check: sediment is visibly piled higher on one side of the structure.

Q8 — D
- Seawall, groyne and breakwater are all hard engineering — three options that are right structures with a false classification. The candidate must sort by category, not by recognition.

chunks.heading: HK Examples

chunks.text:
River energy = The ability of a river to do work (erosion, transportation, deposition)

- Measured by velocity and discharge
- Higher energy = more erosion and transport
- Lower energy = more deposition
chunks.heading: What is River Energy?

chunks.text:
| Factor | Effect on Energy |
|--------|-----------------|
| More water | ↑ Energy |
| Less water | ↓ Energy |

- Discharge = Volume of water passing a point per unit time
- Formula: Q = A × V
  - Q = Discharge (m³/s)
  - A = Cross-sectional area (m²)
  - V = Velocity (m/s)
chunks.heading: 1. Discharge (流量)

chunks.text:
| Factor | Effect on Energy |
|--------|-----------------|
| Steeper slope | ↑ Energy (more potential energy) |
| Gentler slope | ↓ Energy |

- Steeper gradient = faster flow = more energy for erosion
chunks.heading: 2. Gradient/Slope (坡度)

chunks.text:
| Factor | Effect on Energy |
|--------|-----------------|
| Narrow, deep | ↑ Velocity → ↑ Energy |
| Wide, shallow | ↓ Velocity → ↓ Energy |

- Hydraulic radius (R) = A / P
  - Higher R = more efficient flow = more energy
chunks.heading: 3. Channel Shape (河道形狀)

chunks.text:
| Factor | Effect on Energy |
|--------|-----------------|
| Smooth bed (e.g., concrete) | ↑ Energy |
| Rough bed (e.g., boulders) | ↓ Energy |

- Manning's n value measures roughness
chunks.heading: 4. Roughness (粗糙度)

chunks.text:
| Type | Characteristics |
|------|----------------|
| Laminar | Parallel layers, low energy |
| Turbulent | Chaotic, high energy |

- Reynolds number (Re) determines flow type
- Re > 500 = Turbulent flow
chunks.heading: 5. Flow Type (水流類型)

chunks.text:
| Course     | Roughness       | Cross-Section | Hydraulic Radius | Velocity | Discharge | Total Energy | Main Work        |
| ---------- | --------------- | ------------- | ---------------- | -------- | --------- | ------------ | ---------------- |
| Upper  | High (boulders) | Small         | Low              | Low      | Low       | Lower        | Vertical erosion |
| Middle | Medium          | Medium        | Medium           | Medium   | Medium    | Medium       | Transportation   |
| Lower  | Low (smooth)    | Large         | High             | High     | High      | Higher       | Deposition       |

Key factors:
- Roughness: Upper has more boulders → higher friction → lower velocity
- Cross-sectional area: Lower has larger area due to high discharge
- Hydraulic radius (R): Lower has higher R → more efficient flow → higher velocity
- Total energy = velocity × discharge

chunks.text: Research brief for setting the CP2 Data Response Question. Every figure has a source; verify again before the question goes live. Built 2026-09-28.
chunks.heading: CP2 — Hong Kong coastal cases 2024–2026 (DBQ prep)

chunks.text:
- Sea-level rise (HKO) — by 2100 the annual mean sea level at Quarry Bay rises +0.37–0.82 m under SSP2-4.5 and +0.57–1.08 m under SSP5-8.5 (relative to the 1995–2014 average). Historical trend +2.9 mm/yr (1954–2013). HKO also publishes return periods for extreme sea levels: a ~300 cm tidal event goes from roughly a 20-year event today to a 2–3 year event as sea level rises. (hko.gov.hk/en/climate_change/proj_hk_msl.htm)
- Hardening → "living shorelines" — ~16% of HK's coastline is artificial (seawalls, rubble). CEDD issued the Eco-shoreline Guideline (CEO 1/2023); first used at Tung Chung East; pilot living seawalls at Victoria Park Road / Causeway Bay monitored Jul 2022 – Sep 2024; Peng Chau eco-shoreline features under installation, completion Dec 2026 (Marine Dept Notice 246/2025). (Frontiers in Ocean Sustainability 2026; devb.gov.hk "living seawalls"; mardep.gov.hk)
- 26 areas flagged — CEDD's Coastal Hazards Study (2021) identified 26 low-lying coastal residential areas exposed to storm surge + sea-level rise; shoreline management plans follow. (cedd.gov.hk — Topics in Focus: Coastal Enhancement and Shoreline Management)
chunks.heading: 1. Trends (pressure & response)

chunks.text:
- Lung Kwu Tan reclamation — 145 ha (+ Tuen Mun West 45 ha), seawalls + eco-shorelines; gazetted 2 Jan 2026, EIA to ACE 13 Feb 2026; WWF opposed (Sep 2025). (info.gov.hk press release 2026-01-02; eeb.gov.hk ACE papers)
- Kau Yi Chau Artificial Islands — stalled — ~1,000 ha east of Lantau; LegCo reply 10 Sep 2025: still "early planning and study stage", government says it lacks the "necessary conditions" to start. (info.gov.hk LCQ20 2025-09-10; hongkongfp.com 2025-09-11)
- Local adaptation works — Tseung Kwan O promenade flood-protection enhancements + 50,000 sandbags and flood barriers ahead of typhoon season (2026); seawall modification works SE of the airport, 24 months (Marine Dept Notice 70/2026).
chunks.heading: 2. New constructions & mega-projects

chunks.text:
- Hard: dikes/seawalls built after Typhoon Hagupit flooded Tai O in Sept 2008, plus the Emergency Response Plan. (HKU CCSG case bank: Tai O Community Campaign on Disaster Resilience)
- Soft: recycled seashell reefs to dissipate wave energy at the village edge (SCMP — "Stemming the tide: how seashells can restore Tai O's coastal habitat"; classroom version in SCMP Young Post); CarbonCare InnoLab / HKJCDPRI 2016 campaign — 197 villager surveys, 70 elder interviews, workshops → preparedness (soft measure).
chunks.heading: Tai O (west Lantau) — hard + soft + community

chunks.text:
- TNC restores shellfish reefs as "natural coastal defences against storms", reconfigures abandoned oyster farms with volunteers, removes invasive cordgrass, monitors mudflat recovery since 2024 (horseshoe-crab traces returning).
- Northern Metropolis plan includes a Coastal Protection Park between Tsim Bei Tsui and Pak Nai — protection by designation; TNC lobbies for MPA status. HK's largest seagrass expanse; black-faced spoonbill feeding ground. (tnc.org.hk; wwf.org.hk)
- CPP facts verified against primary docs (2026-10-01): coast Tsim Bei Tsui (尖鼻咀) → Pak Nai = 10.7 km (YLDC 13/2024 ¶10 + eco-tourism EOI); park's land part ≈60 ha in two zones — Sha Kiu Tsuen → Tsim Bei Tsui police post, Sheung Pak Nai — mangroves/fish ponds/streams + buffers, sea+land boundaries fixed by AFCD's feasibility study (Dec 2024 → end 2026) (YLDC 13/2024 ¶15). Pairing: 4.8-km promenade between the two eco-tourism nodes (Tsim Bei Tsui = themed-activity node, ~87 ha incl. 21 ha roads; Pak Nai = scenic node, 22 ha / 122,000 m² GFA, ≥50% tourism GFA), developments outside the park on low/low-medium-value land (EOI 2025). Adjacent pressure: Lau Fau Shan extension 411 ha, 48,000–53,000 flats, govt works ≈2030. Official boundary (AFCD CPP Concept & Management Plan 2026, p. 7): coastal band — thin landside strip + ~1–1.5 km offshore, Tsim Bei Tsui → Ha Pak Nai, no Tin Shui Wai; public engagement May–31 Jul 2026 closed. (YLDC 13/2024; nm.gov.hk EOI; afcd.gov.hk CPP Plan)
- Tin Shui Wai River (天水圍河, the 天水圍明渠) — 2.7 km, to be beautified/revitalised with new footbridges + cycle track (YLDC 13/2024 ¶18); phase-1 riverside amenity works completed 2 May 2026, murals/pavilions Jun 2026, long-term 2-km west-bank promenade under the Hung Shui Kiu/Ha Tsuen NDA. Odour/silt/illegal-discharge issues persist; oil spill Dec 2025 traced to an illegal fuelling station. (YLDC 13/2024; news.gov.hk 2026-06-25; info.gov.hk EPD 2025-12-10)
chunks.heading: Pak Nai / Tsim Bei Tsui (Deep Bay, NW) — the flagship soft case

chunks.text: - WWF "Nature-Based Solution" Mai Po programme (2025): managed gei wai, fish-pond and mangrove restoration as a soft buffer; HK–Shenzhen joint mangrove conservation (Jan 2025). Ramsar site. (publications.wwf.org.hk; english.www.gov.cn 2025-01-29)
chunks.heading: Mai Po / Inner Deep Bay — wetlands as buffer

chunks.text:
- TNC pilot shellfish habitat restoration reported progress: oyster reefs improve water quality, fish production and natural coastal defence.

Note: no classic managed realignment exists in HK — nearest equivalents are the wetland/fish-pond buffer and the proposed Coastal Protection Park. Lai Chi Wo has no coastal-protection works (countryside revitalisation only).
chunks.heading: Tolo Harbour (NE) — oyster-reef pilot

chunks.text:
1. Tai O — dikes (hard) + shell reefs (soft) + preparedness campaign (soft). Richest single site.
2. Peng Chau — conventional seawall + eco-shoreline features at its toe (MDN 246/2025, done Dec 2026).
3. Tung Chung East — new seawall with HK's first eco-shoreline on a new reclamation (EP-519/2016 condition; DEVB "living seawalls").
4. Causeway Bay typhoon shelter — pilot sustainable seawall measures, 27-month monitoring (Jul 2022 – Sep 2024) — the evidence base behind the guideline. (Urban comparison.)
5. Lung Kwu Tan — 145 ha reclamation, seawalls + eco-shorelines in one design (Arup); WWF opposes the reclamation itself → "can soft measures justify a hard project?"

Teaching pattern: CEO 1/2023 means every new hard structure carries a soft component; the debate is now "how much soft on the hard, and is it enough". Mai Po is the inverse: soft core with small hard embankments.
chunks.heading: 4. Cases with BOTH hard and soft measures (hybrid)

chunks.text: - Super Typhoon Ragasa (Sept 2025) closed Repulse Bay and Deep Water Bay beaches; reopened 26–29 Sep 2025 after damage checks — coastal "construction" here is soft (repair and re-open, not rebuild). (info.gov.hk press releases 2025-09-26, 2025-09-29)
chunks.heading: 5. Event anchor

chunks.text:
1. "From seawalls to living shorelines" — data: artificial-share %, eco-shoreline timeline, pilot monitoring + HKO SLR projections. Ladder: pattern (SLR trend) → location (site map) → process (wave/sediment mechanics) → change (soft vs hard evaluation).
2. "Protect, adapt or retreat?" — data: the 26 hazard areas, HKO return-period table, LKT vs Kau Yi Chau scale. Strong on evaluation for a specific low-lying community.
3. "Build or don't build?" — Kau Yi Chau reversal (2023 announcement → 2025 pause) vs LKT going ahead; decision stage: trade-offs, stakeholders, sustainability.
4. Hybrid spine (recommended after review) — Tai O or Peng Chau as the spine: pattern (why exposed) → location (where hard vs soft sit) → process (how each dissipates wave energy) → change (evaluate: hard-arm everything, or extend the soft scheme?).

Figures to build when the DBQ is approved: site sketch with hard/soft zones; one data figure (HKO sea-level trend or extreme-sea-level return periods).

docs.path: DSE Geography/CP3/CP3 DBQ/Fangchenggang steel base DBQ (2026).md

chunks.text:
Setting intent
A large-scale city map stem on a genuinely new coastal plant, so the question tests locational factors rather than recall of the textbook cases (Wuhan, Panzhihua, Zhanjiang, Caofeidian). Pairs with CP3 Working Distribution of Steel: this is the "exit the city → move to the coast" trend, drawn at city scale.
Reference papers: modelled on HKDSE 2013 P1 Q2 (plants X/Y, locational advantages read off Figures 2a–2c) and HKDSE 2016 P1 Q2 (site maps with a Key carrying distances, e.g. "(11 km)", "2 km" scale bar). Figure 1a is the site/city map; Figure 1b is the separate SE Asia locator (country borders/names, ASEAN, main ASEAN steel buyers, and the Pinglu Canal 平陸運河 joining the 西江 Xijiang that flows to 廣州 Guangzhou).
chunks.heading: DBQ — Why build a new steel plant at Fangchenggang, Guangxi?

chunks.text:
| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| Site | Qisha coastal industrial park, SE of Fangchenggang city, on the Beibu Gulf |
| Site area | 1,267 ha, mostly reclaimed from the sea (reclamation approved 2015) |
| Designed capacity | iron 8.5 Mt/yr · crude steel 9.2 Mt/yr · finished 8.6 Mt/yr |
| Investment | ≈ ¥639.9 亿 (≈ ¥64 bn) |
| Iron-ore wharf | 200,000 DWT, own railway wharf → plant |
| Milestone | No. 3 blast furnace lit Nov 2024 → phase 1 (10 Mt class) complete |
| Products | hot-rolled plate, high-strength seismic-resistant steel |
| Markets | southern + southwest China; exported to Southeast Asia; on the New International Land–Sea Trade Corridor (rail–sea, via Singapore) |
| Capacity swap | 9.1 Mt steel + 5.41 Mt of inland obsolete capacity closed as this was built (2008 plan) |
| Policy frame | Guangxi Beibu Gulf Economic Area — State Council approval 14 Jan 2008 |
| Distances (from site, straight lines measured on Figure 1a) | city centre ≈ 8 km · Fangchenggang North high-speed station ≈ 17 km · Dongxing / Vietnam border ≈ 34 km · Nanning ≈ 139 km |
chunks.heading: The stem data (all sourced — dates below)

chunks.text:
FIGURE 1a is a large-scale city map of Fangchenggang showing the steel base, its port, railway, roads, water supply and urban area; FIGURE 1b locates the area regionally — country borders and names, the main ASEAN buyers of China's steel, ASEAN (東盟), the Pinglu Canal 平陸運河, the Xijiang 西江 it connects to, and Guangzhou 廣州, the major city on the Xijiang; the KEY FIGURES panel gives the project data. The map shows facts only — no factors are labelled; students identify and elaborate them.

(a) Use FIGURE 1a to describe the location of the Fangchenggang steel base. [3]

(b) With reference to FIGURE 1a, explain THREE locational factors that made this site suitable for developing a new iron and steel plant. [6]

(c) (i) The base covers 1,267 ha and is designed to produce 9.2 Mt of crude steel a year. Calculate the designed output of the plant per hectare of land. Show your working. [2]
    (ii) Explain why the plant was built on land reclaimed from the sea rather than at an inland site. [3]

(d) "Fangchenggang's locational advantages will not last." Do you agree? Use evidence to support your view. [4]

Total: 18
chunks.heading: Question (18 marks)

chunks.text:
- "Near raw materials" — Fangchenggang has no local iron ore or coal. The factor is sea access to imported ore; that reversal is the single most common error.
- Reasons written into the describe part (a) → no credit for the reason.
- Calculation: unconverted Mt, no formula, no units.
- Factors named but not linked to a mechanism ("good transport") → no mark.
- Treating reclamation as an environmental measure rather than a land-supply/port decision.
chunks.heading: Where marks are usually lost

chunks.text:
- Xinhua, 2 May 2019 — 1,267 ha, 9.2 Mt/yr design, 200,000 DWT ore wharf, wharf-to-base railway, products, southern/southwest China + Southeast Asia, New International Land–Sea Trade Corridor with Singapore.
- Baidu Baike — 广西钢铁集团 / 防城港钢铁基地 (accessed 6 Oct 2026) — approved iron 8.5 Mt / steel 9.2 Mt / products 8.6 Mt; total investment ¥639.9亿; reclamation approved 2015 (sea-land use certificate); Qisha coastal industrial park, south-east of the city.
- Wuhan Iron & Steel / Guangxi JV reporting, 2008 — ¥60 bn first-phase investment (80/20); upstream swap closed 9.1 Mt steel + 5.41 Mt inland obsolete capacity.
- Sector reporting, Nov 2024 — No. 3 blast furnace commissioned, phase 1 complete (10 Mt class).
- State Council, 14 Jan 2008 — Guangxi Beibu Gulf Economic Area development plan approved.

docs.title: 1.1 Industrial Location Factors — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP3/Concepts/1.1 Industrial Location Factors (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
`F6_Geography_CP_Summary` flags industrial location factors as "frequently tested" under CP3. Almost every question is a disguised "why here?" — marks come from weighing factors for that specific industry, not listing them.

The move that scores: factor → mechanism → example → link back to the site.
"Near raw materials" scores nothing. "Iron ore and coal are bulky and weight-losing, so transporting them is costly — locating at the source cuts total cost" scores.
chunks.heading: 1.1 Industrial Location Factors — F6 DSE Revision

chunks.text:
Matters when materials are heavy, bulky or perishable relative to the finished product.

- Weight-losing — iron ore → steel, sugar cane → sugar → locate at source
- Perishable — fruit/vegetables → canning or chilling → locate at the farm belt
- Bulk-breaking — imported components consolidated then split → locate at the port
chunks.heading: 1. Raw materials

chunks.text:
Matters when the product is heavier, more fragile or spoils faster than its inputs.

- Weight-gaining — soft-drink bottling (syrup + local water), bricks/blocks → locate at the city
- Perishable finished goods — bakery, ice cream → distribute from the city edge
- High finished-goods transport cost — cement, glass → near the customer
chunks.heading: 2. Market

chunks.text:
- Labour-intensive + low skill — garments, plastic flowers, simple assembly → low-wage regions (classic HK → PRD relocation, 1980s–90s)
- Skilled labour — semiconductors, biotech → near universities / Hong Kong Science Park
- Trade-off — high wages can still win if skill, reliability or productivity is high
chunks.heading: 3. Labour

chunks.text:
- Accessibility to container terminal, expressway, airport
- Decisive where transport is a large share of total cost, and for just-in-time flows (Kwai Chung terminals, Tuen Mun Industrial Estate, Chek Lap Kok for air freight)
chunks.heading: 4. Transport

chunks.text:
- Capital — near finance (Hong Kong CBD, Shenzhen VC money)
- Government policy — industrial estates, tax breaks, mainland special economic zones
- Agglomeration — internal + external economies → see 1.4 Industrial Agglomeration (F6 Revision)
- Footloose industries — software, pharma, high-tech: materials and market barely matter; they chase skilled labour, R&D links and lifestyle (Silicon Valley → 1.3 Silicon Valley Global IT Centre (F6 Revision))
- Personal preference — the owner's home town; a real examiner-approved point
chunks.heading: 5. Other factors

chunks.text:
Industrial inertia (industrial momentum) — an industry stays at its original site even after the locational advantages that first attracted it have weakened or gone. Location factors explain why industry arrives; inertia explains why it does not leave.

The mechanism: the plant's advantages are sunk and local, while the new site's advantages are future and expensive to reach. What keeps an old plant running:
chunks.heading: 6. Industrial inertia — why old plants stay

chunks.text:
- Installed capital — furnaces, presses, buildings are immobile and already paid for. Moving means writing off the whole plant and buying a new one; staying runs gear that is already depreciated.
- Specialised labour — firm-specific skills, long training, unions, workers' housing. Skilled staff will not move, and the new site has to build the skill base from scratch.
- Established linkages — local suppliers, repair and maintenance, specialised transport grown up around the plant (reinforced by 1.4 Industrial Agglomeration (F6 Revision)). Breaking the cluster raises input costs.
- Site costs already sunk — land long bought or on an old lease; in a declining industrial belt land and rates are cheap, so fixed costs stay low.
- Built-in transport — the rail siding, private wharf and access road were paid for generations ago; they cannot be moved with the plant.
- Market position — long-standing contracts, reputation and distribution. Customers buy on delivery reliability, so a move risks the order book.
- Government support — subsidies, tax relief, state-owned employment: the state prefers a slow decline to mass unemployment (1.6 Deindustrialization (F6 Revision)).
- Upgrading in place — retrofitting an existing plant costs a fraction of a greenfield build, so firms modernise rather than relocate.
chunks.heading: 6. Industrial inertia — why old plants stay

chunks.text:
Result: the industry declines in place — ageing plant, gradual closures, overcapacity — instead of relocating.

China example: the inland integrated mills (Anshan, Wuhan, Panzhihua) keep producing even though coastal plants land imported ore and ship out more cheaply. Sunk plant, a specialised workforce, company towns and purpose-built rail hold them there — which is why China unwinds inertia through a capacity-swap rule (1.5:1 — close 1.5 tonnes of inland capacity for every 1 tonne built at the coast) rather than waiting for the mills to move: 9.1 Mt of steel + 5.41 Mt of iron capacity was closed to enable the new Fangchenggang coastal base.

Exam line: "Although the original advantages of the site have declined, industrial inertia — sunk capital, a specialised workforce, established linkages and low residual site costs — keeps the industry at its old location, so it declines gradually rather than relocating."
chunks.heading: 6. Industrial inertia — why old plants stay

chunks.text:
Do not confuse:
- inertia ≠ locational factors — factors attract an industry to a place; inertia keeps it there
- inertia ≠ agglomeration — agglomeration is the pull of clustering; it reinforces inertia (1.4 Industrial Agglomeration (F6 Revision))
- inertia is only a delay — when it finally gives way, the result is deindustrialization and structural unemployment (1.6 Deindustrialization (F6 Revision))
- "why has this industry not moved?" / "why do old plants still operate?" = write inertia, not another list of location factors
chunks.heading: 6. Industrial inertia — why old plants stay

chunks.text:
1. 2–3 factors, each developed one step further than your neighbour
2. One concrete case per factor
3. Closing sentence weighing which factor dominates for that industry
chunks.heading: Answer structure (4–6 marks)

chunks.text:
- Listing with no mechanism
- Applying materials/market logic to a footloose industry
- Forgetting that industries relocate when one factor changes — that is the changing in CP3
- Treating location factors as one-way — "why has this industry not moved?" needs industrial inertia (the reasons to stay), not a fresh list of reasons to come
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Why is steel-making weight-losing, and what does that predict about its location?
2. Why does a bottling plant sit away from where its concentrate is made?
3. Name two factors that pulled HK electronics firms to the PRD, and one that pushes them back today.
4. Why does Silicon Valley ignore raw materials entirely?
5. Which single factor would you argue dominates for a pharmaceutical plant — and why?
6. Why does an inland steel mill such as Panzhihua still operate when a coastal mill can import ore more cheaply? Name the inertia factor in each reason.

docs.title: 2 Industrial Development in China — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP3/Concepts/1.2 Industrial Development in China (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
China's industrial geography is the standard "compare and explain the change over time" vehicle: pre-1949 vs 1949–78 vs post-1978 distribution, then the regional imbalance that the Western Development Strategy answers. From your exam-practice list: "Compare pre-1949 vs post-1978 distribution" and "Impacts on western China."
chunks.heading: 2. Industrial Development in China — F6 DSE Revision

chunks.text:
- Limited industrial development overall
- Two concentrations, for two different reasons:
  - Northeast (Manchuria) — Anshan is THE centre. Heavy industry: iron and steel, machinery, chemicals.
  - Coastal treaty ports — Shanghai, Guangzhou, Tianjin: mainly light industry (textiles, food processing)
- Foreign-controlled enterprises — Japanese capital and technology in the NE, Western/Japanese concessions on the coast; little indigenous capital

Anshan — why there (the locational factors to quote):
| Factor | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Raw materials ← most important | rich iron ore of the Anshan–Qianan belt + Fushun coal nearby |
| Transport | South Manchuria Railway + port access |
| Capital / technology | Japanese colonial investment and engineering |
| Land & water | flat plain, water supply for washing/smelting |
| Market | railway rolling stock, war industry, regional demand |

Dominant factor of this period: raw materials (NE) and port access + foreign capital (coast).

How to use it: one sentence of "before" makes every "after" a comparison instead of a description.
chunks.heading: 2.1 Pre-1949 — the baseline you compare against

chunks.text:
The state, not the market, decided where plants went. Two Five-Year Plans then the Third Front movement.

- 1st Five-Year Plan (1953–57): Soviet aid, the 156 key projects — NE existing base expanded (Anshan), plus new works at Wuhan (Wuhan Iron & Steel, built from the mid-1950s) and Baotou
- 2nd Five-Year Plan (1958–62): industrial push nationwide (also the backyard-steel campaign — note it as quantity without quality)
- Third Front (三線, mid-1960s–70s): industry deliberately moved deep inland for national defence — plants were to survive an invasion

New inland iron & steel centres (the three to name):

| Centre | Why there | Most important factor |
|---|---|---|
| Wuhan (Hubei) | Yangtze river for cheap bulk transport · Daye/Huangshi iron ore nearby · Henan coal · central-China market and labour | transport (river) + nearby raw materials |
| Panzhihua (Sichuan) | high-grade vanadium-titanic magnetite + local coal · Jinsha river water · remote mountain site | defence/strategy (Third Front) + local raw materials |
| Urumqi (Xinjiang) | local coal and oil · far from any border threat path · balanced development of the NW | strategic/defence location + policy |
chunks.heading: 2.2 1949–1978 — planned economy, and the shift inland

chunks.text:
Dominant factors of this period: raw materials + government planning (policy as a location factor) — and the two work together: the state picked sites where inland coal and iron already existed (Daye/Huangshi ore for Wuhan, vanadium-titanic magnetite + local coal for Panzhihua, coal/oil for Urumqi). National defence explains only the inland bias — how far from the coast — not why each individual site was chosen.

Compare with §2.1: raw materials mattered just as much as before; the difference is that a planner, not the market, applied them, and defence was added as a new constraint.

Answer line: pre-1949 = coast + NE for materials/ports/foreign capital → 1949–78 = inland for policy and defence → the distribution is redrawn by the state, not by the market.
chunks.heading: 2.2 1949–1978 — planned economy, and the shift inland

chunks.text:
The driver is policy as a location factor — the same factor as in 1.1 Industrial Location Factors (F6 Revision), now at national scale.

- Special Economic Zones: Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Xiamen, Shantou — first movers, foreign investment, export privileges
- Open coastal cities: Shanghai, Guangzhou, Tianjin, Dalian — the second ring
- Export-oriented manufacturing — "world factory" role: cheap labour + coastal access + port infrastructure → export
- Western Development Strategy — the third ring (below)

Dominant factor of this period: market (access to export ports) + policy incentives (SEZ privileges) — capital and labour are footloose, so the created advantage decides.

Mechanism to write out: coastal location → port access → low export transport cost → FDI concentrates there → jobs and infrastructure follow → cumulative causation (→ 1.4 Industrial Agglomeration (F6 Revision)) → the east–west gap widens.
chunks.heading: 2.3 After 1978 — Reform and Opening

chunks.text:
Why it exists (the problem): the 1978 coastal bias created a widening regional inequality — coast rich, interior poor.

Aims
- Reduce regional inequalities
- Develop western resources
- Improve infrastructure

Measures
- Infrastructure projects (railways, highways)
- Tax incentives
- Education investment

Dominant factor: policy + infrastructure investment, intended to outweigh the west's distance-to-port penalty.

Evaluation spine for a Discuss/Evaluate question: policy and infrastructure can redraw accessibility and pull industry inward, but distance to ports, thin labour markets and lower skills mean the west attracts a different (resource- and domestic-market-oriented) industry than the coast — not a replacement for it.
chunks.heading: 2.4 Western Development Strategy

chunks.text: Technology changes which location factors matter, so it changes where plants can go.
chunks.heading: 2.5 Technology in the 2020s — how the map gets redrawn

chunks.text:
| Technology | Location factor it strengthens / weakens | Effect on the spatial distribution |
|---|---|---|
| Electric arc furnace (EAF) — scrap-based | Weakens iron ore + coal; strengthens scrap supply and market | Mini-mills sit next to where steel is used and scrapped — the dense east (Yangtze & Pearl deltas). Scrap only exists in quantity where there is a big stock of old steel, so the coast keeps its advantage. |
| Hydrogen direct reduced iron (H₂-DRI) with green hydrogen (H₂) | Creates a new factor: cheap renewable energy; still needs high-grade imported ore | Two pulls at once — coastal ports (DR-grade ore arrives by sea: Australia/Brazil/Guinea) and wind/solar regions inland (Xinjiang, Inner Mongolia; the Zhangjiakou pilot uses local wind). Energy, not ore, is what the inland location now offers. |
| Ultra-low-emission (ULE) retrofits + carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) | Environment/regulation becomes a binding cost | Old, inland, city-adjacent blast furnaces are the costliest to abate → they are the ones retired under the 1.5:1 capacity-swap rule; replacements are newer and coastal. |
| Fifth-generation mobile networks (5G), automation and smart factories | Weakens cheap unskilled labour; strengthens digital infrastructure, talent and agglomerated know-how | Labour cost stops being a reason to move inland. Control, research and development (R&D) and sales concentrate in big cities (Shanghai, Hebei) while production runs with few workers — a functional split between headquarters and plant. CISA counts 36 steel enterprises with “excellence-level” smart factories. |
| Remote operation / digital twins | Distance to management matters less | A remote or western site can be run from a coastal city — which makes renewable-energy sites viable when they were not before. |
chunks.heading: 2.5 Technology in the 2020s — how the map gets redrawn

chunks.text:
Synthesis — three simultaneous movements in the 2020s

1. Coastal concentration deepens: import ore → near-zero line → export terminal in one place (Baowu Zhanjiang, commissioned 23 Dec 2025).
2. Inland legacy capacity shrinks: the 1949–78 centres (Wuhan, Panzhihua, Urumqi) survive only by upgrading, or by being the capacity that is retired; no new inland blast-furnace complexes are being built.
3. A new hinterland appears: if cheap green hydrogen matters as much as ports, then energy-rich inland provinces regain a pull they never had — but for hydrogen/EAF plants, not for old-style integrated mills.

(Trend examples and dates are listed immediately below.)

The four-period map (pre-1949 Anshan + ports · 1949–78 inland shift · post-1978 coastal belt · 2020s coastal replacement, bilingual labels) is at the top of this note; PNG in `DSE Geography/CP3/`. Schematic, not to scale.
chunks.heading: 2.5 Technology in the 2020s — how the map gets redrawn

chunks.text:
| Trend | Examples (verified) | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| 1. “Exit the city → move to the coast” (退城沿海) | Caofeidian 曹妃甸 (Tangshan, Hebei — Shougang moved out of Beijing here, 2005–10; deep-water port for 300,000-tonne ore ships) · HBIS Tanggang new district, Laoting 樂亭 (Tangshan) · Baowu Zhanjiang (Guangdong) · JinShengLan (Guangdong, 8 Mt/yr special-steel base; 1,780 mm hot-rolling line broke ground 2026) | Urban mills are closed and rebuilt seaside: deep-water ports for imported ore, sea cooling, more room, and the city loses the pollution. |
| 2. Big coastal replacements under the swap rule | Shandong Steel Rizhao 山東日照 Phase II — ≈ ¥75 bn, 11.5 Mt planned (trade press) | Money is going into replacement capacity at ports, not into greenfield inland mills. |
| 3. Green flagship lines | Zhanjiang near-zero-carbon line, commissioned 23 Dec 2025 (H₂-DRI + EAF, CO₂ −50–80%) · hydrogen pilots at Zhangjiakou (HBIS) and Baowu HyCROF | The “new plant” of the 2020s is a low-carbon line inside a coastal complex, not a whole new complex. |
| 4. Small EAF additions | Electric-arc units approved under capacity replacement (scrap-based, near demand) | Consistent with the 15–20% EAF-by-2030 ambition; mini-mills follow scrap + market, i.e. the east. |
| 5. No net new capacity | 1.5:1 swap rule; crude steel 960.8 Mt in 2025, −4.4% (first sub-billion year since 2018) | “New plant” always means one-in, one-and-a-half-out — total capacity is being cut, and inland legacy capacity is the usual donor. |
| 6. Consolidation | China Baowu ≈ 125 Mt in 2025 — roughly double the world’s No. 2 producer (company/press figures) | The groups that can fund a ¥75 bn or a hydrogen line are the big coastal groups; small inland mills are absorbed or retired. |
chunks.heading: Where new plants are actually going — the 2025–26 trend list

chunks.text: Read the list as one sentence: new steel capacity in China is now coastal, replacement-sized, low-carbon and corporate-owned — the geography is concentrating at ports while total capacity shrinks.
chunks.heading: Where new plants are actually going — the 2025–26 trend list

chunks.text:
Headline data (all sourced)

- Steel industry value-added +6.0% y/y (Jan–Nov 2025) while crude steel tonnage fell 4.4% — less steel, more value (MIIT via steelchina.org).
- Nearly 20 “world-first” steel products launched in 2025 (People’s Daily Online, 29 Apr 2026).
- Electrical (silicon) steel: 8.75 Mt in H1 2025, +12.1% y/y, grain-oriented grades leading; electrical-steel exports > 700 kt in 2025 (SMM).
- Industry profit ¥115.1 bn (2025), margin 1.9% — earned on mix + cost, because selling prices fell ~10% (MEPS: HRC ¥2,956/t, rebar ¥2,785/t).

Examples — the products behind those numbers
chunks.heading: Value-added steel — selling quality instead of tonnes

chunks.text:
| Value-added product | Example | End use | Why it earns more |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electrical / silicon steel | Shougang 0.1 mm ultra-thin grain-oriented sheet (world first); Baosteel high-grade GO | transformers, EV and motor cores, appliance motors | thinness and magnetic efficiency = tight tolerances; few mills can make it |
| High-speed rail wheels | Masteel (China Baowu) wheels | CRH / Fuxing high-speed trains | safety-critical forging; qualification is the barrier to entry |
| Automotive sheet | deep-drawing and ultra-high-strength grades | car bodies, EV structures | spec-driven, contracted with the assembler — not a spot commodity |
| Ship plate / heavy wide plate | hull and LNG-carrier plate | shipyards, offshore, pipeline | sold to named yards on certification, not on tonnage |
| (typical set — no 2025 figure attached) | bearings, tools, high-rail steel | machinery | higher margin, replaces imports |

The counterweight you must mention: value-added is largely sold at home, while the export basket tilts low — semi-finished billet exports hit 14.82 Mt in 2025 (record, >2.3× y/y, 25-year high) and the average export unit price fell 10.2% (CISA via Japan Metal Daily/BigMint; MEPS).
chunks.heading: Value-added steel — selling quality instead of tonnes

chunks.text:
Why this matters for a location question (CP3 link): high-end grades need skilled labour, R&D, quality control and closeness to demanding customers (car plants, shipyards, appliance makers) — so value-added production reinforces market + agglomeration + know-how, i.e. the eastern clusters. Bulk, low-value products (billet, rebar) need only ore, energy and a port — so they can be made anywhere cheap, and are what China ships out.

One-sentence version: China is moving up the value chain at home (electrical steel, rail wheels, automotive plate) while exporting the low end — which keeps high-value steel in the east and bulk steel at the ports.
Exam answer line: technology shifts the dominant location factor from raw material and cheap labour to capital, energy price, digital infrastructure and environmental compliance — so 2020s plants cluster at ports (ore), renewable-energy zones (hydrogen) and demand/agglomeration centres (scrap, talent), while older inland integrated mills decline.
chunks.heading: Value-added steel — selling quality instead of tonnes

chunks.text:
| Period | Where | Pattern | Most important factor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-1949 | NE (Anshan) + coast | heavy industry in NE; light industry at treaty ports | raw materials (NE) / port + foreign capital (coast) |
| 1949–1978 | inland — Wuhan, Panzhihua, Urumqi | state-built inland steel centres | raw materials + government planning (defence sets the inland bias) |
| Post-1978 | coast — SEZ, open cities | export-oriented manufacturing belt | export market + policy incentives |
| WDS onward | west | resource + domestic-market industry | policy / infrastructure (overcoming distance) |
| 2020s (tech-driven) | coastal green replacements + energy-rich inland (H₂ / EAF) | brownfield inland declines; new capacity is coastal or renewable-powered and automated | energy price + environmental compliance + port access (cheap labour no longer decides) |
chunks.heading: 2.6 At a glance — period → pattern → dominant factor

chunks.text:
The coastal shift does not empty the interior overnight. Industrial inertia means the plant stays where it is even after the advantages that created it have weakened.

Why an inland mill (Anshan, Wuhan, Panzhihua) is still running:

- Sunk capital — an integrated mill is a mountain of immobile, already-depreciated equipment; moving means paying for a whole new plant while abandoning the old one
- Specialised workforce and company towns — furnace crews with firm-specific skills, plus the housing, schools and services built around the works; the labour will not move, and the coastal plants hire their own staff anyway
- Linkages already in place — local coke and spare-parts supply, repair shops, and the railway built to serve mine and mill (agglomeration working in reverse: leaving the cluster costs money)
- Low residual site cost — land long since paid for, cheap in a declining inland city
- Employment and stability — a state-owned mill's closure means regional unemployment, so the state keeps it going or slows the decline
- Upgrading instead of moving — ultra-low-emission retrofits let an old mill meet new environmental standards in place rather than relocate
chunks.heading: 2.7 Industrial inertia — why the old inland plants keep running

chunks.text:
What finally overcomes inertia: coastal advantage plus policy. Imported ore landed at a deep-water port beats a long inland haul, and the 1.5:1 capacity-swap rule forces the closures that firms would not choose themselves — 9.1 Mt of steel + 5.41 Mt of iron inland capacity closed to release the quota for the Fangchenggang coastal base. Inertia is exactly why the swap has to be rule-based.

Exam line: "New coastal plants reach imported ore more cheaply, yet inland mills such as Panzhihua keep producing because of industrial inertia — sunk capital, a specialised workforce and established rail and linkages — so government removes them through a capacity-swap rule rather than waiting for them to close."

Full inertia list and the "stay vs move" logic: 1.1 Industrial Location Factors (F6 Revision) §6.
chunks.heading: 2.7 Industrial inertia — why the old inland plants keep running

chunks.text:
- Describe/Explain: period → location pattern → the factor that caused it
- Compare: in pairs across periods (1949 vs 1978 vs pre-1949), never two separate paragraphs
- Evaluate: measure + effect + limitation, then a judged conclusion
- "Locational factors" question: name the factor → give the mechanism → state which factor dominated in that period and why
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Listing SEZs without saying what an SEZ changes (policy → cost/incentive → location decision)
- Forgetting the causal chain from coastal policy to regional imbalance
- Describing the Western Development Strategy without stating the inequality it targets
- Skipping 1949–1978 — a "compare pre-1949 and post-1978" answer with no middle period loses the change-over-time mark
- Naming Panzhihua/Wuhan/Urumqi without saying why there (the factor, not just the name)
- Describing the coastal shift as if inland mills simply closed — inertia explains the delay; say what keeps them running and what finally removes them
- Writing 1949–78 as “policy only” — raw materials still decide the individual site; policy and defence decide the direction of the shift
- Treating technology as a bonus point instead of a location factor — say which factor it strengthens or weakens, then the effect on distribution
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Why was Anshan the industrial centre before 1949, and how does that reason differ from Shanghai's?
2. Why did Wuhan, Panzhihua and Urumqi all become iron & steel centres between 1949 and 1978 — name the raw material each site had, and the factor they share.
3. Why did industry hug the coast before 1949, and how did that differ from the reason it did after 1978?
4. What did an SEZ actually offer that a normal city did not?
5. Explain how export-oriented manufacturing amplifies the east–west gap.
6. Two aims + two measures of the Western Development Strategy — and one limitation of each.
7. Which location factors from 1.1 does China deliberately manufacture through policy?
8. Explain why a shift to electric arc furnaces favours the east, while hydrogen DRI could favour inland renewable-energy regions — two technologies, two geographies.
9. Why does automation reduce the importance of cheap labour as a location factor, and what replaces it?
10. China’s value-added output rose (+6.0%) while tonnage fell (−4.4%). Explain why value-added production strengthens market/agglomeration factors, while bulk billet exports strengthen only raw material + port factors.
11. Explain, using industrial inertia, why Panzhihua still produces steel although a coastal plant such as Fangchenggang lands imported ore more cheaply — three reasons, and what finally removes the inland capacity.
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
- Steel output fell to 960.8 Mt in 2025 (−4.4% YoY) — below 1 billion tonnes for the first time since 2018 (seven-year low), driven by the property slump. Government policy now explicitly aims to cut output and prune overcapacity (2025–2026), with a 1.5:1 capacity-swap rule. Finished-steel exports hit a record 119 Mt (≈134 Mt on the broader customs line) — up to ~29% of global steel trade, triggering CBAM/tariff friction and a new export-licence regime (Jan 2026).
- Green steel flagship: Baosteel Zhanjiang — China's first million-tonne-scale near-zero-carbon line, fully commissioned 23 Dec 2025 (hydrogen-based shaft furnace + EAF, CO₂ cut 50–80%); sector target is 15–20% EAF share by 2030 (actual still ~10%).
- Location theme is still live: new capacity must replace old capacity — so growth shows up as coastal relocation and green replacement, not new inland plants.
- Full detail, dates and sources: CP3 Update Cases 2025-2026 · data brief: DBQ Angles - China Iron and Steel (CP3)
