docs.title: 3 Silicon Valley — Global IT Centre — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP3/Concepts/1.3 Silicon Valley Global IT Centre (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
Your exam-practice list: "Favourable factors for global IT centre." Silicon Valley is the footloose-industry case study — the proof that materials and market stop mattering once an industry is footloose, and the standard example of agglomeration + cumulative causation in one place. It is also the anchor for multi-point production, your 12-mark Section C stem: "Account for the locational factors of the headquarters of the IT industry in the US. Why does the IT industry in the US at present commonly adopt the mode of multi-point production?"
chunks.heading: 3. Silicon Valley — Global IT Centre — F6 DSE Revision

chunks.text:
- Climate — pleasant weather helps attract and retain mobile, highly skilled staff (a pull for people, not a production input)
- Silicon — the raw material for chips and the valley's name; not actually used now, so it is a historical accident, not a current location factor. Say that explicitly — examiners reward the correction.
chunks.heading: Physical factors

chunks.text:
- Stanford University — research and a talent pool; the pipeline from lab to start-up
- Venture capital — availability of investment for unproven ideas
- Skilled workforce — deep tech expertise, easy to move between firms
- Entrepreneurial culture — innovation mindset, tolerance of failure
- Agglomeration — clustering of firms, suppliers and services (→ 1.4 Industrial Agglomeration (F6 Revision))
chunks.heading: Human factors (the ones that earn marks)

chunks.text:
- Defense industry — Cold War military contracts seeded early demand and R&D funding
- Reverse brain drain — returning overseas Chinese and other immigrant engineers
chunks.heading: Historical factors

chunks.text:
Definition (say it exactly): one product is designed, fabricated, assembled, tested and sold in different countries, with each stage placed where that stage's requirements are cheapest, coordinated by one TNC through digital networks. It is a single product, many places — not many separate factories.

Your Figure 2: five stages, five locations, one firm.
chunks.heading: 3.2 Multi-point production — the concept

chunks.text:
| Stage                         | Where (typical)                      | Dominant locational factor                                 | Why that factor                                                               |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1. Headquarters & R&D         | US — Silicon Valley, Austin, Seattle | Knowledge agglomeration + capital                          | universities, venture capital, skilled labour, entrepreneurial culture (§3.1) |
| 2. Design of chips & software | United States                        | Highly skilled / creative labour + IP protection           | design needs engineers and secrecy, not factory space                         |
| 3. Chip fabrication           | Taiwan, South Korea, Japan           | Enormous capital + stable power/water + supplier proximity | a fab costs billions; TSMC ≈ 70% of global foundry revenue (2026)         |
| 4. Assembly & testing         | China, Vietnam, India                | Semi-skilled labour at low wage + export infrastructure    | high labour content per unit, low value per shipping box                      |
| 5. Global market              | Worldwide                            | Market access                                              | distribution, after-sales, local standards                                    |
chunks.heading: 3.2 Multi-point production — the concept

chunks.text:
Why firms adopt it — the mechanisms, not just the list
1. Stages need different factors — no single place can host all five cheaply (front needs knowledge and capital; middle needs lower-cost skilled labour; end needs market access).
2. Components are light and high value-to-weight — cheap to air-freight, so distance costs little.
3. Trade liberalisation — inputs cross borders tariff-free (WTO; China joined 2001; export processing zones).
4. Digital coordination — HQ can control far-flung lines in real time; one design file becomes thousands of units anywhere.
5. Risk is spread — an interruption at one point can be absorbed by another (and firms can serve regional markets locally).

12-mark skeleton: state what the mode is → two stage-to-stage factor contrasts with mechanism ("fabs need capital and power, assembly needs cheap semi-skilled labour, so the two cannot sit together") → one enabling technology or policy → one caution (it works only while trade and communications stay open).
chunks.heading: 3.2 Multi-point production — the concept

chunks.text:
|                                      | PAST: globalisation of production (1990s–2010s)                                                                                                                                        | NOW: regionalisation & resilience (2020s)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Driver                           | cost minimisation + market opening                                                                                                                                                         | risk minimisation + market access                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Locational factors that mattered | cheap semi-skilled labour · export zones & FDI incentives · tariff-free trade (WTO, China 2001) · containerisation + air freight · telecom · scale of China's workforce and its market | proximity to the market (near-shoring) · political alignment / "friend-shoring" · government subsidies · rising Chinese wages · automation (wage matters less) · land + reliable power for fabs and data centres · deliberate redundancy — "China + 1"                      |
| Spatial pattern                  | long, single-threaded chains with one dominant assembly base — China, the "world's factory"                                                                                            | chains broken into regional blocs (Americas / East Asia / Europe); assembly disperses to India, Vietnam, Mexico; the knowledge front-end stays concentrated                                                                                                                   |
| Evidence                         | Apple still sources 75% of iPhone shipments from China (Feb 2026)                                                                                                                      | India's share quadrupled to 25% since 2022 · US–Taiwan deal, 15 Jan 2026 — US$250 bn of Taiwanese investment in US chips · Nvidia US$1.5 bn Ohio campus, 4.25 GW, from 2028 · China's own "3+2" self-supply map (Beijing/Shanghai/Shenzhen logic, Wuhan/Hefei memory) |
chunks.heading: 3.3 The globalisation it was born in — and the trend now

chunks.text:
Read it as one sentence: the old globalisation moved production to the cheapest place; the new trend moves it to the safest reachable place — and it moves stages, not whole firms.

Two traps:
- Saying production "left China" — it has not: China still holds 75% of iPhone shipments; the shift is marginal and stage-by-stage (some assembly to India/Vietnam), not a wholesale exit.
- Giving the new trend with no factors — "companies are diversifying" earns nothing. Name the factor and the mechanism: "tariff and export-control risk raises the cost of concentrating in one country, so firms add a second source even though it is dearer."
chunks.heading: 3.3 The globalisation it was born in — and the trend now

chunks.text: Technology has pushed this map twice, in opposite directions.
chunks.heading: 3.4 How technology change reshapes the spatial pattern

chunks.text:
| Technology | The factor it changes | The spatial effect |
|---|---|---|
| Internet, cloud, video, ERP | makes coordination across continents nearly free | Spread — splitting production into stages became possible at all: the original globalisation |
| Containerisation + air freight | makes distance cheap; IT goods are high value-to-weight | Spread — HQ in the US, fab in Taiwan, assembly in Vietnam, market worldwide |
| Automation / robots | weakens cheap semi-skilled labour | Partial re-concentration — assembly no longer must chase the lowest wage, so lines move toward the market (US, Mexico); note the jobs do not return in the same numbers |
| Advanced lithography (EUV), nanometre nodes | makes capital, power, water and supplier density decisive | Concentration of the middle stage — TSMC ≈70% of foundries; fabrication clusters in Taiwan/Korea/Japan even while everything else spreads |
| AI + cloud computing | creates a new stage whose factor is cheap land + cheap reliable power, not labour | A new point on the map: data centres shift inside countries — Atlanta overtakes Northern Virginia (CBRE H1 2026); Nvidia's 4.25 GW Ohio campus |
| 5G / IoT | real-time control of many small lines | Deeper multi-point — more, smaller, more scattered plants are controllable by one HQ |
| Remote collaboration tools | weakens "talent must live next to HQ" | Mild dispersion of R&D nodes (Austin, Seattle already in Figure 2) — but agglomeration of knowledge keeps the front end clustered in Silicon Valley |
chunks.heading: 3.4 How technology change reshapes the spatial pattern

chunks.text:
The line to memorise: technology first spread production (cheap communications + freight), and now re-clusters parts of it (automation + extreme capital intensity + energy costs). Multi-point production never meant "production everywhere" — it means each stage in the place that fits it, and technology keeps re-deciding which places fit.

Answer structure — "how does technology affect the spatial pattern of multi-point production?"
1. Name the stage affected (front / middle / end)
2. Name the technology
3. State the factor it strengthens or weakens
4. Give the direction — spread, concentrate, or regionalise — with a named example
5. Judgement: technology enables the pattern; geography and politics decide where it actually lands
chunks.heading: 3.4 How technology change reshapes the spatial pattern

chunks.text:
History (defense contracts, Stanford) → first firms → talent and capital attract more firms → agglomeration economies + knowledge spillover → cumulative causation → dominance becomes self-reinforcing.

That chain converts a factor list into an explanation, which is where the higher marks sit.
chunks.heading: The argument to build

chunks.text:
1. Group factors: physical / human / historical (or push–pull)
2. For each, state the factor and the mechanism ("VC funds high-risk ideas that banks won't → founders can start firms locally → firms cluster")
3. Finish with cumulative causation: why the advantage persists rather than why it started
4. One caveat: rising costs, congestion or competition (Shenzhen, Tel Aviv, Bangalore) — evaluation marks
chunks.heading: Answer structure (typical 6–8 marks)

chunks.text:
- Writing "silicon is available" as a current factor — it isn't
- Describing Silicon Valley as rich in raw materials or near a market
- Giving factors with no mechanism — "good climate" needs "attracts mobile skilled workers who can choose where to live"
- Forgetting to say why it lasts (cumulative causation), not only why it began
- Describing multi-point production without the stages — "made in many countries" is description; stage → factor → place is explanation
- Treating past globalisation and the 2020s trend as the same story — the driver changed from cheapest to safest
- Saying "production has left China" (it hasn't: 75% of iPhones) or giving the new trend with no factor and no mechanism
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Which of Silicon Valley's factors would survive if the firms all moved away? Which would not?
2. Why is Stanford a location factor for firms, not just for students?
3. Explain the link between venture capital and agglomeration.
4. What role did the defense industry play before the valley was famous?
5. Evaluate: will Silicon Valley's dominance continue? Give one factor for and one against.
6. Figure 2 has five stages. For stages 1, 3 and 4, name the dominant factor and explain why no single country can host all five cheaply.
7. Why did technology enable multi-point production in the 1990s, and why is automation now reversing part of it?
8. "The new trend is simply a return of production to the USA." Evaluate this statement. (Hint: China 75%, India 25%, and which stages actually move.)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
- Reshoring is now contractual: US–Taiwan trade deal (15 Jan 2026) commits $250bn of Taiwanese investment in US semiconductors, energy and AI.
- Export controls are speeding Chinese self-supply: China's 2026–2030 five-year priorities are 7/5nm logic, memory (YMTC, CXMT, HBM), lithography, equipment localisation and EDA — arranged in a "3+2" regional model (Beijing/Shanghai/Shenzhen for logic; Wuhan/Hefei for memory).
- The bottleneck moved from chips to land + power: Nvidia's $1.5bn Ohio campus (4.25 GW, OpenAI 20-year lease, from 2028); Atlanta overtook Northern Virginia for data-centre space under construction (CBRE H1 2026).
- Supply-chain drift: China still 75% of global iPhone shipments, India quadrupled to 25% since 2022.
- Full detail, dates and sources: CP3 Update Cases 2025-2026

Source note: CP3_Industrial_Location_Detailed_Notes · figure: CP3 Data Question Set - IT Industry (2026 Update) · index DSE_SUMMARY
chunks.heading: 2025–2026 update (use this for currency marks)

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
Your exam-practice list: "How cumulative causation promotes industrial clusters" and "Cost-effectiveness of clustering." These are the mechanism questions — the two highest-value definitions in CP3, because both are pure reasoning you can reproduce without memorising data.
chunks.heading: 4. Industrial Agglomeration — F6 DSE Revision

chunks.text:
The chain to write, in order:

1. Initial advantage — something (a port, a university, a policy, luck) starts the first industry
2. Linkages — forward linkages (closer to customers) and backward linkages (closer to suppliers) pull related firms in
3. Labour market — a pool of skilled workers forms; workers move between firms, firms move to workers
4. Knowledge spillover — ideas spread between firms through informal contact and staff movement
5. Infrastructure — shared roads, power, utilities, services are built and then under-used without more firms

Each step makes the next one cheaper → the cluster grows without any new external cause. That is the definition to prove, not just state: "an initial advantage sets off a self-reinforcing chain in which each round of growth makes the next round more likely."

Exam phrasing tip: write the chain as "because… which in turn…" — causal connectives are what the mark scheme rewards.
chunks.heading: 4.1 Cumulative causation — "growth begets growth"

chunks.text:
- Bulk-buying — lower input costs
- Specialisation — workers become experts
- Financial — better access to capital (larger, more legible firm)
chunks.heading: Internal economies (benefits a firm gets from growing itself)

chunks.text:
- Infrastructure — shared roads, power
- Labour pool — ready, already-trained workforce
- Spillover effects — knowledge sharing, supplier and service concentration

The distinction examiners test: internal = size of the firm; external = location among other firms. Write it as a contrast sentence and you have a free mark.
chunks.heading: External economies (benefits a firm gets from being *next to other firms*)

chunks.text: Clustering is not free: land and rent rise, congestion, competition for staff, environmental pressure, and diseconomies of scale. A cluster can also lock a region into decline — which is exactly what Part 6 covers.
chunks.heading: 4.3 The limits (evaluation marks)

chunks.text:
- Explain "cumulative causation": define in one line → walk the 5-step chain → give one named example (Silicon Valley, Shenzhen, Kwai Chung)
- Discuss cost-effectiveness: internal vs external economies as two columns of mechanism, then a limitation
- To what extent: benefits for the firm / for the region, then when the benefits stop
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Confusing internal with external economies
- Describing that firms cluster instead of why each step causes the next
- No example — a named cluster with one specific detail anchors the reasoning
- Forgetting diseconomies in a "discuss"/"evaluate" question
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Define cumulative causation in one sentence, then give four links in the chain.
2. Forward vs backward linkage — give one industry example of each.
3. Why is a skilled labour pool an external economy?
4. Two internal and two external economies, with the mechanism for each.
5. When does agglomeration start working against a region?

Source note: CP3_Industrial_Location_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

docs.title: 5 Transnational Corporations (TNCs) — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP3/Concepts/1.5 Transnational Corporations TNCs (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
Your exam-practice list: "Evaluation of LDC attractiveness as a TNC location" and "Impacts of TNCs on host countries." Both are Discuss / Evaluate questions — you must weigh, not describe.
chunks.heading: 5. Transnational Corporations (TNCs) — F6 DSE Revision

chunks.text:
- Operations in multiple countries
- Global production networks — components made in several places, assembled elsewhere
- Decision-making centralised in headquarters, production decentralised
- Constantly seeking lowest-cost / best-fit locations — which is why they are the living example of location-factor trade-offs from 1.1 Industrial Location Factors (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: 5.1 What a TNC is (definition first — it's free)

chunks.text:
For the TNC
- Lower labour costs — the usual first answer, but give the mechanism (wage share of unit cost falls → unit cost falls → price competitiveness rises)
- Less regulation — looser environmental and labour rules lower compliance cost
- Growing markets — producing where the new consumers are
- Tax incentives — host-government concessions, free-trade zones

For the LDC (host)
- Job creation — direct employment plus linked service jobs
- Technology transfer — skills, methods, equipment knowledge
- Infrastructure — ports, power, roads built to serve the plant
- Export earnings — foreign currency
chunks.heading: 5.2 Why set up in an LDC

chunks.text: Employment · technology transfer · infrastructure development · export growth
chunks.heading: Positive

chunks.text: Exploitation of labour (low wages, poor conditions) · environmental damage · dependency on foreign capital (profit repatriated to HQ, vulnerable to the TNC leaving) · limited local linkages (inputs imported, so the money circulates outside the country)
chunks.heading: Negative

chunks.text:
1. Conditions matter — impacts differ by country, industry and whether local linkages exist
2. Short run vs long run — jobs and infrastructure now; dependency and repatriated profits if skills and suppliers don't develop locally
3. Who gains — host economy vs consumers vs the TNC's shareholders
4. Judged conclusion — e.g. "attractive to LDCs for jobs and technology, but only where policy forces local sourcing and skills transfer; otherwise the gains leak out."
chunks.heading: The evaluation spine

chunks.text:
- Listing positives with no mechanism
- Treating "cheap labour" as the whole story (forget regulation, market access, incentives)
- No limitation or judgement in an Evaluate question — that's the ceiling on the mark
- Forgetting profit repatriation / weak local linkages — the classic negative points
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Define "TNC" in one sentence with the two-part headquarters/production split.
2. Two reasons an LDC attracts a TNC, each with its mechanism.
3. Explain why export earnings and job creation can coexist with dependency.
4. What limits technology transfer in practice?
5. Evaluate: should an LDC welcome a TNC? Structure a 8-mark answer.

Source note: CP3_Industrial_Location_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
It is the closing half of CP3's story: location factors change → industry moves → the original region deindustrializes.香港 is the natural case study — you lived through it, and it links straight back to 1.1 Industrial Location Factors (F6 Revision).
chunks.heading: 6. Deindustrialization — F6 DSE Revision

chunks.text:
- Rising labour costs — the wage advantage disappears; firms follow cheaper labour elsewhere (HK → PRD)
- Automation — machines replace workers, so cheap labour stops being decisive and plants consolidate
- Globalisation — production can be fragmented and offshored anywhere; transport and communication costs fell
- Competition from LDCs — lower-cost producers undercut on price
- Service sector growth — land, capital and labour shift to higher-value services (finance, logistics, tourism); the pull side of the same shift

The linking sentence that earns marks: "deindustrialization is not an accident — it is what happens when the factors that once located industry change sign: the same labour and cost logic that brought manufacturing now removes it."
chunks.heading: 6.1 Causes — connect each to a location factor that flipped

chunks.text:
- Job losses — manufacturing employment falls first and fastest
- Economic decline — output, exports and linked suppliers shrink
- Social problems — unemployment, out-migration of young workers, community decline, inequality between regions still making things and those that aren't
- Need for retraining — the policy response: reskill workers for the service economy; without it, structural unemployment persists
chunks.heading: 6.2 Impacts — short run vs long run

chunks.text: Cheap labour and export access pulled manufacturing in → after 1978 PRD wages undercut HK → factories relocated → HK factories closed → employment shifted to services → retraining and new industry absorbed part of the workforce. Add: the government's role in that absorption for evaluation marks.
chunks.heading: The Hong Kong spine (one paragraph you can adapt)

chunks.text:
- Explain causes: cause → mechanism → where the industry went
- Discuss impacts: economic / social / for whom, plus a time dimension
- Evaluate policy: retraining works if skills match the new jobs — give the limitation (age, education, geography of new jobs)
chunks.heading: Answer structure

chunks.text:
- Listing causes with no link to location factors (the examiner wants the change)
- Treating deindustrialization as purely negative — some regions gain the services
- No case study — HK makes any answer concrete
- Forgetting the feedback: retraining and service growth are the region's response, not part of the cause
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Explain how rising labour costs produce deindustrialization — in one causal chain.
2. Why does automation weaken the very factor that once mattered most?
3. Two economic and two social impacts, each with a mechanism.
4. Why is retraining a response rather than a cause?
5. Evaluate: did deindustrialization harm Hong Kong overall? Give a judged answer.

Source note: CP3_Industrial_Location_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

docs.title: AI-era IT demand and hardware assembly — where the work is going
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP3/Research/AI-era IT demand and hardware assembly - where the work is going.md

chunks.text:
Purpose: One note that holds the finished figures and the summary behind them, for CP3 (industrial location, deindustrialization, transnational corporations) and for the industry research in Indian IT Outsourcing & AI Employment Tracker.
Scope note: Software services and hardware assembly move differently. The first barely relocates; the second relocates constantly. Both are here because the contrast is the teaching point.
Compiled: 2026-10-26. Every figure was built from primary sources, numerically QC'd (zero layout problems) and visually verified.
chunks.heading: AI-era IT demand and hardware assembly — where the work is going

chunks.text: AI is not triggering a general reshoring to the United States. It is doing three different things in three different places at once: deepening India's position through in-sourcing (global capability centres now take the work rather than the client), reshuffling genuinely domestic US demand for a narrow band of work, and spreading the commoditised middle across nearshore Latin America and Central Europe. Separately, AI is compressing the price of the same work — vendors earn more in total while charging less per deal — and hollowing out entry-level hiring. Meanwhile in hardware, the assembly layer is the thing that actually moves, and it is moving from China to India, Vietnam and Mexico.
chunks.heading: 1. The one-paragraph answer

chunks.text:
| Figure                                                             | File                                                                                | What it shows                                                                                  |     |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|             | `AI-era IT demand - world map and trends FY2026.png` (+ `.pdf`)            | Where outsourced software and IT services demand is deepening, and the four channels of change |     |
|  | `India IT sector 2016-2026 - employment hiring and revenue.png` (+ `.pdf`) | FY2016–FY2026: sector employment, revenue, net hiring, vendor headcount, in-house vs outsourced   |     |
|  | `India outsourcing vendors - bi-year profits FY2016-FY2026.png` (+ `.pdf`) | Net income indexed to each company's own FY2016 base, net margin, and the margin spread        |     |
|           | `IT hardware assembly - where it is moving FY2026.png` (+ `.pdf`)          | Where IT hardware assembly is moving, the assembly line expanded, and who captures the value        |     |
chunks.heading: 2. The figures

chunks.text:
The route no longer looks like "outsourcing to India." It looks like in-sourcing to India, by companies that have already built Indian operations.

- India hosts 2,117 global capability centres — a multinational's own in-house delivery centre, as opposed to work contracted out to a vendor firm — across 3,728 units, employing ~2.36 million people and generating $98.4 bn in FY26. Revenue has grown ~9.9% a year over five years, against ~6.2% for headcount
- 506 Forbes Global 2000 companies now run a centre in India, up from 423 five years ago
- The number of such centres is up 32% since FY21; ~500 new centres in five years (Anthropic, Marriott, Lufthansa, FedEx, Medtronic, General Mills among them)
- Only 13% still run on cheap labour alone; 43% are capability-building, 39% own end-to-end work and domain expertise, 5% are AI-led with executive mandates
- 63% of them run their company's Americas headquarters from India
- They employ 28% of the world's in-house AI talent in this sector (250,000+) and rank #1 on AI hiring intensity

Hiring by companies' own centres is now outrunning hiring by vendor firms:

| | FY2024 | FY2025 | FY2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| In-house (company's own centre) | 60,000 | 110,000 | 200,000 |
| Outsourced (vendor firm) | 50,000 | 100,000 | 110,000 |
chunks.heading: Channel 1 — India in-sourcing (strongest effect)

chunks.text: (Xpheno via Business Standard. Note: an earlier draft of the world map carried 300,000 for FY24 IT services — a transcription error, corrected against the source.)
chunks.heading: Channel 1 — India in-sourcing (strongest effect)

chunks.text:
Not a reversal of outsourcing, and not primarily AI-driven. The drivers are geopolitics, tariffs and supply-chain visibility; AI is an enabler, not the cause.

- 247,000 US manufacturing jobs announced in 2025 via reshoring and foreign direct investment; 244,000 in 2024 — five consecutive years above 240,000; >2.3 million since 2010 (Reshoring Initiative 2025 Annual Report, 23 Oct 2026)
- 88% of 2024 announcements were in high or medium-high tech sectors; leading industries were computer & electronics, electrical equipment (EV batteries, solar) and transportation equipment
- Tariffs were cited in 454% more cases in 2025 than 2024; government incentives in 49% fewer
- US manufacturing costs remain 10–50% higher than offshore — the Reshoring Initiative's own caveat, and the reason most sourcing decisions still go offshore
- Case evidence: Vanguard moved roles back from Infosys to Malvern, Pennsylvania; Provalus insourced to Alabama
- Deloitte (2024): ~70% of executives had brought functions in-house over five years
- Indeed Hiring Lab: US software-dev postings +15% since Claude Code, but total postings still −7%, and 27.5% below pre-pandemic. Of the gain, 71% was senior-level and 37% carried AI titles
chunks.heading: Channel 2 — US reshoring (real, but narrow)

chunks.text:
- Latin America: IT outsourcing market $70.85 bn (2024) → $126.3 bn (2030), growing 10.1% a year (Grand View Research). Colombia's ecosystem grew >22% in 2025; Mexico and Costa Rica are also growing service exports
- Central & Eastern Europe in-house centres: $27.11 bn (2026) → $41.97 bn (2031), growing 9.18% a year; Poland alone 53.88% of that market (Mordor)
- Europe overall in-house centre market: $102.9 bn (2026) → $148.38 bn (2031)
chunks.heading: Channel 3 — Nearshore and Eastern Europe (the real middle)

chunks.text: - IBPAP forecast: 1.85–2.14 million IT and business-process services jobs by 2028, down from ~2.5 million — AI eats call-centre entry work
chunks.heading: Channel 4 — The Philippines loses the low end

chunks.text:
HCLTech CEO C. Vijayakumar, Q4 FY26 earnings call, 21 Apr 2026: AI causes 2–3% annual deflation in deal values — a $100m deal now signs closer to $80m.

- Mechanism: time-and-materials billing. A firm that becomes 50% more productive bills less for the same work.
- Analyst estimate: a 3–3.5% annual drag on industry revenue if the pattern persists
- Implication: AI efficiency shows up as revenue deflation unless contracts move to outcome-based pricing — which is still mostly piloted
chunks.heading: The deflation mechanism (this is the finding a snapshot can't show)

chunks.text:
Net income indexed to each company's own FY2016 base (=100):

| | FY16 | FY18 | FY20 | FY22 | FY24 | FY26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TCS | 100 | 129 | 125 | 152 | 184 | 194 |
| Infosys | 100 | 116 | 118 | 144 | 152 | 157 |
| HCLTech | 100 | 118 | 123 | 145 | 149 | 150 |
| Wipro | 100 | ~100 | 109 | 133 | ~109 | 117 |
| Tech Mahindra | 100 | 135 | 143 | 198 | 84 | 171 |

(Tech Mahindra's FY24 dip is a one-off impairment, not an operating collapse.)

Net margin tells the uncomfortable half:

| | FY16 | FY18 | FY20 | FY22 | FY24 | FY26 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TCS | 17.9% | 21.0% | 18.3% | 20.0% | 19.1% | 18.4% |
| Infosys | 16.0% | 18.3% | 16.4% | 18.2% | 17.1% | 16.4% |
| HCLTech | 18.1% | 17.4% | 15.6% | 15.7% | 14.3% | 12.8% |
| Wipro | ~15.4% | ~15.4% | ~15.4% | ~15.8% | ~12.3% | 11.9% |

HCLTech's margin has fallen ~5pp over the decade; Wipro's ~3.5pp. Profit rises because revenue rises faster than margin falls — but pricing power is eroding.
chunks.heading: Profits are up, margins are down
Revenue per employee — the productivity story

chunks.text:
- US / UK / EU onshore: $130–220/hr
- Central & Eastern Europe, Latin America: $40–80/hr
- India: $25–65/hr
- Off-the-shelf model: $200,000/yr onshore staff + $5,000/mo tokens vs $1m managed offshore
- Offshore is still 3–4× cheaper. Global outsourcing >$525 bn (2025), +8–9%; offshore software development $178 bn
- ISG: Americas technology services spend $27.5 bn, +61% — but 426 managed contracts, −11% YoY, a fourth straight quarterly decline. Fewer, bigger deals.

The slogan that captures it: Velocity + Context + Compute > Cheap Labour.
chunks.heading: The rate bands (why the arbitrage narrowed but did not vanish)

chunks.text:
AI is compressing the price of outsourced work and shrinking the volume of junior work, while the market grows and total profits rise. The hypothesis was right about the pressure and wrong about the outcome. Entry-level hiring is where the damage is real — net hiring fell from 600,000 (FY22) to 135,000 (FY26).

Watch for: in-house hiring slowing and US postings rising above pre-pandemic. Neither has happened.
chunks.heading: The refined verdict

chunks.text:
Value added by function, 45 global value chains (Iacovone, Grossman & Zepeda 2015):

| Function | Share of value |
|---|---|
| R&D, production services, marketing | 30% |
| Headquarters | 27% |
| Distribution | 21% |
| Final assembly | 16% |
| Logistics | 5% |

Assembly carries the volume but captures the least of it — so it is the cheapest place to start removing China exposure. Malaysia is the clean example: 13% of global chip packaging but only ~6% of semiconductor export value.
chunks.heading: Why assembly moves first

chunks.text:
Solder paste print → Paste inspection (SPI) → Pick & place → Reflow oven → Optical inspection (AOI) → X-ray/ICT/FCT test → Depanel, coat, pack

- 50–70% of surface-mount (SMT) defects originate at the paste-print step (Field; Cal Poly; SMTA)
- 30–50% of assembly cost is test and rework
- Labour concentrates in handling, rework, test and box build — the repeatable steps, which is exactly what relocates
chunks.heading: The surface-mount assembly line (SMT)

chunks.text:
iPhone assembly share — the sharpest series:

| | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 |
|---|---|---|---|
| China | 83% | 74% | 72% |
| India | 14% | 23% | 27% |

(Smart Analytics Global; Counterpoint puts India at ~26% for 2026 — estimates diverge.)

Share of global manufacturing exports:

| | 2022 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|
| China | 28.3% | 27.1% | 26.1% |
| Vietnam | 2.8% | 3.4% | 3.9% |
| Mexico | 2.4% | 2.7% | 2.9% |
| India | 2.1% | 2.5% | 2.8% |

Robot density (2024, per 10,000 manufacturing workers) — the automation mechanism:

South Korea 1,220 · Singapore 818 · Germany 449 · Japan 446 · United States 307 · China 166 · world average 132

China leads on installed stock (295,000 robots, 54% of global deployments) but density now sits below the US — the arithmetic of why assembly leaves a country whose labour is no longer cheap. (IFR recalculated China on new National Bureau of Statistics employment data; the 2023 figure of 470 is not comparable.)

Back-end specialisation:
- Vietnam — 62% of global Apple AirPods assembly (Q1 2026); ~$200bn of electronics exports (2024)
- Malaysia — 13% of global chip packaging and test
- Philippines — electronics exports $39bn (2024) → $46bn (2025) → $54bn forecast (2026)
- Taiwan — 60% of world foundry revenue
- Mexico — $108bn of electronics exports
chunks.heading: Country trends

chunks.text: China is losing share, not volume. It still holds ~$1.06trn of electronics exports. This is diversification, not decoupling — companies added capacity in Vietnam, India and Mexico while expanding China. Friend-shoring investment outside China reached $310bn in 2025, up 72% from 2022, but that is additive capacity, not a transfer out of China.
chunks.heading: The caveat

chunks.text:
- CP3 Industrial location — assembly moves to where labour is cheapest and automation is densest; robot density explains why Korea and Singapore keep assembly while China loses it
- CP3 Deindustrialization — the Philippines case: a country whose comparative advantage was low-cost labour losing that advantage to AI
- CP3 TNCs — these in-house centres are the modern form of a transnational corporation's offshore footprint; 63% run the company's Americas headquarters from India
- CP3 China — China is holding volume and losing share; the mechanism is tariff and value-chain risk, not demand collapse
- Related vault notes: CP3 Update Cases 2025-2026 · 1.6 Deindustrialization (F6 Revision) · 1.5 Transnational Corporations TNCs (F6 Revision) · Indian IT Outsourcing & AI Employment Tracker

Exam-leakage note
The figures above print values. If a DBQ sub-part asks students to compute or compare any of these numbers, use the un-annotated version or strip the printed values — a footnote that enumerates percentages leaks them equally.

chunks.text:
Purpose: Track whether AI is displacing demand for Indian software engineers, and track the outsourced (off-site) job market in India.
Why this is trackable: India services revenue, headcount and exports are published quarterly (vendor filings) and annually (RBI survey, NASSCOM). Job-posting indices are published monthly (Naukri JobSpeak, Indeed Hiring Lab, Xpheno). All are re-published on a known annual cycle — so a tracker with a fixed indicator set will accumulate signal rather than noise.
Next scheduled update: see `Cron schedule` at the foot.
Companion note: AI-era IT demand and hardware assembly - where the work is going — the four channels of change (India in-sourcing, narrow US reshoring, nearshore/Central Europe, the Philippine low end), the FY2016–FY2026 ten-year series, the bi-year vendor profit and margin tables, the AI-deflation mechanism, and the hardware-assembly side of the story.
chunks.heading: Indian IT Outsourcing & AI Employment Tracker

chunks.text:
The hypothesis is NOT supported at the aggregate level — but it IS supported at the entry level.

The distinction matters more than the verdict:

| Level | Evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Aggregate employment | Tech sector employment rose to 5.95 mn in FY26 from 5.815 mn (NASSCOM), +2.3% | ❌ Not replaced |
| Aggregate revenue | Sector revenue +6.1% to $315 bn FY26 (NASSCOM); software services exports +8.2% to $221.4 bn (RBI, FY26) | ❌ Not replaced — the market is growing |
| Off-site (outsourced) share | 91.7% of software exports delivered off-site (RBI FY26) | ❌ Offshoring is more entrenched, not less |
| Entry-level / fresher | 55% of 651 surveyed IT firms reported a decline in entry-level hiring; net hiring fell to 140,000 in FY26 from 600,000 in FY22 (Xpheno) | ✅ Replaced — this is where the damage is |
| AI jobs vs losses | AI hiring 83,100 vs documented layoffs/attrition 31,921 → net +51,179 (Nomura, Aug 2026) | ❌ AI is creating more than it cuts, so far |

The real story: AI is not shrinking the pie — it is changing who gets hired. The "bench model" (mass hire freshers, train them on the job) is broken; AI eats the junior tasks freshers used to do, so firms hire fewer juniors and more experienced AI-adjacent staff.
chunks.heading: 1. Verdict on the hypothesis (as of 2026-10-24)

chunks.text: The number that best tracks the hypothesis: net hiring per year (currently 140,000, down from 600,000 in FY22) combined with entry-level hiring as a share of total. If AI is genuinely replacing demand for engineers, net hiring goes negative and stays negative. It has not.

chunks.text:
Track these as tripwires. If any fires, the hypothesis gains support:

| Tripwire | Threshold | Current reading | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | Tech sector employment (I4) falls two consecutive years | FY26: +2.3% (rising) | Two years of decline = structural, not cyclical |
| T2 | Top-6 vendor headcount falls two consecutive quarters | Q2 FY27: 4 of 5 added (rising) | Vendor filings are audited; two down quarters is real |
| T3 | Net hiring (I14) turns negative | FY26: +140,000 | Negative net hiring = the hypothesis working |
| T4 | Net hiring falls >50% YoY again | FY22 600k → FY26 140k (already −77% cumulative) | Pace of decline is the real story |
| T5 | AI job creation drops below documented losses | +51,179 net (Aug 2026) | The crossover point |
| T6 | Export revenue (I1) declines YoY | FY26: +8.2% | If the market shrinks, headcount follows |
| T7 | Off-site share (I3) falls sharply | 91.7% | Offshoring being reversed would be a shock |

And the tripwires that would falsify the hypothesis (i.e. confirm that AI is not replacing demand):

chunks.heading: 6. Cron schedule

chunks.text:
1. Title shifting. Job postings move from "Software Engineer" to "Generative AI Leader" / "AI Engineer" — a fall in software postings is partly relabelling. Global software postings are −27.5% vs pre-pandemic, but 69.3% of Q1 2026 postings were senior-level, and India's software share of all postings is rising in most large economies (Indeed Hiring Lab).
2. Restructuring ≠ layoffs. TCS's FY26 headcount fall was framed as a "$6 bn AI overhaul" and "workforce restructuring"; most exits were at normal attrition (11–15%). Count net, not gross exits.
3. OCP exclusion. RBI's $221.4 bn excludes overseas commercial presence. Using it as "total" understates the market; the $239 bn figure includes it. Keep both, label each.
4. The 24,000 vs 51,000 conflict is not a conflict. Top-6 exits (92,000, of which 24,000 net IT/engineering reduction) and Nomura's AI-hiring-vs-losses (+51,179) measure different things — gross churn vs AI-attributable net.
5. Don't use US data as a proxy for India. Indeed Hiring Lab indices are US. India's cycle has decoupled (ManpowerGroup: India tops global hiring confidence while US postings sit 27.5% below pre-pandemic).
6. Attrition rising ≠ employment falling. India Inc attrition rose to 18% while employment grew. Churn and headcount are separate series — track both, never infer one from the other.

(added 2026-10-07 — why old plants still operate after the original advantages have gone)
- Installed capital: plant and machinery are immobile and already paid for — relocation means writing them off

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
This is the conceptual spine of CP4. Almost every CP4 essay ultimately asks: does this measure balance the three pillars? A definition drop-in earns a mark early, then earns more when you use it as a judging criterion in your conclusion.
chunks.heading: 4.1 Sustainable Development — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
"Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs." — World Commission on Environment and Development, 1987

Why it matters in an answer: it hands you two testable ideas — needs now vs needs later, and the idea that the two can conflict. Any policy that improves today by borrowing from tomorrow (draining an aquifer, spending a city's whole land reserve) fails the test even if it looks successful.
chunks.heading: The definition (learn it verbatim)

chunks.text:
Don't just list them. Use them as a checklist for judging any urban measure:

1. Economic — can the city afford it, and does it keep working?
- Mechanism: efficiency + growth + jobs pay for maintenance; a scheme nobody can afford to run decays within a decade.
- Look for: cost, funding source, jobs created, ongoing revenue.

2. Environmental — does it stay within the resource base?
- Mechanism: resources conserved and pollution controlled now = the future generation's stock is intact.
- Look for: energy saved, emissions cut, waste reduced, land/habitat protected.

3. Social — do people actually gain, and is it fair?
- Mechanism: benefits concentrated on the wealthy create long-run instability; community participation increases compliance (people maintain what they helped design).
- Look for: equity, access, quality of life, participation.

Answer structure for "Discuss/Evaluate a sustainable measure"
1. One line of definition (the three pillars).
2. Pillar by pillar: evidence the measure delivers economic, environmental, social gains — one specific HK example each.
3. The tension: name where the pillars conflict (e.g. green space = environmental win, but land that could be housing = economic/social cost).
4. Verdict sentence: net contribution to sustainability, and under what condition.
chunks.heading: The three pillars — and how to actually use them

chunks.text:
The move that separates bands: you are not asked whether a measure is good, but whether it is sustainable — i.e. whether the gain survives the trade-off over time.

Common marks lost
- Quoting the definition but never using it again — it must return in your judgement.
- Treating the pillars as three unrelated bullet lists instead of a trade-off.
- "Sustainable" used as a synonym for "environmental" — social and economic pillars disappear.
- No named example: the syllabus demands Hong Kong or a real place, not hypotheticals.
chunks.heading: The three pillars — and how to actually use them

chunks.text:
1. Rewrite the 1987 definition in one sentence without using the word "future".
2. Why does a policy that maximises jobs but pollutes a river fail as sustainable development?
3. Give a HK example that scores on the social pillar only — then say what it costs the other two.
4. Explain the difference between sustainability and conservation.
5. Use the three pillars to judge one measure you know. Which pillar wins, and which loses?

Source notes: CP4_Sustainable_City_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · fieldwork link 2027 HKDSE Geography Assessment Framework
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Urban problems are the "problem" half of a problem–solution essay. Examiners want you to show cause → effect, not just a shopping list of complaints. The classic failure is describing what is wrong without explaining why it happens in cities.
chunks.heading: 4.2 Urban Problems — F6 Revision

chunks.text: Every urban problem is a density effect — people, vehicles, industry and waste packed into a small area outstrips the space and infrastructure available. That single idea links the three groups below.
chunks.heading: The organising principle: cities concentrate

chunks.text:
- Air pollution — vehicle emissions and industrial fumes are released where population density is highest, so exposure is concentrated too. Mechanism: more journeys + idling traffic in a street canyon → poor dispersion → health costs.
- Water pollution — industrial waste and sewage overload treatment capacity; runoff from paved surfaces carries oils into channels.
- Waste disposal — consumption is high and land is scarce; landfill capacity runs out before waste generation falls. Mechanism: no land → transport cost rises → pressure to incinerate.
- Noise pollution — traffic and construction; a sensory environmental problem with direct health effects (sleep, stress), which is why it is examined separately from air quality.
chunks.heading: 1. Environmental problems (the physical symptoms)

chunks.text:
- Housing shortage — demand from population growth + migration exceeds supply; land price is the transmission mechanism, so high property prices and shortage are the same problem stated twice.
- Traffic congestion — peak-hour demand exceeds road capacity. Mechanism: time lost, fuel wasted, emissions rise — note how this loops back into the environmental group.
- Squatter settlements — informal housing appears where formal housing is unaffordable; it is both a symptom of inequality and a cause of poor services.
- Social inequality — the wealth gap concentrates advantage in some districts, producing spatial divides (rich/poor neighbourhoods) that shape access to jobs and services.
chunks.heading: 2. Social problems (the human symptoms)

chunks.text:
- Aging facilities — infrastructure built for an earlier population needs replacement, and deferred maintenance compounds the cost.
- Insufficient services — healthcare and education provision lags population growth in expanding districts.
- Energy supply — rising demand (air-conditioning, electronics) strains generation and supply; in import-dependent cities this becomes an economic and security issue, not just a technical one.

Answer structure for "Explain urban environmental / social problems"
1. State the problem in one line (definition or evidence).
2. Give one cause with a mechanism — "because …, which leads to …".
3. Give one consequence (who is affected, and how badly).
4. Link to another problem where genuine (congestion → air pollution → health).
For a full essay: two problems from different groups, each fully developed, then a sentence on why they are interconnected — that linkage is the top-band move.
chunks.heading: 3. Infrastructure problems (the systems symptom)

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Listing 8 problems in 8 fragments — one developed problem beats four named ones.
- Describing rural or global problems in an urban question.
- Cause and effect reversed ("air pollution causes traffic").
- Facts without a Hong Kong anchor when the question implies a city case.
- Treating social problems as only "poor people" — housing, congestion and inequality are structural, not personal.
chunks.heading: 3. Infrastructure problems (the systems symptom)

chunks.text:
1. Explain how congestion causes air pollution, then how that air pollution creates a social cost.
2. Why are housing shortage and high property prices essentially one problem?
3. A city builds new roads to solve congestion. Using mechanisms, explain why congestion may return.
4. Distinguish an environmental from an infrastructure problem using the example of waste.
5. Name one urban problem in Hong Kong and one in an LDC city — what differs, and why?

Source notes: CP4_Sustainable_City_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · framework 2027 HKDSE Geography Assessment Framework

docs.title: 4.3 Sustainable City Features — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP4/Concepts/4.3 Sustainable City Features (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
This is the "solution" half of every CP4 essay, and it matches the 2027 Section B fieldwork module "Building a Sustainable City" (the module that replaced Climate Change). Expect data-response items where you must identify a feature from a figure and then evaluate it.

The formula for every feature: measure → mechanism → pillar → limit
"Green roofs reduce the urban heat island effect (measure) because vegetation absorbs less heat than concrete and provides evaporative cooling (mechanism), advancing environmental sustainability (pillar) — but they are expensive to maintain on old buildings (limit)."
One sentence, all four elements, three marks.
chunks.heading: 4.3 Sustainable City Features — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
- Energy efficiency — insulation and efficient systems cut electricity demand for cooling/heating → lower emissions and lower running cost → environmental and economic pillars.
- Water conservation — rainwater harvesting and reuse reduce demand on supply systems; matters most where supply is stressed.
- Natural lighting — daylighting reduces lighting electricity; design feature (orientation, atriums) rather than add-on technology.
- Green materials — recycled/recyclable content lowers embodied energy; closes the loop on construction waste.
- Certification — schemes such as BEAM Plus give a measurable standard, which turns "green" from a claim into evidence for an exam answer.
chunks.heading: 1. Green building

chunks.text:
- Public transit (MTR, buses, trams) — high-capacity modes cut cars-per-journey → less congestion and less emissions. Mechanism: mode shift, not just new vehicles.
- Cycling and walking — zero-emission short trips; needs safe, connected infrastructure or people revert to cars.
- Pedestrian zones — remove vehicles from a street → air/noise improvement plus commercial footfall (a social/economic gain).
- Electric vehicles — cut tailpipe emissions; be precise: benefit depends on how the electricity is generated, and they do not solve congestion or road space.
chunks.heading: 2. Sustainable transport

chunks.text:
- Reduce → reuse → recycle → recover → dispose, in that order of preference — the hierarchy itself is examinable.
- Recycling (three-colour bins) — diverts material from landfill but depends on public participation and market prices for recyclables.
- Composting — organic waste becomes soil condition; also cuts landfill methane.
- Incineration with energy recovery — shrinks volume and generates electricity, but produces emissions and ash, and needs steady feedstock.
- The structural point: a city with no spare land has to move up the hierarchy, because disposal has nowhere to go.
chunks.heading: 3. Waste management

chunks.text:
- Parks — recreation, mental health, and permeable surface for drainage.
- Urban forestry / tree planting — shade + evapotranspiration cools streets; absorbs CO₂ and filters pollutants.
- Vertical gardens and roof gardens — green the built-up core where ground land is unavailable; reduce roof temperatures and building energy use.

Answer structure for "Discuss measures to build a sustainable city"
Pick three features from different groups (one building, one transport, one waste/green) → for each: mechanism + a named HK example + one limitation → close by judging which feature gives the largest gain for a land-scarce city.

Common marks lost
- Feature named, mechanism missing ("trees are good").
- No example — HK specifics (MTR, three-colour bins, I·PARK1, BEAM Plus) are cheap marks.
- Claiming EVs = zero pollution without the energy-generation caveat.
- Ignoring land scarcity: in Hong Kong, every measure competes for space — that trade-off is the evaluation.
- Repeating the same pillar three times instead of showing economic, environmental and social gains.
chunks.heading: 4. Green space

chunks.text:
1. Explain how a green roof cools a city — give the physical mechanism, not just the label.
2. Why does public transport reduce two different urban problems?
3. Using the waste hierarchy, explain why incineration is a step above landfill but below recycling.
4. Give one limitation of each: green building, electric buses, urban parks.
5. A city can fund one measure only. Which do you choose for a land-scarce city, and why?

Source notes: CP4_Sustainable_City_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · fieldwork module 2027 HKDSE Geography Assessment Framework

docs.title: 4.4 Hong Kong Case Studies — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP4/Concepts/4.4 Hong Kong Case Studies (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Hong Kong is the examinable city for CP4 — the syllabus specifies urban problems and sustainability in Hong Kong. Examiners reward named, specific evidence (an actual project, an actual scheme), and penalise generic "the government should…" statements. Treat each item below as a quote-able case.
chunks.heading: 4.4 Hong Kong Case Studies — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
- The problem: ageing buildings in older districts (weak structure, no lift, poor ventilation) coexist with heritage value.
- Mechanism of the trade-off: demolition + higher-density redevelopment increases floor area and modernises housing, but irreversibly removes streetscapes and community networks.
- Both sides must appear: renovation/conservation keeps social continuity and embodied materials (environmental + social); redevelopment delivers capacity and safety (economic). The examinable judgement is which district, which building, and who decides — density gains in one place can push pressure onto another.
chunks.heading: 1. Urban renewal — the core conflict

chunks.text:
- MTR expansion — rail as the spine of the network: high capacity, electric, punctual; mechanism = mode shift from private cars and cross-harbour road traffic. Note the linked land-use point: MTR stations concentrate development (rail + property integration), which is itself a sustainability argument (transit-oriented development).
- Bus route restructuring — feeder and trunk reorganisation reduces duplicated routes and transfers; a network efficiency measure rather than a new technology.
- Electric buses — cut tailpipe emissions along the densest corridors, improving street-level air quality where exposure is highest. Caveat worth making: the gain depends on how electricity is generated.
chunks.heading: 2. Transport

chunks.text:
- Imported electricity from the Mainland — Hong Kong generates little of its own fuel supply; imports diversify sources and can lower cost and local emissions, but create dependency (a vulnerability in an evaluation answer).
- Renewable pilot schemes — solar on government buildings, schools and slopes. Be honest about limits: dense high-rise shading and land scarcity cap yield, so renewables currently contribute a small share. The examinable point is why a wealthy, land-scarce city still struggles with renewables.
chunks.heading: 3. Energy

chunks.text:
- Three-colour recycling bins — source separation raises recovery, but participation and market prices for recyclables determine success.
- Landfill extension — all three strategic landfills have been approaching capacity for years; extension buys time, costs money and faces NIMBY siting opposition.
- Incinerator (I·PARK1 / the WTE facility) — volume reduction plus energy recovery; trade-offs are emissions control costs, ash disposal, and public acceptance.
- The structural narrative examiners like: no land → disposal cannot expand → the city must move up the waste hierarchy (reduce/reuse/recycle).

Answer structure for a HK case study question
1. Name the scheme/project precisely.
2. Explain the mechanism of benefit (what it changes, physically or behaviourally).
3. State which pillar(s) it advances.
4. Give one limitation specific to Hong Kong (land, density, cost, dependency, participation).
5. Verdict: effective to what extent — and under what condition.
chunks.heading: 4. Waste

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Describing the scheme without saying why it helps (no mechanism).
- Inventing numbers — if you don't know a figure, argue from structure instead of guessing.
- Claiming success where the mechanism is weak (bins exist ≠ recycling happens; EVs ≠ clean grid).
- Ignoring land scarcity, the single most Hong Kong-specific constraint.
- Using an LDC example in a Hong Kong question.
chunks.heading: 4. Waste

chunks.text:
1. Explain the urban-renewal trade-off using two of the three pillars.
2. How does MTR expansion reduce both congestion and air pollution?
3. Why is importing Mainland electricity both a gain and a risk?
4. Use the waste hierarchy to justify incineration in a land-scarce city, then give its strongest objection.
5. Name three Hong Kong waste measures and state, for each, what determines whether it actually works.

Source notes: CP4_Sustainable_City_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · fieldwork module 2027 HKDSE Geography Assessment Framework
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
This is the "who delivers it" section. Answers that name measures but never identify the actor (planner, government, community) lose the mechanism. The examinable distinction is regulation vs incentive vs participation — three different levers with different strengths.
chunks.heading: 4.5 Planning Strategies — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
- Zoning — assigns residential, commercial, industrial and other uses to land. Mechanism: it prevents incompatible mixing (industry next to homes) and anticipates problems rather than fixing them later. Limit: rigid zones can create long commutes when jobs and homes are separated — a genuine sustainability cost.
- Building control (height, density, setbacks) — sets how much can be built. Mechanism: density limits protect light/ventilation; controlled density near transit supports public-transport viability. Tension: high density makes efficient services but can worsen overcrowding.
- Green belts — land reserved from development. Mechanism: they permanently cap urban sprawl and protect recreational/ecological space. Limit: they raise land prices inside the boundary and can push development further out — say so; it is a top-band evaluation point.
chunks.heading: 1. Town planning — shaping land use

chunks.text:
| Lever | How it works | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|---|
| Regulation — emission standards, mandatory requirements | Sets a floor; non-compliance is penalised | Immediate, universal coverage | One-size-fits-all; can be gamed; no reward for exceeding the floor |
| Economic incentive — environmental taxes, charges, green-building subsidies | Changes the price, so behaviour changes voluntarily | Flexible, encourages innovation | Cost of administration; may be too weak to change behaviour |
| Provision/investment — building transit, bins, treatment works | Government supplies the alternative | Enables change that individuals cannot | Expensive; needs maintenance; dependent on budgets |

Use the table's logic in essays: regulation stops the worst behaviour, incentives encourage the best, provision makes either possible.
chunks.heading: 2. Government policies — three levers

chunks.text:
- Public consultation — residents' knowledge (noise, traffic, local use) improves decisions; mechanism = better information + perceived legitimacy, so schemes face less opposition.
- NGO participation — environmental groups monitor, campaign and run programmes that government does not have capacity for; they also hold decision-makers accountable.
- Education/awareness — changes individual behaviour (littering, recycling, energy use). Honest evaluation: education is slow and uncertain — it works only where alternatives exist. A person told to recycle with no nearby facility will not.

Answer structure for "Evaluate planning strategies for a sustainable city"
1. Group measures by actor: planning (regulation) / government (incentive + provision) / community (participation).
2. For each: mechanism → named example → one strength and one limitation.
3. Show interaction: regulation without provision fails; provision without participation fails (bins without habits).
4. Conclude: which combination suits a land-scarce, high-density city, and why.
chunks.heading: 3. Community involvement — the social pillar in action

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Confusing a policy with its outcome ("the government bans pollution" ≠ cleaner air).
- Treating community involvement as free support — consultation costs time and can delay projects.
- Missing the green-belt counter-argument (higher prices / displaced development).
- No actor named: "something should be done" scores nothing.
- Forgetting Hong Kong's context — density and land scarcity change which lever works best.
chunks.heading: 3. Community involvement — the social pillar in action

chunks.text:
1. Explain how zoning reduces an environmental problem before it occurs.
2. Distinguish an environmental tax from an emission standard — mechanism and trade-off.
3. Why does a recycling campaign fail if no collection system exists?
4. Give one way green belts help sustainability and one way they harm it.
5. Which lever would you use to make buildings more energy-efficient — regulation, incentive, or provision? Justify with a mechanism.

docs.title: 4.6 Challenges of Sustainable Development — F6 Revision
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP4/Concepts/4.6 Challenges of Sustainable Development (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
This part is the evaluation engine of CP4. Every "Discuss / Evaluate / To what extent" question is answered here: a measure is only sustainable if the conflict it creates is acceptable and the implementation is feasible. Students who reach for these arguments leave the top band; students who only praise measures do not.
chunks.heading: 4.6 Challenges of Sustainable Development — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Development vs conservation
- Mechanism: land is finite — a site used for a park or preserved habitat is unavailable for housing or commerce, and vice versa. Every green-space decision in a land-scarce city has an opportunity cost.
- Signature case logic: urban renewal — rebuild (capacity, safety) or conserve (heritage, community, embodied materials).

Economic vs environmental (short-term vs long-term)
- Mechanism: environmental measures carry upfront cost and often delayed, diffuse benefits, while businesses and governments are rewarded on short horizons. Hence "we cannot afford it now" recurs — and is the argument sustainability is designed to answer (borrowing from the future generation).
- Example logic: green building standards raise construction cost but cut decades of running cost.

Individual vs collective
- Mechanism: sustainable outcomes are aggregate — one extra car, one unrecycled bag seems trivial alone, but multiplied by the population it defines the problem. Individuals bear private costs (effort, money) for collective gains → free-rider behaviour.
- Example logic: recycling participation; why incentives or regulation are often needed alongside education.
chunks.heading: 1. Conflicts — the three trade-offs

chunks.text:
- Cost — sustainable technology and retrofits are expensive; budgets compete with housing, health and transport. Public acceptance of charges/taxes is weak, so funding is politically fragile.
- Technology — solutions are not equally available: renewable generation is limited by land and weather in a dense city; some treatments need skills or infrastructure the city lacks. "Technically possible" ≠ "available here".
- Public acceptance / behavioural change — measures that change routines (separation of waste, fewer car trips, higher charges) meet habit and resistance; without compliance, the mechanism never fires. This is the single most common reason a well-designed scheme fails.

Answer structure for the top-band evaluation
1. Acknowledge the measure's benefit (one sentence, with mechanism).
2. Name the specific conflict it creates (which two pillars clash).
3. State the implementation constraint (cost / technology / acceptance) in this city's context.
4. Resolve or weigh them: under what condition does the benefit survive the trade-off?
A closing sentence of this form is worth a mark on its own: "The measure is sustainable only if its upfront cost is met and public compliance is secured; otherwise it shifts rather than solves the problem."
chunks.heading: 2. Implementation issues — why measures underdeliver

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Listing conflicts as abstract nouns with no mechanism ("there are trade-offs").
- No Hong Kong context — these arguments must be attached to a real case.
- Evaluating only cost, ignoring acceptance and technology (examiners award each distinct constraint).
- Treating conflict as failure: sustainability is managed conflict — say how it is managed.
- Contradicting yourself: praising a measure earlier, then denying all costs later.
chunks.heading: 2. Implementation issues — why measures underdeliver

chunks.text:
1. Explain the development-vs-conservation conflict using one Hong Kong site or project.
2. Why do environmental benefits arrive later than economic costs — and why does that matter for policy?
3. Use the free-rider idea to explain why education alone may not deliver recycling.
4. Give one cost, one technology limit and one acceptance problem facing a waste measure in Hong Kong.
5. Complete: "This measure is sustainable only if …" — then defend the sentence with two mechanisms.
