docs.title: Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP5/Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts.md

chunks.text:
1. Hot and dry summer → High evaporation

  • Strong sunlight and high temperature increase evaporation rate

  • Water evaporates from soil surface

2. Water table + Capillary action

  • Water table = top of groundwater

  • Capillary effect draws water upward through soil pores against gravity

3. Water rises, carrying salts

  • Water moves from water table to surface

  • Dissolved salts (e.g., NaCl) are carried upward with the water

4. Water evaporates, salts remain

  • Surface water evaporates

  • Salts are left behind in topsoil

5. Over-irrigation worsens the problem

  • Excess water raises the water table

  • More capillary action = more water movement

  • Irrigation water adds more salts

  • More evaporation = more salt accumulation

6. Result

  • White salty crust forms on surface

  • Soil becomes unsuitable for plant growth
chunks.heading: Soil Salinisation: Step-by-Step Explanation

chunks.text:
Predicted Grade Test P1.pdf
• Potential Evaporation (PE): Maximum evaporation possible if unlimited water available. Depends on temperature, humidity, wind, solar radiation.

• Actual Evaporation (AE): Actual water evaporated. Limited by water availability.

• Precipitation (P): Water input from rainfall.
  ───

Key Relationships

1. When P > Ep (Precipitation exceeds potential evaporation)

  • Soil moisture surplus

  • Ea = Ep (all potential evaporation is met)

  • Excess water → runoff or groundwater recharge

2. When P < Ep (Precipitation less than potential evaporation)

  • Soil moisture deficit

  • Ea = P (evaporation limited by water supply)

  • Soil dries out, moisture reserves depleted

3. Always true: Ea ≤ Ep

  • Ea cannot exceed Ep (can only evaporate what's available or what atmosphere can take)
chunks.heading: Relationship Between Hydrological Components

chunks.text:
|              | Saline Soil                                     | Salinisation                                                              |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Cause    | Natural climate conditions                      | Human activity (misuse of irrigation)                                     |
| Location | Southern California (arid climate)              | Irrigated agricultural areas worldwide                                    |
| Process  | Hot + dry → high evaporation → no rain to leach | Over-irrigation → water table rises → capillary action → salts accumulate |
| Example  | Imperial Valley's natural salt-affected soil    | Imperial Valley (Salton Sea area)                                         |

Key Difference:

  • Saline soil = Natural

  • Climate creates it (hot, dry, low rain)

  • "This land is naturally saline"

• Salinisation = Human-induced

  • Irrigation misuse creates it

  • "Poor irrigation practices caused salinisation"
chunks.heading: Saline soil vs Salinisation

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
The framework expects you to apply concepts accurately and consistently to contemporary issues. CP5 questions ask you to sort factors into the right system and then explain how each factor limits or raises output — a factor list alone earns little.
chunks.heading: 5.1 Agricultural Systems — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
The agricultural ecosystem (the farm as a natural system)
- Solar energy — the ultimate input: sunlight drives photosynthesis, so radiation, day length and cloudiness set the ceiling on yield.
- Water — rainfall or irrigation; both deficiency and surplus damage crops.
- Soil — nutrients, structure, drainage; soil fertility is what a season can draw on.
- Labour — the human work force available at planting/harvest peaks.
- Capital — money inputs: machinery, seeds, fertiliser.

The economic system (the farm as a business)
- Land — the space, and its rent/cost — an economic, not physical, constraint.
- Labour — as hired/paid work: wage cost and availability, not raw effort.
- Capital — as investment: machinery, loans, creditworthiness.
- Management — technology and skills: crop choice, timing, marketing.

The classic exam trap
Labour and capital appear in both systems — so naming them isn't enough. You must say which sense you mean: "labour as a physical input (enough hands at harvest)" vs "labour as a cost (wage rates)". The distinction is the mark.
chunks.heading: 1. Production factors — two systems, don't mix them

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Explain factors affecting agricultural productivity"
1. Select the factors the question's system actually uses (physical vs economic).
2. For each: state it → give the mechanism ("high temperature increases the rate of photosynthesis, so …") → quantify or exemplify where possible.
3. Finish with the binding constraint: which single factor is limiting yield here — the factor that can't simply be added.
chunks.heading: 1. Production factors — two systems, don't mix them

chunks.text:
| | Subsistence | Commercial | Organic |
|---|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Feed the household | Sell for profit | Sell, using natural methods |
| Scale | Small, often fragmented | Large, mechanised | Varies (small → large) |
| Technology | Low, traditional | High, capital-intensive | Low synthetic inputs; skilled knowledge needed |
| Surplus / risk | Little surplus → high famine risk | Surplus + storage → buffer | Lower yields, higher price/premium market |

Why the spectrum matters in essays: movement from subsistence → commercial is exactly the process CP5 calls agricultural development, and it is the main long-run answer to famine. Organic sits on its own axis — it is about method, not scale: it can be practised on a smallholding or a corporate farm.

Mechanisms worth quoting: commercial farming raises output through machinery, irrigation, fertiliser and improved seed, and reduces volatility through storage and market access; subsistence farming's thin surplus means one bad season becomes hunger.

Answer structure for "Compare subsistence and commercial farming"
Two developed comparisons (scale, technology, surplus/market), each with a consequence for food security, then a judgement: which performs better under drought, and what the trade-off is (yield vs cost, self-sufficiency vs dependency).
chunks.heading: 2. Types of farming — a spectrum, not three boxes

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Mixing systems — putting "rent" in the ecosystem or "sunlight" in the economic system.
- Describing farming types without linking to productivity or food security.
- Value-judgement without mechanism ("farming is bad for the environment").
- Ignoring the binding constraint — students describe what could change, not what is actually limiting yield.
chunks.heading: 2. Types of farming — a spectrum, not three boxes

chunks.text:
1. Sort: fertiliser, rent, sunlight, manager's skill, irrigation water, loan interest — ecosystem or economic system? Justify each.
2. Why does the same word "labour" need two different explanations in an exam?
3. Explain how a shift from subsistence to commercial farming reduces famine risk — give the chain of causes.
4. State one way organic farming is weaker than conventional, and one way it is stronger.
5. In a semi-arid region, identify the binding constraint and explain why adding capital alone won't raise yield.

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · 5.2 Sahel Region (F6 Revision) · 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
The Sahel is the syllabus's famine-belt case study. Questions nearly always ask you to separate physical from human causes and then weigh which dominates — so build the two lists separately, then argue their interaction.
chunks.heading: 5.2 Sahel Region — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Location — a semi-arid band immediately south of the Sahara, running across Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad and Sudan. Its position between desert and savanna is the source of its vulnerability: it sits on the margin where rainfall becomes unreliable.

Climate
- Semi-arid, roughly 100–400 mm per year — below or at the edge of what reliable rain-fed cropping needs.
- High temperature year-round → high evapotranspiration, so effective moisture is even lower than the rainfall suggests.
- Frequent, unpredictable drought — the rainfall total is less dangerous than its variability: years of plenty, then failure.
- High year-to-year variation — makes planning impossible and prevents surplus accumulation.

Degradation problems
- Desertification — the desert edge advances as vegetation cover is lost.
- Soil erosion — wind on bare ground and sheet wash in short storms remove the fertile layer.
- Water scarcity — rivers and shallow wells fall; groundwater is slow to recharge.
- Nutrient depletion — harvested crops remove nutrients that are not replaced, so yields fall even in good years.
chunks.heading: 1. Physical environment

chunks.text:
- Rapid population growth — more mouths and more land needed per household; output per person falls even if total output rises.
- Traditional farming methods — low input, low yield, no buffer; fallow periods shorten as land gets divided.
- Overgrazing — stocking numbers exceed carrying capacity → vegetation stripped → soil exposed.
- Deforestation — trees cut for fuel and to clear land → windbreaks lost, erosion accelerated, rainfall cycle disrupted.
- Poverty — cannot buy fertiliser, irrigation, seed or insurance, so cannot escape the low-yield trap.
- Limited infrastructure — no roads to move surplus to deficit areas, no storage → food exists but cannot reach hunger.
- Political instability and debt — conflict and fiscal pressure divert spending from agriculture and relief.
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors (the amplifier)

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Explain why the Sahel is prone to famine / evaluate physical vs human causes"
1. Physical: low, variable rainfall + high evapotranspiration → unreliable yields (mechanism in two steps).
2. Human: population growth, overgrazing, deforestation → degradation → yields fall further.
3. Interaction (the top band): physical conditions set the exposure; human actions determine the severity. Drought alone is a hazard; drought + degraded soil + no storage + no transport becomes famine.
4. Verdict: human factors are the more actionable, physical factors the more unavoidable — state which you judge dominant and why.

Common marks lost
- Listing causes without mechanism — "desertification" named, never explained.
- Treating the Sahel as the Sahara: it is the marginal band, not desert.
- No interaction argument — physical/human lists with nothing connecting them.
- Confusing drought (a hazard) with famine (a food-system failure) — they are not synonyms.
- Missing infrastructure: famine is often about distribution, not total production.
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors (the amplifier)

chunks.text:
1. Explain how 100–400 mm of rainfall becomes a food-security problem through two separate mechanisms.
2. Why does high temperature worsen rainfall scarcity?
3. Trace the chain: overgrazing → vegetation loss → soil erosion → lower yield.
4. Distinguish drought from famine in one sentence each, then state how one leads to the other.
5. Give one case where the Sahel had enough food produced but people still went hungry — what failed?

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · 5.4 Famine Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision) · Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Southern California is the MDC farming counter-case to the Sahel: a highly productive region where the constraints are environmental (water) rather than poverty. The examiner's favourite task is compare — so keep the structure parallel to 5.2 Sahel Region (F6 Revision).
chunks.heading: 5.3 Southern California — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Advantages
- Mediterranean climate — dry, sunny summers with a wet winter: warm growing season with no summer rainfall stress provided water is supplied; low humidity also reduces fungal crop disease.
- High sunshine / radiation — strong photosynthesis → high yields and good fruit quality; long growing season allows multiple harvests.
- Fertile soil — alluvial deposits on valley floors and fans from rivers carrying eroded material; naturally high nutrient status.
- Irrigation water from the Colorado River — the single factor that converts an arid climate into one of the world's most productive agricultural regions (it also imports water from hundreds of km away, which is the vulnerability).

Challenges
- Water scarcity — rainfall insufficient in the growing season; supply depends on distant, over-allocated rivers.
- Arid climate — high evapotranspiration means applied water is lost quickly; droughts recur.
- Soil salinity — irrigation raises the water table; evaporation leaves salts in the topsoil → yields fall. (See Common Mistakes in CP5 concepts for the step-by-step salinisation mechanism and the saline soil / salinisation distinction.)
chunks.heading: 1. Physical factors

chunks.text:
- Advanced technology — mechanisation, controlled-environment growing, monitoring; raises yield per hectare and per worker.
- Irrigation systems — drip and sprinkler networks make precise water application possible; technology is what turns the physical advantage into production.
- Capital investment — funds for equipment, cold storage, processing and transport to distant markets.
- Government support — water infrastructure, subsidies, research and regulation.
- Research institutions — universities and agricultural research develop varieties and techniques (bred for heat, disease, market) — this is the classic external economy of scale for a farming region.

Answer structure for "Compare the Sahel with Southern California" / "Explain productivity differences"
1. Compare on matched axes: climate & water, soil, technology & capital, markets/infrastructure.
2. For each axis, give the mechanism and name the binding constraint in each region (Sahel: rainfall variability; S. California: water supply).
3. Note the deep similarity: both are limited by water — one lacks it entirely, the other must import it. The difference is capital and technology, not climate luck.
4. Verdict: which region's agriculture is more sustainable, and why (dependency on imported water vs dependency on rainfall)?
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Calling Southern California "wet" — its summers are dry; irrigation is doing the work.
- Listing technology without mechanism ("modern technology helps").
- Explaining salinisation in one clause — examiners want the sequence: irrigation → water table rises → evaporation → salts accumulate → osmotic damage → yield falls.
- No comparison — two descriptions side by side with no matched axes.
- Ignoring that irrigation imports the problem: Colorado River over-allocation is a genuine sustainability limit.
chunks.heading: 2. Human factors

chunks.text:
1. Explain why a dry summer is an advantage for crop quality, then state what it costs.
2. Give the four-step mechanism of soil salinisation and one way to prevent it.
3. Which single human factor would you add to the Sahel to raise yield most — and why does it work in California?
4. Compare the binding constraint in the Sahel with that in Southern California.
5. Is Southern California agriculture sustainable? Argue both sides, then judge.

docs.title: 5.4 Famine — Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP5/Concepts/5.4 Famine Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
"Why do famines occur?" is the single most reliable CP5 question. The top band depends on two distinctions: hazard vs famine, and trigger vs root cause.
chunks.heading: 5.4 Famine — Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
A severe shortage of food causing widespread hunger and death.

Note what the definition implies: famine is about access and distribution, not only total tonnage. A region can produce food and still starve if people cannot buy, move or receive it.
chunks.heading: 1. Definition

chunks.text:
These recur in nearly every case — learn them as a diagnostic checklist:

1. Semi-arid regions — low, unreliable rainfall: output swings wildly year to year.
2. Limited resources and poor infrastructure — no roads, storage or markets, so surplus can't move and deficit can't be reached.
3. Economic problems — poverty and debt: no purchasing power, no buffer, no insurance, debt servicing diverts spending from food.
4. Political problems — conflict and instability: displacement, aid blocked, farms abandoned, governance of reserves fails.
5. Environmental degradation — deforestation and soil erosion reduce the land's carrying capacity, so the same weather now produces less food than it used to.

The pattern to spot: each characteristic both raises the chance of crop failure and removes a buffer against it. That double action is why famine-prone areas are trapped.
chunks.heading: 2. Characteristics of famine-prone areas

chunks.text:
Natural causes (usually the trigger)
- Drought — the classic trigger: a run of failed rains cuts yield sharply.
- Floods — wash away topsoil, seed and standing crop; silt and waterlogging damage land.
- Pest outbreaks — locusts, rusts, blight destroy crops rapidly and across borders.
- Climate variability — the underlying pattern: unpredictable onset and intensity of rains makes planting decisions a gamble.

Human causes (usually the root cause and the severity multiplier)
- War and conflict — destroys farms, kills/livestock, blocks aid, displaces farmers from planting seasons.
- Rapid population growth — more consumers; smaller plots per household; soil rested for shorter periods.
- Land degradation — erosion, salinisation, deforestation → progressively lower yields (a slow-onset cause).
- Poor governance — corruption or mismanagement of reserves, price controls that discourage supply, delayed warnings.
- Trade policies — export of food during shortage, or tariffs/price policy that keeps food unaffordable domestically.
chunks.heading: 3. Causes — separate trigger from root cause

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Explain why famine occurs in X"
1. State the trigger (one natural cause, with mechanism: "failed rains reduced rain-fed yield by …").
2. Show the root causes that turn shortfall into famine: infrastructure, poverty, governance, conflict.
3. Make the explicit argument: a physical hazard becomes famine only when the food system cannot respond — with one sentence of evidence (storage, roads, purchasing power).
4. Conclude which is more decisive for prevention — because that determines the policy.

Common marks lost
- Using drought and famine interchangeably.
- Only natural causes listed → lands mid-band; human causes are where the marks are.
- No mechanism for any cause ("floods damage crops" — how, and what happens next?).
- Ignoring distribution: food aid exists but cannot reach people.
- No named case (Sahel required by the syllabus).
chunks.heading: 3. Causes — separate trigger from root cause

chunks.text:
1. In one sentence each: hazard, trigger, root cause, famine.
2. Explain how debt contributes to famine without any crop failure at all.
3. Why does poor infrastructure matter twice — at the moment of failure and after it?
4. Give a natural and a human cause, and show how they interact in one region.
5. A country exports food during a shortage. Explain, with mechanisms, how policy can cause famine.

docs.title: 5.5 Combating Famine — Solutions (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/CP5/Concepts/5.5 Combating Famine Solutions (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Solutions questions are evaluative by design: "To what extent can short-term measures solve famine?" or "Can GM crops solve world hunger?" The distinction examiners reward is relief vs development — one buys time, the other removes the cause.
chunks.heading: 5.5 Combating Famine — Solutions (F6 Revision)

chunks.text:
Emergency relief
- Food aid — immediate calorie supply; mechanism: bypasses a failed harvest. Limits: arrives after the peak, undercuts local farmers' prices (so the next harvest is damaged), depends on logistics and security.
- Water supply — tankers, wells, purification: prevents dehydration and water-borne disease, which is what often kills after the food shortage.
- Medical care — treats malnutrition and disease; hunger weakens immunity, so disease epidemics follow famine.
- Refugee support / camps — concentrates vulnerable people where aid can reach them; costs host regions and can create dependency.

Food supply management
- Food imports — raise national availability quickly; cost: foreign exchange, shipping time, price exposure.
- Emergency reserves — strategic stock released when prices spike; needs holding cost and honest management.
- Price controls — keep food affordable; risk: discourage supply, create black markets, so the policy can worsen availability.

The key judgement: short-term measures reduce mortality but do nothing about the cause. Repeat the cycle without development.
chunks.heading: 1. Short-term measures (relief — buys time)

chunks.text:
Agricultural development
- Irrigation — decouples production from rainfall variability (the Sahel's binding constraint).
- Drought-resistant crops — raise the yield floor in poor years, which matters more than peak yield.
- Fertilisers and improved seed — restore soil nutrients, lift productivity.
- Modern technology — mechanisation, monitoring, training: raises yield and reduces post-harvest loss.

Infrastructure
- Roads — link farms to markets; move surplus to deficit areas during failure.
- Storage — grain stores/silos prevent spoilage and let surplus be held across bad years (directly attacks year-to-year variability).
- Markets — give farmers price information and an incentive to grow surplus.
- Water systems — rivers, dams, wells: supply and flood/drought moderation.

Economic & social development
- Education — better farming practice, family planning, and ability to read warnings/prices.
- Healthcare — reduces the disease burden that converts malnutrition into death.
- Job creation and trade — purchasing power: famine is as much an income problem as a production problem.
chunks.heading: 2. Long-term solutions (development — removes the cause)

chunks.text:
For: higher yields; pest resistance (less crop loss); drought tolerance (stability in bad years); nutritional enhancement (e.g. fortified staple). Each point needs a mechanism: pest resistance → fewer plants lost → higher effective yield.

Against: uncertain health effects (long-term, disputed — say "contested", don't assert harm); dependency on corporations (patented seed, annual purchase, market power); environmental risk (gene flow to wild relatives, effect on non-target species); loss of traditional seed varieties (genetic diversity that future breeding needs).

Answer structure for "Can X solve famine?"
1. Define what "solve" requires — sustained food availability, access and stability.
2. Show what the measure delivers (mechanism + evidence).
3. Show what it does not address (e.g. food aid doesn't fix infrastructure; GM doesn't fix conflict or purchasing power).
4. Compare short-term vs long-term explicitly, then judge: necessary but not sufficient is usually the defensible verdict — with the condition that would make it sufficient.
chunks.heading: 3. GM crops — the set-piece debate

chunks.text:
Common marks lost
- Treating relief as a solution rather than a stopgap.
- GM debate asserted instead of argued — one-sided answers cap at mid-band.
- No mechanism ("irrigation helps" — why, and which constraint does it remove?).
- Ignoring cost, sustainability or local capacity — evaluative questions award marks for feasibility.
- No case reference (Sahel, Southern California) to anchor the argument.
chunks.heading: 3. GM crops — the set-piece debate

chunks.text:
1. Distinguish emergency relief from agricultural development using one measure each, with mechanism.
2. Explain two ways storage reduces famine risk beyond simply holding food.
3. Why can food aid damage the next season's local production?
4. Give two arguments for and two against GM crops, each with a mechanism.
5. A donor may fund one long-term project only: irrigation, roads, or education. Which do you choose for the Sahel — defend with two mechanisms.

Source notes: CP5_Combating_Famine_Detailed_Notes · index DSE_SUMMARY · 5.4 Famine Causes & Characteristics (F6 Revision) · 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture (F6 Revision)
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Sustainable agriculture is where CP5 joins CP4 — the same three-pillar test applied to farming. Data-response items regularly use the organic farming table in your source notes, so practise reading it and drawing cautious conclusions.
chunks.heading: 5.6 Sustainable Agriculture — F6 Revision

chunks.text:
Environmental — conserve resources (soil, water, biodiversity), reduce pollution (agrochemicals, runoff), protect ecosystems.
- Mechanism: soil is a non-renewable asset on human timescales — farming that mines soil fertility yields more this decade and less the next.

Economic — must remain profitable and efficient, and respond to markets.
- Mechanism: a farm that cannot cover costs abandons the practice; sustainability that isn't affordable doesn't persist.

Social — fair labour conditions, community benefit, food security.
- Mechanism: farming systems that destabilise rural communities (or price food out of reach) fail the pillar even if yields are high.

The examinable tension: environmental measures often lower yield or raise cost short-term; economic pressure pushes the other way. Sustainable agriculture is the balance point, and questions ask you to locate it.
chunks.heading: 1. Principles — the three-pillar test for farming

chunks.text:
- Crop rotation — alternate crops across seasons: different species draw different nutrients and host different pests → soil nutrients maintained and pest cycles broken, reducing fertiliser and pesticide need. Also breaks disease carry-over.
- Organic farming — natural fertilisers (compost, manure) and no synthetic pesticides → no chemical runoff, better soil structure and organisms. Cost: lower yields, more labour, more knowledge, and produce must fetch a premium to remain economic.
- Agroforestry — trees integrated with crops/livestock: shade and shelter reduce heat/wind stress and water loss; multiple outputs (fruit, timber, fodder, crops) spread income risk; roots hold soil.
- Water management — drip irrigation delivers water to roots with minimal evaporation (critical where water is scarce); rainwater harvesting stores wet-season water for dry-season use; recycling/treated reuse reduces demand on freshwater. Each attacks a specific loss pathway rather than just "saving water".
chunks.heading: 2. Practices — mechanism for each

chunks.text:
| Country | Organic area (M ha) | Share (%) | Income/capita (USD) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Australia | 12.3 | 2.8 | 34,923 |
| Brazil | 0.9 | 0.3 | 9,567 |
| USA | 1.6 | 0.5 | 45,592 |
| China | 2.3 | 0.4 | 5,383 |
| Italy | 1.1 | 9.0 | 30,353 |
| UK | 0.6 | 3.8 | 35,130 |

What the table actually supports
- Absolute area is led by Australia (land availability), but share is led by Italy (9.0%) — so "who leads" depends on which measure you choose. Say which you are using.
- Higher-income countries generally show higher shares (Italy, UK) — consistent with consumers paying a premium and with stricter regulation/market maturity.
- China's large area but tiny share (0.4%) shows a large agricultural sector with little organic conversion.
- The source notes also record: the USA resists large-scale adoption because of lower yields and higher costs — the economic-pillar objection in one line.

Careful reading: correlation with income ≠ causation; and land area ≠ share. Examiners award the distinction.
chunks.heading: 3. The organic farming case data (and how to read it)

chunks.text:
Answer structure for "Evaluate sustainable agriculture measures"
1. Name 2–3 practices with mechanism (rotation, drip irrigation, agroforestry).
2. Judge each against the three pillars — environmental gain, economic cost, social effect.
3. Use one piece of evidence (the organic table, or a named region).
4. Conclude with the condition for success: premium markets, water savings, or policy support — whichever the mechanism requires.

Common marks lost
- Practices listed with no mechanism or no evaluation.
- Quoting organic yields as "worse" without the market/premium context.
- Claiming organic = sustainable by definition — it can fail the economic pillar.
- Mixing CP4 urban language into a farming question.
- Reading the table loosely (area vs share confusion).
chunks.heading: 3. The organic farming case data (and how to read it)

chunks.text:
1. Explain how crop rotation reduces fertiliser use — the mechanism, not the label.
2. Give one economic and one environmental argument against expanding organic farming.
3. Using the table, state which country leads on area and which on share, and why the difference matters.
4. Why is drip irrigation more sustainable than flood irrigation in an arid region?
5. Apply the three pillars to agroforestry: one gain and one cost for each pillar.

chunks.heading: CP5 Update Cases 2025–2026 — Combating Famine

chunks.text:
- Sudan — Darfur/Kordofan, Sep 2025. IPC confirmed Famine (Phase 5) in El Fasher (North Darfur) and Kadugli (South Kordofan); 21.2 million people (45%) in IPC Phase 3+, including 375,000 in Catastrophe; malnutrition above the 30% famine threshold in 4 Greater Darfur localities. Conflict + siege + aid blockade. — IPC Famine Review Committee Report, Sudan, Oct 2025.
- Gaza Strip, Aug–Sep 2025. First IPC-confirmed famine in the Middle East: ~641,000 in Phase 5; ~98% of cropland damaged or inaccessible; 12,000+ children acutely malnourished in July (six-fold rise since January). Man-made famine, collapse of local agriculture. — WHO/FAO/UNICEF/WFP IPC analysis, 22 Aug 2025.
- Sahel / West & Central Africa, 2025 lean season. 52 million people in Cadre Harmonisé Phase 3+ across 13 countries (Nigeria 30.6 m, Chad 3.3 m, Niger 2.2 m, Mali 1.5 m); 2,600 in Catastrophe in Ménaka/Tessalit, Mali; staple-cereal prices 10–200% above the 5-year average. Conflict + climate + price inflation. — CILSS/PREGEC, March 2025.
- South Sudan, Sept 2025–July 2026. 5.97 million in Phase 3+ (42%); 28,000 in Phase 5 Catastrophe (17,000 Luakpiny/Nasir, 11,000 Fangak); Luakpiny/Nasir at risk of Famine. Protracted conflict + refugee return from Sudan. — IPC South Sudan Snapshot, Sept 2025.
- Yemen, May 2025–Feb 2026. 17.1 million (49%) in Phase 3+, projected 18.1 million (52%) by Feb 2026, 41,000 in Phase 5 (Hajjah, Al Hodeidah, Amran); food assistance cut from 3.6 m recipients (2024) to zero from July 2025. Failure of combating measures — aid cuts drive famine. — IPC Yemen Special Brief, 27 June 2025.
chunks.heading: Causes of famine

chunks.text:
- Horn of Africa (Somalia, Kenya, Ethiopia), Dec 2025. Historic failed Oct–Nov rains: 20–25 million need food assistance; Somalia's Bay/Bakool non-irrigated harvest projected <10% of average; maize +19% above the 5-year average (Kitui), red sorghum +25% (Baidoa); livestock milk down about one-third (Mandera). — FEWS NET East Africa Alert, 23 Dec 2025.
- Europe, June 2026 heatwave. Record June heat cut the EU+UK grain harvest by 9 million tonnes (lowest since 2018), about €2 bn lost revenue; France −3.4 m t of maize, Hungary −2.4 m t, Spain −1.4 m t. Climate shock to staple crops in industrial agriculture. — The Guardian, 22 July 2026 (Coceral/ECIU).
- Pakistan — Indus Plains, 2022 monsoon floods. 2.67 million acres (13.3%) of Punjab cropland and 287,000 ha (16.5%) of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa cultivable land inundated; 15% of Punjab's rice region submerged; major crops = 81.2% of total agricultural losses. Flood-driven crop failure. — Springer, "Assessing Agrometeorological Damage after the 2022 Pakistan Floods", 2025.

chunks.heading: CP6 Update Cases 2025–2026 — Disappearing Green Canopy

chunks.text:
- Brazilian Amazon, Aug 2024–Jul 2025. INPE/PRODES recorded 5,731 km² of primary forest cleared — down 12.07% from 6,518 km² and the lowest rate in 11 years; Mato Grosso the only state to rise (+25%). Falling deforestation overall, regional reversal. — INPE / Gov.br (PRODES 2025).
- Bolivia (Amazon basin), 2025. About 20% of non-fire primary forest loss across the Amazon (~150,000+ ha), the highest per-area loss rate in the basin; agriculture and the Santa Cruz soy frontier are the main drivers. — MAAP #244 / Amazon Conservation.
- DR Congo, 2025. 560,000 ha of primary forest lost (third-largest globally), non-fire loss at an all-time high; 86% of DRC loss since 2002 linked to shifting cultivation, charcoal and conflict-driven displacement. — Global Forest Watch 2026 / Univ. of Maryland GLAD.
- Indonesia, 2025. Primary-forest loss rose 14% year-on-year — 433,751 ha cleared, an 8-year high — reversing a decade of decline; palm oil and mining remain key drivers. — Mongabay / Auriga / WRI GFW.
- Malaysia (Sarawak), 2024–25. Indigenous Penan/Kenyah communities filed a High Court suit over 54,478 ha of native customary land after clearing continued for oil-palm planting in Belaga, in breach of MSPO rules barring post-2019 forest conversion. — Eco-Business, Aug 2025.
chunks.heading: Causes of deforestation

chunks.text: - Canada boreal forest, 2025 season. By Oct 2025, 8.3 million ha burned (>5,600 fires) — 2nd-worst season on record after 2023 (18.8 Mha); 2023–2025 Canadian wildfires released more CO₂ than the previous 15 years combined. — Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre / Nature Reviews Earth & Environment 2026.
chunks.heading: Fire and climate as causes

chunks.text:
- EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), Dec 2025. Regulation (EU) 2025/2650 postponed application to 30 December 2026 (30 June 2027 for small operators) — covering cattle, cocoa, coffee, palm oil, rubber, soya and wood imports. Policy measure against imported deforestation, delayed. — Council of the EU, 18 Dec 2025.
- China afforestation, 2025. 8.47 million ha of land greened (3.56 M ha afforestation + 4.93 M ha grassland restoration), national forest coverage up to 25.1%; the Three-North programme delivered 8.77 M ha of desertification control. Large-scale afforestation as a success story. — National Forestry & Grassland Administration, 2026 report.

docs.title: CP7 — Borneo 2025 Super El Niño: Fires, Peat, Rainfall, Canals

chunks.text:
A self-contained teaching unit built around the October 2026 Borneo / Indonesia fire event during the developing super El Niño. The data were assembled in October 2026; some figures compare the present event with the 2019 analogue and the 2020 dry-season baseline.

Source scope. Every figure in this folder is derived from public, no-auth datasets: NASA FIRMS (thermal anomalies), ESA Sentinel-2 L2A (10 m optical), Pantau Gambut "From Concessions to Consequences" (Aug 2025), Open-Meteo ERA5 reanalysis (1981–2026), Sarawak Department of Irrigation and Drainage (DID) iHydro hourly water level.

Verified claims (QC passed). Analytic QC runs in-script for every figure (0 text-out-of-canvas failures, label probes confirmed, percentile/headline numbers printed). Vision QC (model-side) confirmed the visual content of every Sentinel-2 panel and the position of every annotation.

chunks.heading: Sources & links

chunks.text:
- Thermal anomaly ≠ fire. VIIRS picks up gas flares, kilns, and sun glint too. For peat fires specifically, ESA WorldCover 2021 + peatland mask is a better proxy.
- Global Peatland Map 2.0 (Greifswald / UNEP) overestimates peat extent in Indonesia and Malaysia — that caveat is mandatory whenever you cite the country's 6 Mha peatland figure.
- Reanalysis ≠ gauge. ERA5 is a 12-point grid, not point measurements. For exam-style defensible trend claims, the GRDC daily records (free registration) are the upgrade.
- Sentinel-2 cloud cover varies. 2025 is 21% cloud, 2019 is 13% — your "more fires" comparison is on the visible ground, not a cloud-fooled change.

chunks.heading: CP7 Update Cases 2025–2026 — Global Warming

chunks.text:
- Global temperature, 2025. Mean surface temperature 1.44 °C ± 0.13 above 1850–1900; 2023–2025 the first three-year period averaging above 1.5 °C; WMO confirms 2025 as the third-warmest year on record. — WMO, 14 Jan 2026.
- Sea level, 2025. Global mean sea level ~111.2 mm above the 1993 satellite baseline — a record high for the 14th consecutive year; 2025 annual rise 0.08 cm (La Niña-suppressed) against a long-term 0.44 cm/yr trend. — AMS State of the Climate 2025; NASA Sea Level Portal.
- Glacier loss, 2025 hydrological year. Glaciers lost 408 ± 132 Gt of mass — equivalent to 1.1 mm of sea-level rise; six of the seven highest mass-loss years have occurred since 2019. — Nature Reviews Earth & Environment / WGMS (Welty et al., 2026).
- Antarctic sea ice, 1 Mar 2025. Annual minimum 1.98 million km² — tied for second-lowest in the 47-year record, 860,000 km² below the 1981–2010 average; fourth straight minimum under 2 million km². — NSIDC, 6 Mar 2025.
chunks.heading: Evidence and causes

chunks.text:
- Europe, summer 2025 heatwaves. At least 35,000 excess deaths across four back-to-back heatwaves; 46 °C in Germany (28 June), 45.8 °C in Spain; over 80 million Europeans experienced above 40 °C. — The Guardian, 25 Aug 2026; BBC.
- Pakistan, 15 Aug 2025. Buner cloudburst dropped ~150 mm of rain in one hour; at least 222 killed province-wide (208 in Buner); 2025 monsoon total about 1,000 deaths. — AFP; Dawn, 16 Aug 2025.

chunks.text:

- Renewables, 2025. Global renewable capacity reached 5,149 GW, a record +692 GW (+15.5%) added in 2025 (solar PV +511 GW); renewables now 49.4% of global capacity. — IRENA Renewable Capacity Statistics 2026; Reuters, 31 Mar 2026.

chunks.heading: 2.1 Distribution

chunks.text:
Granite (5 steps):
1. Magma generated
2. Magma rises but stops underground
3. Slow cooling → large crystals
4. Solidifies
5. Uplift → exposed

Tuff (5 steps):
1. Volcanic eruption
2. Ash ejected into air
3. Ash settles
4. Compaction → tuff
5. Uplift → exposed
chunks.heading: Formation Processes：

chunks.text:
- Formation: Intrusive igneous rock (plutonic)
- Texture: Coarse-grained (large crystals)
- Weathering: Easily weathered in hot/wet climate
- Products: Grus (sandy soil), corestones, tors
- Landscape: Rounded hills, gentler slopes

chunks.heading: 2.2 Sedimentary Rocks

chunks.text:
1. Weathering & erosion break existing rock into sediment (sand, mud, pebbles).
2. Transportation carries it (river, wind, sea).
3. Deposition — sediment settles in layers when the water slows; each layer is laid down horizontally (original horizontality).
4. Compaction — burial under later layers: weight squeezes water out, grains pack tighter.
5. Cementation — minerals (silica, calcite, iron oxides) precipitate in the pore spaces and glue grains together.
6. The two last steps together = lithification — sediment becomes rock.
chunks.heading: How sedimentary rock forms (the chain, in order)

chunks.text:
| Feature | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Bedding plane | Surface between two layers — marks a change in deposition conditions (grain size, material) |
| Stratification | The layering itself; layers may be folded or faulted by later internal forces (compression) |
| Fossils | Organic remains preserved between layers — a sedimentary signature (igneous rocks have none) |
| Grain size | Conglomerate (pebbles) → sandstone (sand) → mudstone (mud); finer = quieter deposition |
chunks.heading: Key features you must be able to use

chunks.text:
- Layered sedimentary rocks occur mainly in the northeast (Tolo Harbour / Sha Lo Tung area — Devonian sandstone & mudstone, over 300 million years old).
- Recent alluvium (unconsolidated sediment) fills the northwestern New Territories lowlands.
- Contrast for identification: HK granite = coarse-grained, massive (no bedding), well-jointed; sedimentary = visible layers + bedding planes.
chunks.heading: Hong Kong context

chunks.text:
- Sedimentary rock origin: deposition in layers → burial → compaction → cementation → bedding planes separate the layers.
- Why weaker than granite: often bedded and porous — water enters along bedding planes/joints → breaks down faster (links 4.1 Weathering).
chunks.heading: Exam chains

chunks.text:
1. A rock shows clear layers and a fossil. Name the rock type and the process that bound its grains. → Sedimentary; cementation (with compaction).
2. What forms a bedding plane? → A surface between two layers, formed when deposition conditions change.
3. Layers in the rock are bent into a curve — external or internal process? → Internal (compression/deformation after the rock formed).

chunks.heading: 2.3 Metamorphic Rocks

chunks.text:
Metamorphic rock is a minor part of Hong Kong by area — your distribution table in 2.1 ROCK TYPES IN HONG KONG gives it as "minor, NWNT" — but it is the rock with the most distinctive landform and the most serious engineering consequence in the whole syllabus. It is the answer to solution weathering, and the reason Yuen Long is not as safe to build on as it looks.

| Rock type | HK coverage |
|---|---|
| Volcanic (Tuff) | 48% |
| Granite | 30% |
| Sedimentary | 10% |
| Metamorphic | Minor (NWNT) |
chunks.heading: Why metamorphic rock matters in Hong Kong

chunks.text:
1. A parent rock already exists — igneous, sedimentary or the older version of a metamorphic rock.
2. It is buried deeper, so temperature and pressure both rise (geothermal gradient, roughly 1 °C per 30–100 m, plus the weight of overburden).
3. Over millions of years the minerals re-crystallise in the solid state — they do not melt. The rock stays solid throughout.
4. Textures change: crystals grow, minerals re-sort into layers (foliation), and the rock becomes harder and denser.
5. Uplift and erosion eventually expose it at the surface.

The key exam point: metamorphism is heat + pressure, NOT melting. If it melts and cools again it is igneous, not metamorphic. And it is an internal process.
chunks.heading: How metamorphic rock forms (the chain, in order)

chunks.text:
| Parent rock (before) | Process | Metamorphic rock (after) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Limestone (sedimentary, carbonate) | heat + pressure → recrystallisation | Marble | still soluble — the HK case |
| Mudstone / shale (sedimentary) | heat + pressure → foliation | Slate | splits into thin flat sheets |
| Sandstone (sedimentary) | heat + pressure → recrystallised quartz | Quartzite | very hard |
| Various igneous | heat + pressure → banding | Gneiss | banded, coarse-grained |
| Various | heat + pressure → strong foliation | Schist | visible mica flakes |

Rock-cycle chain in one line:
magma cools → igneous; sediment accumulates and lithifies → sedimentary; heat & pressure → metamorphic (marble from limestone, slate from mudstone).
chunks.heading: Parent rock → metamorphic rock — the pairs you must be able to state

chunks.text:
| Property | Granite | Tuff | Marble |
|---|---|---|---|
| Origin | intrusive igneous | extrusive igneous | metamorphic (from limestone) |
| Solubility | insoluble | insoluble | soluble in weak acid |
| Structure | coarse, jointed | fine, resistant | recrystallised, foliated, fissile |
| Main HK landform | rounded hills, tors | rugged peaks, hexagonal columns | karst: sinkholes, caves, solution cavities |
| Main HK problem | deep weathering, landslip | steep slopes, lack of flat land | unstable ground, subsidence |

Granite and tuff are both insoluble — they weather and erode but they do not dissolve. Marble is the exception, and that single property explains every landform and every engineering problem below.
chunks.heading: Why marble behaves differently from granite and tuff

chunks.text:
1. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and the soil → forms weak carbonic acid.
2. The acidic water reacts with the carbonate in marble → the rock dissolves.
3. Dissolution works along joints and bedding planes, widening them.
4. Over hundreds of thousands of years the joints become solution cavities, caves and sinkholes.
5. The result is karst topography.

Exam line: solution weathering = acidic water dissolving soluble rock such as limestone or marble. It is chemical, not physical, and it requires a soluble carbonate rock.
chunks.heading: Solution weathering — the mechanism, step by step

chunks.text:
| Landform | Description |
|---|---|
| Solution cavity | Enlarged joint or bedding plane underground |
| Cave | Cavity large enough to enter |
| Sinkhole | Surface collapse into a cavity |
| Karst topography | The whole landscape of pits, cavities and lost surface drainage |
chunks.heading: The landforms karst produces

chunks.text:
Marble and other metamorphic rock are concentrated in the north-west New Territories, especially along the Yuen Long – Tuen Mun belt. The Hong Kong Housing Authority also identifies marble cavity at Ma On Shan and in the Tung Chung reclamation area.

| Location | Region type | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Yuen Long | NW New Territories, Yuen Long River basin | The classic marble cavity area; flat alluvial lowland |
| Tuen Mun / Kam Tin | NW New Territories, belt continues | Marble bedrock, in places under thick superficial deposits |
| Ma On Shan | eastern New Territories | Marble cavity recorded by the Housing Department |
| Tung Chung reclamation | Lantau, reclaimed land | Marble cavity beneath a reclamation platform |
| Sheung Shui | NW New Territories | Near the northern end of the belt |

The distribution pattern: marble follows the old limestone outcrop belt, which runs across the north-west New Territories. The flat, low-lying areas around Yuen Long and the Tuen Mun coast are where the marble is buried under recent alluvium, so it is invisible at the surface — which is precisely why the problem is dangerous.
chunks.heading: Distribution — where marble is found in Hong Kong

chunks.text:
- The flatness is misleading. The Yuen Long lowland is flat because the Yuen Long River deposited alluvium over an older limestone / marble surface. The flatness is recent and it hides the karst underneath rather than indicating safe ground.
- Marble cavity can only carry a very small extra load. Cavities are voids — there is nothing to build on.
- The rock may be unreachable. At one Yuen Long site the rock stratum lay deeper than 175 m from ground level, beyond ordinary pile types.
chunks.heading: The Yuen Long trap — flat land that is not safe

chunks.text:
Both are on the Housing Authority site "New Foundation Construction Technology for Sites with the Presence of Marble Cavity" (15 July 2022).

| Project | Problem found | Solution | Why it works |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wang Fu Court, Yuen Long | Very large marble cavity ~60 m below ground level; rock at >175 m at some points — normal pile foundations could not reach or spread the load | Buoyancy Raft Foundation — BIM was used to model the geological profile and produce a 3-D print-out, then a raft was designed to float the building on the soil stratum rather than transfer load to rock | Spreads the load across the soil instead of transferring it to the cavity |
| Long Ching Estate, Yuen Long | Marble cavity at a relatively deep level — common pile types ineffective | Shaft-Grouted Barrette — grouting around the perimeter of the pile to increase the thickness of soil in contact | Increases friction between pile and soil, giving adequate support for taller buildings |
chunks.heading: Two real foundation solutions (Hong Kong Housing Department)

chunks.text:
Exam use: "Yuen Long has flat land — why can't you build easily everywhere?"
→ The flat land is alluvium deposited over marble. The soluble carbonate bedrock has been dissolved along joints, leaving cavities and sinkholes that can only carry very small loads — and may lie too deep for ordinary piles. Developers must use special foundations (buoyancy raft, shaft-grouted barrette) after ground investigation.
chunks.heading: Two real foundation solutions (Hong Kong Housing Department)

chunks.text:
| Rock | Parent rock | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Marble | limestone | recrystallised carbonate, soluble — the HK case |
| Slate | mudstone | foliated, splits into thin flat sheets, very fissile |
| Schist | various | strongly foliated, visible mica flakes |
| Gneiss | various | banded, coarse-grained |
| Quartzite | sandstone | very hard, recrystallised quartz |

Marble from limestone and slate from mudstone are the two pairs students must be able to state in the rock-cycle chain.
chunks.heading: Other metamorphic rocks — know the names, low exam weight

chunks.text:
- Metamorphic rock origin: an existing rock is buried → temperature and pressure rise → minerals re-crystallise in the solid state (no melting) → foliation / banding → uplift and erosion expose it.
- Why marble gives karst: marble is carbonate and soluble → rainwater is weakly acidic → dissolution along joints → cavities, caves, sinkholes.
- Why weak for building: cavities are voids with very low bearing capacity → foundations fail or need special design.
- Contrast with granite: granite weathers in place and can be eroded away; marble dissolves and is removed from within.
chunks.heading: Exam chains

chunks.text:
1. What two conditions must increase for a rock to become metamorphic, and what must not happen? → Temperature and pressure must rise; the rock must not melt (if it melts and solidifies it becomes igneous).
2. Name the parent rock and the metamorphic product for two pairs. → Limestone → marble; mudstone → slate (also sandstone → quartzite).
3. A rock is foliated and splits into thin flat sheets. Name it and its parent. → Slate, from mudstone.
4. Why does solution weathering happen in marble but not in granite? → Marble is carbonate, so soluble in weak acid; granite contains no carbonate and is insoluble.
5. Name the four landforms karst produces. → Solution cavity, cave, sinkhole, karst topography.
6. Where in Hong Kong is marble cavity found? → Yuen Long, Tuen Mun, Ma On Shan and Tung Chung.
7. Why is Yuen Long's flat land not automatically safe to build on? → It is alluvium deposited over marble; the soluble carbonate bedrock has been dissolved along joints, leaving cavities that carry very little load and may lie too deep for ordinary piles.
8. A site has a marble cavity about 60 m deep and rock beyond 175 m. Which two foundation types would the Housing Department consider, and why? → Buoyancy Raft Foundation (spreads load on the soil stratum rather than transferring it to rock) and Shaft-Grouted Barrette (perimeter grouting increases pile–soil friction for support of taller buildings).

docs.title: 3.3 Faults in Hong Kong
docs.path: DSE Geography/EP1/3.3 Faults in Hong Kong.md

chunks.text:
Part of: EP1_Dynamic_Earth_HK — PART 3: INTERNAL PROCESSES (see 3.2 Faulting)
Related: EP1_Dynamic_Earth_Glossary · hk_geology_cases · 2. Internal forces and processes
chunks.heading: 3.3 Faults in Hong Kong

chunks.text:
- A fault = fracture in rock with movement along it (a joint has no movement).
- Fault zones are bands of crushed, fractured rock — planes of weakness: water flows along them, weathering and erosion work faster, engineering is harder.
- Hong Kong's major faults run NE–SW.
chunks.heading: Basics

chunks.text:
1. Valleys & gorges follow faults — crushed rock erodes faster along the fault line, so streams and valleys develop along it (e.g., Tolo Channel, a fault-controlled drowned valley).
2. Drainage alignment — streams grow along NE–SW / NW–SE joint-and-fault patterns, giving a trellis-like drainage grain.
3. Water along faults — fault zones carry groundwater (springs, seepage); tunnels meeting a fault zone get water ingress and need reinforcement (e.g., railway tunnels through fault zones — see hk_geology_cases).
4. Coastline inlets — drowned fault valleys become inlets and typhoon shelters.
chunks.heading: How faults shape the physical landscape

chunks.text:
| Link | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| Corridors attract settlement | Fault valleys give flatter land + water → roads, villages and towns line the valleys |
| Fractured rock constrains development | Fault-zone rock = weaker foundations, groundwater seepage → higher engineering cost, landslip risk near cut slopes |
| Linear infrastructure | Roads and tunnels are routed around, or engineered across, fault zones (reinforcement, drainage) |
| Limited local effect | Modern urban spread follows transport and economy strongly — faults are locally decisive, not the whole pattern |
chunks.heading: How faults affect where people build

chunks.text:
1. Define fault → NE–SW trend of major HK faults.
2. Landscape paragraph: line valleys/gorges (Tolo Channel) → drainage alignment → groundwater/springs.
3. Urban paragraph: valleys = settlement corridors; fault rock = foundation/tunnel constraints; give one case phrase each.
4. Relative-importance judgement: faults set the underlying physical frame (where flat land and water are), but human/transport/economic factors decide the final distribution — faults matter most locally (a corridor, a tunnel route).
chunks.heading: Essay plan (describe + discuss relative importance)

chunks.text:
1. Name two landform signs of a fault on a landscape map. → Linear valley/gorge; aligned stream segments.
2. Why does a fault zone trouble tunnel builders? → Fractured rock collapses easily + groundwater flows along the zone → reinforcement and drainage needed.
3. In an essay, how do you handle "relative importance"? → Give faults a mechanism each for landscape and settlement, then judge: pattern-setter physically, locally decisive, but transport/economy modify the final spread.
chunks.heading: Self-check

chunks.text: Weathering = breakdown of rocks in situ (at the place) by weather factors.

- Definition: Rocks expand when heated, contract when cooled. Repeated expansion/contraction → stress → cracking.
- HK Context: Not common, usually happens on rock in exposed area (e.g, coastal area, hill top)

Process:
- Intense heating in summer daytime cause rock to expand
- Cooled by sudden raining in summer
- Repeated cycles → stress → cracks develop
- Result: Rock breaks into smaller pieces
- Note: Less significant than chemical weathering in HK
chunks.heading: a) Thermal Expansion (Temperature Changes)

chunks.text:
- Definition: Salt crystals grow in rock pores
- HK Context: Coastal areas (beaches, cliffs) — especially exposed coastal granite (Cheung Chau, Lamma, Po Toi, Sai Kung coast)
- Process:
  1. Sea spray lands on rock
  2. Water evaporates → salt crystals remain
  3. Crystals grow → pressure on rock
  4. Rock breaks
- Result (the FORM it produces): Honeycombed rock surface — a pitted, cavernous pattern of small cavities
- Examples:
  - Cheung Chau — Fa Peng Rock (花瓶石), Rock of the Ringing Bell (叮噹石), Human Head Rock (人頭石)
  - Lamma Island — coastal granite faces
  - Coastal cliffs in Sai Kung, Lantau
chunks.heading: b) Salt Crystallization (in coastal areas)

chunks.text:
Form vs Process — the single most common mistake in Paper 2
"Honeycomb" is the FORM (the appearance), not the PROCESS (the mechanism).
| | Answer |
|---|---|
| Process (what is doing the work) | Salt crystallisation — sea spray → salt enters pores → evaporation → crystals grow → pressure → grains break out. Physical weathering. |
| Form (what you can see) | Honeycomb / honeycombed rock surface — small pits and cavities |
| Landform term (not a DSE syllabus term — do not use in an exam) | Tafoni / alveolar weathering |
Exam trap: HKEAA 2024 Paper 2 Section D Q1(c)(i) asked "What is the physical weathering process shown?" — most candidates wrongly answered "honeycomb weathering". The examiner expected salt crystallisation.
Rule of thumb: if the question asks for a process, name the agent (salt crystallisation, thermal expansion, hydrolysis). If it asks for a form or feature, name the appearance (honeycomb, spheroidal, block disintegration).

One exception — honeycomb in carbonate rock is chemical
The rule above holds for coastal granite. But in the Tung Chung / Tolo Harbour marble clasts within tuff breccia, small cavities that also look like honeycomb form by solution of the carbonate (chemical / karst), not by salt. Check the rock type before answering.
chunks.heading: b) Salt Crystallization (in coastal areas)

chunks.text:
- What it is: A pitted, cavernous rock surface of closely-spaced small cavities, like a honeycomb
- Where in HK: Coastal granite — Cheung Chau (Human Head Rock), Lamma Island
- Why the pattern is cellular: It develops on the weathered surface of a well-jointed granite boulder; salt crystallisation removes grains from the softer, more weathered zones, and the harder rock stands as the walls between pits
- Often occurs together with:
  - Spheroidal weathering → corestone → tor (the boulder shape, e.g. Fa Peng Rock)
  - Block disintegration → the boulder breaks along its joints
  - Granular disintegration → grains shed and collect at the base
- Exam wording: "salt crystallisation (physical weathering) produces a honeycombed surface on coastal granite"
chunks.heading: 1c. Honeycomb Weathering (the FORM produced by salt crystallisation)

chunks.text: Hong Kong's hot/wet climate = rapid chemical weathering
chunks.heading: 2. Chemical Weathering (MAIN in HK)

chunks.text:
- Definition: Water reacts with minerals → changes them
- Process:
  1. Feldspar (in granite) + water → kaolin (clay)
  2. Clay is soft → easily eroded
- Reaction: Feldspar + H₂O → Kaolin + silica
- Result: Granite becomes grus (sandy soil)
- Examples: Lion Rock, Kowloon - granite weathered to grus
chunks.heading: a) Hydrolysis (Most Important!)

chunks.text:
- Definition: Iron minerals react with oxygen + water → rust
- Process:
  1. Iron minerals (biotite, hornblende) in rock
  2. + Oxygen + Water → iron oxide (rust)
  3. Rock becomes red/brown coloured
  4. Weakens rock structure
- Result: Pink/red colour in granite, weakened rock
- Examples: Red-coloured granite in Hong Kong
chunks.heading: b) Oxidation

chunks.text:
- Definition: Acidic water dissolves carbonate minerals (calcite, dolomite) in soluble rock such as limestone or marble
- HK Context: Limited carbonate bedrock in HK. The case study is the marble belt of Yuen Long – Tuen Mun in the NW New Territories — metamorphosed carbonate bedrock buried under thick superficial deposits, with karst cavities. It is controlled under "Area Number 2 of the Scheduled Areas" for foundation works (CEDD GCO Publication 2/90).
- Process:
  1. Rain absorbs CO₂ → forms weak carbonic acid
  2. Acid + calcium carbonate → dissolves
  3. Rock dissolves → karst features (caves, sinkholes, solution cavities)
- Examples: Yuen Long – Tuen Mun marble belt (NW NT) — karst topography, sinkholes and buried cavities (CEDD GCO Publication 2/90)
chunks.heading: c) Solution (only for Carbonate Rocks — Marble in HK)

chunks.text:
- Definition: Plant roots grow into cracks → pry rocks apart
- HK Context: Common in areas with vegetation
- Process:
  1. Seed germinates in crack
  2. Roots grow deeper and wider
  3. Roots widen cracks → mechanical break
- Examples: Common in forest areas
chunks.heading: a) Root Growth (Biological)

chunks.text:
- Definition: Lichens/mosses produce acids that break down rock
- HK Context: Humid climate supports lichen growth
- Process:
  1. Lichens attach to rock surface
  2. Produce organic acids
  3. Acids break down minerals
  4. Rock weakens
- Examples: Found on granite and volcanic rocks
chunks.heading: b) Organic Acids (Biological)

chunks.text:
| Type | Process | HK Importance |
|------|---------|---------------|
| Hydrolysis | Water + feldspar → clay | MOST IMPORTANT |
| Oxidation | Iron + O₂ → rust | Very important |
| Salt crystallisation | Salt crystals grow in pores → rock breaks | Important on exposed coastal granite — produces the honeycomb form |
| Thermal expansion | Temperature changes | Less important |
| Solution | Acid dissolves carbonate rock (limestone, marble) | Limited (only in carbonate bedrock — Yuen Long – Tuen Mun marble belt) |
| Biological | Roots/acids | Important locally |
chunks.heading: Summary: Weathering in HK

chunks.text:
1. Hot climate — higher temperature = faster reactions
2. High rainfall — lots of water for reactions
3. Dense vegetation — adds organic acids
4. Long exposure time — rocks at surface for millions of years
chunks.heading: Why Chemical Weathering is Fast in HK

chunks.text:
Weathering breaks rock → erosion removes the broken material

| Weathering | → | Erosion |
|------------|---|---------|
| Hydrolysis → grus | → | Water washes away grus |
| Oxidation → weak rock | → | Wind/rain removes weak rock |
| Roots widen cracks | → | Gravity causes rocks to fall |
chunks.heading: Weathering → Erosion

chunks.text:
| English | Chinese |

| Physical weathering | 物理風化 |

| Honeycomb weathering (the FORM) | 蜂窩狀風化（形態） |
| Tafoni (not a DSE syllabus term) | 蜂窩穴 |

Form vs process, in one line for the glossary:
Process = salt crystallisation (物理風化) → Form = honeycomb (蜂窩狀風化).
Answer the process when the question asks "what process"; answer the form when it asks "what feature / what form".
chunks.heading: Key Terms

chunks.text:
1. Water enters rock cracks
2. Reacts with feldspar minerals
3. Feldspar transforms to clay (kaolin)
4. Clay is soft → easily eroded
5. Result: Grus (sandy soil)
chunks.heading: Hydrolysis:

chunks.text:
1. Iron minerals in rock
2. Exposed to oxygen + water
3. Iron oxidizes (rusts)
4. Rock becomes red-coloured and weak
5. Result: Weakened rock structure
chunks.heading: Oxidation:

chunks.text:
1. Sea spray lands on exposed coastal rock
2. Salt enters the pores and cracks of the granite
3. Water evaporates → salt crystals form inside the pores
4. Crystals grow → crystallisation pressure pushes grains apart
5. Grains are loosened and shed
6. Result: Pitted, cavernous honeycomb surface (Cheung Chau, Lamma)
chunks.heading: Salt crystallisation (physical):

chunks.text:
1. Seeds land in rock cracks
2. Roots grow and expand
3. OR lichens produce acids
4. Rock breaks down
5. Result: Physical breakdown
chunks.heading: Biological:

chunks.text:
| Location | Weathering Type | Result |
|----------|----------------|--------|
| Lion Rock | Hydrolysis | Grus soil, corestones |
| Kowloon Peak | Hydrolysis + Oxidation | Red granite, boulder fields |
| Castle Peak | Hydrolysis | Deep weathering |
| Yuen Long – Tuen Mun | Solution | Karst topography, sinkholes, buried cavities in marble |
| Cheung Chau (Fa Peng Rock, Human Head Rock) | Salt crystallisation | Honeycombed rock surface (on a spheroidally-weathered tor) |
| Lamma Island | Salt crystallisation | Honeycombed coastal granite faces |
| Sai Kung coast | Salt crystallization | Coastal erosion |
chunks.heading: Hong Kong Examples

chunks.text:
Erosion = removal and transport of weathered material by agents (water, wind, ice, gravity).

Key difference: 
- Weathering = breakdown in place
- Erosion = transport away
chunks.heading: Definition: Erosion

chunks.text:
- Definition: Raindrop impact detaches and splashes soil particles
- HK Context: First stage of erosion on bare slopes
- Process:
  1. Raindrops hit bare soil surface
  2. Impact detaches soil particles
  3. Splash disperses particles
  4. Particles become suspended in water
- Result: Soil particles lifted and transported
- Note: Most effective on bare soil; vegetation cushions impact
chunks.heading: a) Rainsplash Effect

chunks.text:
- Definition: Water flows as thin sheet across surface, removing uniform layer
- HK Context: Common on bare slopes after vegetation removed
- Process:
  1. Rain falls as sheet
  2. Water flows as thin sheet across surface
  3. Removes fine particles evenly
  4. Surface lowers gradually
- Result: Uniform lowering of surface
- Synonym: Sheet erosion
chunks.heading: b) Sheetwash

chunks.text:
- Definition: Small channels (rills) form where water concentrates
- HK Context: After heavy rain on bare slopes
- Process:
  1. Sheet flow concentrates
  2. Small channels form (<30cm deep)
  3. Water flows faster in channels
  4. More erosion in rills
- Example: Early stage of gully formation
chunks.heading: b) Rill Erosion

chunks.text:
- Definition: Deep channels formed by concentrated flow
- HK Context: Areas with intense rainfall, bare slopes
- Process:
  1. Rills deepen over time
  2. Channels become >30cm deep
  3. Gullies difficult to cross
  4. Very irreversible
- Examples: Castle Peak, Lantau trails
chunks.heading: c) Gully Erosion

chunks.text:
- Definition: Erosion by flowing water in streams
- HK Context: All year-round in streams
- Process:
  1. Water flows in channel
  2. Hydraulic action (water force)
  3. Abrasion (sediment grinds bed)
  4. Attrition (rocks hit each other → smaller)
- Examples: Shing Mun, Tai Lam Chung
chunks.heading: d) Stream/River Erosion

chunks.text:
Definition: Erosion by sea waves on coastline
- HK Context: Long coastline with cliffs
- Process:
  1. Waves crash against cliff
  2. Hydraulic action (air compressed in cracks)
  3. Cliff collapses
  4. Debris removed by longshore drift
- Examples:
  - Lung Ha Wan (Cape D'Aguilar)
  - Sharp Island
  - Sai Kung coastline
  -
chunks.heading: 2. Wave Erosion (Coastal)

chunks.text:
1. Bare slope — Vegetation removed (human activity/fire)
2. Rainsplash effect — Raindrops hit soil, detach particles
3. Sheetwash (sheet erosion) — Water flows as thin sheet, removes fine particles
4. Rill formation — Small channels form (<30cm deep)
5. Rill deepening → Gully (>30cm deep)
6. Gully widening — Network of gullies develops
7. Valley formation — Extended erosion → valley
chunks.heading: Step-by-Step: Rill → Gully → Valley

chunks.text:
| Factor | Reason |
|--------|---------|
| Heavy rainfall | Summer monsoons, intense storms |
| Steep slopes | Rapid runoff |
| Dense development | Slope cutting, vegetation removal |
| Tropical climate | Fast weathering → loose material |
| Limited soil | Thin soil washes away easily |
chunks.heading: Why Erosion is Serious in HK

chunks.text:
| Location | Erosion Type | Features |
|----------|-------------|----------|
| Castle Peak | Water erosion (gullies) | Badlands, deep gullies |
| Lantau | Gully erosion | Mountain trails |
| Sai Kung | Wave erosion | Sea cliffs, caves |
| Shing Mun | Stream erosion | River channels |
| Road cuttings | Landslide/rockfall | Steep slopes |
chunks.heading: Hong Kong Examples

chunks.text:
| Method | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Vegetation | Plant grass/shrubs to hold soil |
| Retaining walls | Support slopes |
| Terracing | Reduce slope angle |
| Drainage | Control water flow |
| Slope reinforcement | Wire meshes, soil nails |
chunks.heading: Preventing Erosion in HK

chunks.text:
| English | Chinese |
|---------|---------|
| Erosion | 侵蝕作用 |
| Weathering | 風化作用 |
| Hydraulic action | 沖蝕作用 |
| Abrasion | 磨蝕作用 |
| Attrition | 磨損作用 |
| Sheet erosion | 片蝕 |
| Rill erosion | 細溝侵蝕 |
| Gully erosion | 溝蝕 |
| Mass movement | 塊體運動 |
| Landslide | 山泥傾瀉 |
| Longshore drift | 沿岸漂移 |
chunks.heading: Key Terms

chunks.text:
| | Weathering | Erosion |
|---|-----------|---------|
| Definition | Breakdown in place | Removal & transport |
| Location | At the place | Moving away |
| Agents | Temperature, water, chemicals | Water, wind, gravity |
| HK example | Hydrolysis → grus | Gullies, landslides |
chunks.heading: Summary: Weathering vs Erosion

chunks.text:
Mass Movement = movement of rock/soil downslope due to gravity.

Key concept: Shear stress vs Shear strength

| Term | Definition |
|------|-------------|
| Shear stress | Force pulling slope down (gravity + water weight) |
| Shear strength | Resistance of slope to movement (cohesion + friction) |

When movement occurs: Shear stress > Shear strength
chunks.heading: Definition: Mass Movement

chunks.text: Rapid movement of rock/soil downslope along a sliding surface.
chunks.heading: Definition

chunks.text:
| Factor | Effect on Landslide |
|--------|---------------------|
| INCREASES Shear Stress | |
| Heavy rain | Water adds weight → more stress |
| Steep slope | Higher gravity component → more stress |
| Additional load | Buildings/structures on slope |
| DECREASES Shear Strength | |
| Rainwater | Reduces friction between particles |
| Loss of vegetation | Roots no longer hold soil |
| earthquakes | Ground shaking reduces stability |
chunks.heading: Using Shear Stress & Strength:

chunks.text:
1. Factors increase shear stress (heavy rain adds weight)
2. Factors decrease shear strength (water reduces friction)
3. Shear stress > Shear strength
4. Slope fails → rapid movement along sliding plane
chunks.heading: Process:

chunks.text:
| Role | How it works |
|------|-------------|
| 1. Adds weight | Water fills soil pores → increases mass → increases shear stress |
| 2. Reduces friction | Water lubricates between soil particles → reduces shear strength |
| 3. Increases pore water pressure | Water pressure pushes particles apart → reduces contact between grains |
| 4. Creates surface of rupture | Weakest plane where failure occurs |
chunks.heading: Role of Water in Landslide:

chunks.text:
1. Rainwater enters soil
2. Fills pores (spaces between particles)
3. Adds weight → Shear stress increases
4. Pore water pressure rises → pushes particles apart
5. Contact between particles decreases → Friction reduced
6. Shear strength decreases
7. Surface of rupture forms (weakest plane in soil)
8. Shear stress > Shear strength → Landslide!
5. Landslide occurs
chunks.heading: Detailed Water Role:

chunks.text:
| Factor                 | How it affects                     |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Steep slope        | Higher shear stress                |
| Heavy rain         | Increases weight, reduces friction |
| Lack of vegetation | No root binding                    |
| Human activity     | Slope cutting, construction        |
| Earthquake         | Shaking weakens slope              |
| Soil type          | Loose soil less stable             |
chunks.heading: Factors Affecting Landslide:

chunks.text:
- 2016 Sau Mau Ping landslide
- 2018 Tsing Yi landslide
- Road cuttings after heavy rain
chunks.heading: HK Examples:

chunks.text: Free-falling of detached rocks from steep cliffs or slopes.
chunks.heading: Definition

chunks.text:
| Factor | Effect on Rockfall |
|--------|---------------------|
| INCREASES Shear Stress | |
| Gravity | Pulls loose rocks down |
| Earthquakes | Shakes rocks loose |
| DECREASES Shear Strength | |
| Weathering | Breaks bonds between rocks |
| Ice (not in HK) | Frost wedging expands cracks |
| Root growth | Pries rocks apart |
chunks.heading: Using Shear Stress & Strength:

chunks.text:
1. Weathering loosens rocks (hydrolysis, oxidation)
2. Joints/cracks develop in rock
3. Root growth or earthquake pushes rock
4. Water enters cracks → adds weight + reduces friction
5. Bond breaks (shear strength = 0)
6. Gravity pulls rock down → free fall
chunks.heading: Process:

chunks.text:
- Adds weight to loose rocks
- Reduces friction between rock and cliff face
- Freezes in cracks (not common in HK)
- Hydrolysis/oxidation weakens rock bonds
chunks.heading: Role of Water in Rockfall:

chunks.text:
| Factor | How it affects |
|--------|----------------|
| Steep cliff | More likely to fall |
| Weathering | Weakens rock bonds |
| Joints/fissures | Planes of weakness |
| Earthquake | Shakes rocks loose |
| Freeze-thaw | Not common in HK |
chunks.heading: Factors Affecting Rockfall:

chunks.text:
- Road cuttings on highways
- Lion Rock area
- Kowloon Peak cliffs
chunks.heading: HK Examples:

chunks.text:
| | Increases Stress | Decreases Strength |
|---|---|---|
| Landslide | Rain weight, steep slope, earthquake | Water reduces friction, no vegetation |
| Rockfall | Gravity, earthquake, roots | Weathering breaks rock bonds |

Key equation: When Shear stress > Shear strength → Mass movement occurs
chunks.heading: Summary: Shear Stress vs Shear Strength

chunks.text:
| Condition | Effect |
|-----------|--------|
| Heavy summer rain | Saturated soil = more weight + less friction |
| Steep slopes | High stress |
| Tropical climate | Fast weathering = weak rocks |
| Development | Slope cutting = unstable slopes |
| Lack of vegetation | No root binding |
chunks.heading: HK Conditions for Mass Movement

|---------|---------|
| Mass movement | 塊體運動 |
| Shear stress | 剪切應力 |
| Shear strength | 剪切強度 |
| Landslide | 山泥傾瀉 |
| Rockfall | 岩石倒塌 |
| Slope stability | 斜坡穩定性 |
| Friction | 摩擦力 |

chunks.heading: Key Terms

chunks.text:
Corestones' Definition: Rounded boulders formed by spheroidal weathering
Tors' Definition: Exposed rock outcrops standing above surroundings

Formation Process (Step-by-Step:

1. Initial cracks — Granite has perpendicular joints (vertical and horizontal)
2. Water infiltration — Rainwater seeps into cracks
3. Chemical weathering — 
   - Hydrolysis: Feldspar + water → kaolin (clay)
   - Oxidation: Iron minerals (biotite, hornblende) + oxygen + water → iron oxide (rust)
4. Spherical weathering — Corners weather faster than edges → becomes rounded
5. Core remains — Hard inner core remains as rounded boulder (corestone)
6. Weathered material — Upper granite becomes kaolin (clay)
7. Erosion — Weathered material removed by running water
8. Exposed bedrock — Hard unweathered granite emerges as tor
9. Joints control shape — Spacing of joints determines tor shape

Key Concepts:
- Spheroidal Weathering: Corners weather fastest (3 faces) → rounded shape
- Oxidation: Iron minerals rust → red/brown colour (pink granite in HK)
- Hydrolysis: Feldspar breaks down to clay

Examples: Amah Rock, Lion Rock
chunks.heading: Tors:

chunks.text:
Definition: Depression channels formed by intense erosion

Formation Process (Step-by-Step):

1. Dry season (winter) — Hong Kong has dry winter; soil dries out and cracks form
2. Bare surface — Slope has little vegetation (human activity/fire)
2. Rainsplash effect — Raindrops hit soil → detach soil particles → splash disperses soil
3. Sheet erosion — Water flows as thin sheet across surface → removes loosened particles
4. Concentration — Water concentrates in small channels
5. Rill formation — Small channels (rills) develop
6. Gully erosion — Rills deepen → gullies (>30cm deep)
7. Badlands — Complete drainage pattern, network of gullies

Key Concepts:
- Rainsplash effect — Raindrop impact detaches soil particles; most effective on bare soil
- Sheet erosion — Uniform removal of surface layer
- Rill erosion — Small channels forming
- Gully erosion — Deep channels, irreversible
- Vegetation role — Roots hold soil; removal → erosion
- Slope angle — Steeper slopes = faster erosion

Examples: Castle Peak
chunks.heading: Gullies and Badlands:

chunks.text:
| Area                         | Features                 |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Lion Rock / Kowloon Peak | Corestones, tor clusters |
| Castle Peak              | Badlands, gullies        |
| Cheung Chau              | Granite rocks, sea caves |

chunks.text: Volcanic landforms are features created by volcanic activity, including the volcanic rocks themselves and the erosional features that develop on them.
chunks.heading: What are Volcanic Landforms?

chunks.text:

chunks.heading: Volcanic Rock Types in Hong Kong

chunks.text:
Formation:
- Compact tuff resists erosion
- Surrounding softer rocks erode faster
- Result: Steep hills and ridges remain

Examples:

- Needle Hill (532m)
- Grassy Hill (647m)

Formation:

- Less resistant rocks around erode away

Examples:
- Tai Mo Shan (tuff and rhyolite)
- Castle Peak (volcanic tuff)

Formation:

Examples:

chunks.heading: Hong Kong Volcanic Areas

chunks.text:
- Differential erosion: Hard volcanic rocks resist erosion → form peaks/ridges
- Tuff: Most common volcanic rock in HK (compact, resistant)
- Weathering: Tropical climate causes chemical weathering → breakdown of rocks

chunks.text:
Part of: EP1_Dynamic_Earth_HK — PART 5: LANDFORMS
Related: EP1_Dynamic_Earth_Glossary · 5.1 Granite Landforms · 5.2 Volcanic Landforms · hk_geology_cases
chunks.heading: 5.3 Hong Kong UNESCO Global Geopark

chunks.text:
- Hong Kong National Geopark (2009) → UNESCO Global Geopark (2015).
- Two regions:
  - Volcanic Region (southeast) — High Island / Sai Kung: hexagonal volcanic columns (rhyolitic tuff), volcanic landforms → see 5.2 Volcanic Landforms.
  - Sedimentary Region (northeast) — Tolo Harbour / Yan Chau Tong: layered Palaeozoic sedimentary rocks, coastal landforms → see 2.2 Sedimentary Rocks.
chunks.heading: What it is

chunks.text:
| Zone | Management idea |
|---|---|
| Core | Most sensitive geology — visitor access kept minimal; sightseeing from the water, no landing encouraged |
| Special | Limited basic facilities — suited to education and training visits |
| Integrated | Highest capacity — full facilities concentrate visitors here so the sensitive areas stay protected |

- Carrying capacity = the maximum visitor load an area takes without degrading its geological values.
chunks.heading: Zone logic (why areas are zoned differently)

chunks.text:
Yes (appropriate):
- Geologically unique value → protection is justified; zoning controls impact.
- Education — visitors learn geology/ecology on site.
- Sustainable local income (boat tours, facilities) without extracting the resource.
- Controlled carrying capacity spreads visitors to the integrated zone.

Limits / costs:
- Footfall and litter erode the formations; once damaged, geological features do not regenerate (non-renewable heritage).
- Disturbance to ecology and tranquillity.
- If visitor numbers exceed carrying capacity, values decline — judge the zoning as the deciding factor.

Judgement shape: appropriate if zoning + carrying capacity are enforced; the uniqueness of the geology raises the protection bar.
chunks.heading: Discussion scaffold — is it appropriate to open a site to tourism?

chunks.text:
1. Why is landing discouraged in the core zone? → Most sensitive geology — minimize physical contact; sightseeing from boats.
2. Which zone should carry the shops/visitor centre? → Integrated — concentrate facilities and numbers there, protecting the other zones.
3. Give one economic benefit and one risk of geotourism. → Sustainable local income vs footfall erosion if carrying capacity is exceeded.
