docs.title: EP1 Geological Features in Hong Kong — Rock Characteristics, Internal/External Processes (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/EP1/EP1 Geological Features in HK (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why this is on the paper
Your own EP1 revision sheet lists three learning objectives (22 Oct 2026 scan): understand the geological background of different regions in Hong Kong, understand the relationship between geological processes and their resultant landforms, and understand how those landforms affect local urban development. Question 2 of the F6 first term test paper (18 marks, landslide) and Question 3 (18 marks, rocks and Geopark) both require candidates to name HK examples and explain how the process made them — naming a landform without the process scores nothing.
chunks.heading: EP1 Geological Features in Hong Kong — F6 DSE Revision

chunks.text: The rule: every geological feature in Hong Kong is rock characteristics + a process acting on it → a landform → a consequence for people. A candidate who can only recall the landform cannot earn the mechanism marks; the marks are in the arrow between the boxes.
chunks.heading: The concept that carries the marks

chunks.text: Each photo is from your own EP1.8 revision sheet, labelled with the example it shows. Read the caption and the process together — that pairing is what earns the mechanism marks.
chunks.heading: Part A — Rock-process-landform photo bank

chunks.text:
![Lai Chi Chong — minor fold in sedimentary rock](figures/EP1_proc_p01_1.png)

Folding — sedimentary strata compressed, buckled into a fold. The compressional force comes from the Lianhuashan Fault Zone.

![Folded strata cross-section with stress directions](figures/EP1_proc_p01_3.png)

Annotated diagram: which direction the rock was pushed, and how the fold formed.
chunks.heading: Folding

chunks.text:
![Hong Kong major NE–SW fault lines](figures/EP1_proc_p01_2.png)

Faulting — rock breaks and displaces horizontally along NE–SW major fault lines. Note the systematic NE–SW trend: this is why HK fault valleys all run the same way.

![Shing Mun Valley and Shing Mun River](figures/EP1_proc_p02_1.png)

Long narrow valley along a fault — the crushed rock in the fault zone erodes faster than the granite either side, so the valley is thin, steep-sided and follows the fault exactly.
chunks.heading: Faulting

chunks.text:
![Mafic dyke within parental granite](figures/EP1_proc_p03_1.png)

A mafic dyke intrudes granite. The dyke is more resistant than its host rock, so after denudation it stands out as a ridge or headland while the granite is eroded back.

![Basaltic dyke within parental tuff](figures/EP1_proc_p03_2.png)

The same principle in tuff host rock.

![Granite exposed as a batholith](figures/EP1_proc_p03_3.png)

Denudation strips the overlying rock and leaves the granite batholith exposed as rounded hills.
chunks.heading: Volcanism — internal

chunks.text:
![Sharp Peak — extinct volcanic cone](figures/EP1_proc_p04_1.png)

Extrusive volcanism built a cone; it is now extinct and denudation has steepened the slopes.

![Tai Mo Shan — high-altitude upland](figures/EP1_proc_p04_2.png)

Tuff from extrusive volcanism. Because tuff is fine-grained and resistant, Hong Kong's high ground is volcanic, not granite — this is the single most common student error.

![High Island — hexagonal columnar joints in tuff](figures/EP1_proc_p04_3.png)

Tuff cools and contracts, producing regular hexagonal columns. This columnar jointing is precisely why High Island is a UNESCO Global Geopark site.
chunks.heading: Volcanism — external

chunks.text:
![Po Toi Island / Cheung Chau — sheeting joints](figures/EP1_proc_p05_1.png)

Pressure release: overlying rock is eroded away, the underlying granite expands, and it cracks parallel to the surface in sheeting joints.

![Buddha Hand Rock, Po Toi Island](figures/EP1_proc_p05_2.png)

Continued block disintegration along those sheeting joints.

![Bread Rock of a granitic boulder, Castle Peak](figures/EP1_proc_p05_3.png)

Block disintegration — the boulder breaks along its joints.

![Sharp Island — Pineapple Bun Rock](figures/EP1_proc_p06_1.png)

Exfoliation: onion-like layers peel off the boulder as the surface alternately heats and cools. This is thermal expansion/contraction — not pressure release, and characteristically found in tuff, not granite.
chunks.heading: Physical weathering — pressure release and block disintegration

chunks.text:
![Deep weathering profile](figures/EP1_proc_p06_2.png)

Chemical weathering works downward, producing a deep zone of altered rock above fresh rock. In Hong Kong's hot humid climate this zone is deep — which is why granite slopes are unstable.
chunks.heading: Chemical weathering

chunks.text:
![Rhino Rock](figures/EP1_proc_p07_1.png)

Rhino Rock (Ho Man Tin) — a granite tor: spheroidal weathering rounds the block, then erosion strips the surrounding regolith and leaves the corestone standing.

Form vs Process — the most common Paper 2 mistake
"Honeycomb" is the FORM, not the PROCESS.
| | Answer |
|---|---|
| Process | Salt crystallisation — sea spray → salt enters pores → evaporation → crystals grow → pressure → grains break out. Physical weathering. |
| Form | Honeycomb — a pitted, cavernous surface of small cavities |
| Landform term (not a DSE syllabus term — do not use in an exam) | Tafoni / alveolar weathering |
HKEAA 2024 Paper 2 Section D Q1(c)(i) asked "What is the physical weathering process shown?" — most candidates wrongly answered "honeycomb weathering". The expected answer was salt crystallisation.
On exposed coastal granite (Cheung Chau, Lamma), salt crystallisation produces the honeycombed surface. Exception: in the Tung Chung / Tolo Harbour marble clasts, similar cavities form by solution (chemical / karst) — check the rock type first.
chunks.heading: Salt crystallisation and honeycomb weathering

chunks.text:
![Castle Peak / Tai Lam — gully and badland](figures/EP1_proc_p07_2.png)

Sheet erosion, then rill and gully erosion, cut the weathered granite soil into a badland.

![Tor at Shek O hillslope](figures/EP1_proc_p08_1.png)

Spheroidal weathering leaves a corestone; erosion removes the surrounding regolith and the corestone is left exposed as a tor.

![Scar and scree below a slope](figures/EP1_proc_p08_2.png)

Mass wasting — slumping of slope material leaves a scar, and debris accumulates as scree at the foot of the slope.
chunks.heading: Erosion and mass movement

chunks.text:
![Strata and bedding planes in sedimentary rock](figures/EP1_proc_p09_1.png)

Sedimentation lays down layers; the bedding planes are the weaknesses that later processes exploit.

![Long Lok Shui, Tung Ping Chau — chert interbed](figures/EP1_proc_p09_2.png)

Sedimentation plus a submarine volcanic eruption: a chert bed within the strata.
chunks.heading: Sedimentary rocks and bedding

chunks.text:
![Lai Chi Chong — tuffaceous sandstone](figures/EP1_proc_p10_1.jpg)

Sedimentation plus extrusive volcanism — volcanic ash settles into the sedimentary rock.

![Devil Fist, Bluff Head](figures/EP1_proc_p10_2.png)

Folding, then weathering and erosion along the folded bedding.
chunks.heading: Mixed: folding + weathering + erosion

chunks.text:
1. Name the rock and its characteristics — "granite, an intrusive igneous rock, coarse-grained and massively jointed" (1–2 marks).
2. Name the process — chemical weathering (spheroidal) / faulting / wave erosion / marine erosion (2 marks).
3. Explain the mechanism in steps — joints → water infiltration → hydrolysis of feldspar to clay → corners weather faster → corestone → erosion removes regolith → tor (3–4 marks).
4. Give the HK example — Amah Rock, Lion Rock, Castle Peak badlands (1 mark).
5. Land on the human consequence — weak foundations, landslip risk, or flat land for housing (1–2 marks).
chunks.heading: Answer structure (typical 8–12 mark mechanism question)

chunks.text:
- Naming a landform with no process — "Castle Peak has badlands" scores 0 beyond the example mark. The mark scheme wants "sheet → rill → gully erosion on bare granite soil".
- Confusing granite and tuff resistance — students often say granite is harder. Correct: granite is coarse and jointed (so it weathering-weathered easily in HK's hot humid climate); tuff is fine-grained and more resistant overall, giving steeper landforms.
- Ignoring that a dyke is more resistant than its host rock — Tsing Yi / Lantau coastlines are shaped because the dyke outlives the granite, not because the granite is hard.
- Treating a fault valley as "low flat land" automatically good for building — a fault zone is also crushed, fractured rock = weak foundation and groundwater seepage. Fault valleys attract settlement and constrain it.
- Dropping the region name — every mark in a "geological regions" question is anchored to a named region (Sha Tin, Tai Mo Shan, Yuen Long, Chi Ma Wan…), not to Hong Kong in general.
chunks.heading: Common marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Why does granite produce badlands but tuff produce sharp ridges? → Granite is coarsely jointed and weathers to loose regolith → sheet/rill/gully erosion; tuff is fine and resistant → mass movement and stream erosion cut sharper relief.
2. Why is Silvermine Bay a bay and the headland next to it a headland? → Differential erosion: the resistant dyke stands, the weaker granite is eroded back.
3. What process made the long narrow valley at Shing Mun? → Faulting along a NE–SW line → crushed rock → faster erosion along the fault → Shing Mun Reservoir and gorge.
4. A student says "granite is hard so it makes high mountains". Correct them. → Granite in HK weathers readily (hot, humid, jointed); the high rugged peaks are tuff/volcanic, granite gives rounded hills and tors.
5. Yuen Long has flat land — why can't you build easily everywhere? → Underlying metamorphic rock (marble) is weak/fissile → foundation problems and subsidence, so flatness alone isn't enough. (Stronger answer: marble is soluble, so dissolution along joints produces karst — sinkholes and cavities.)
6. A student writes "exfoliation happens when pressure is released, as in Po Toi Island." Correct them. → Po Toi Island shows sheeting joints, caused by pressure release. Exfoliation is thermal expansion/contraction, acts on small boulders, and is characteristically tuff — Pineapple Bun Rock, Sharp Island is the example.
7. Name the two features a slope failure leaves behind, and say which is upslope. → Scar (head scarp, upslope, where the mass detached) and scree (talus, at the foot, where debris accumulates, grain size decreasing downslope).
8. Why is a fault valley a transport corridor but a poor place to build? → The same crushed rock that is easy to excavate is fractured and water-bearing. CKR crosses 7 fault zones; the West Drainage Tunnel crosses 8 major faults with inflow to 150 L/min and Q-value 0.03.
9. What is the parent rock of marble, and why does marble behave differently from granite in Hong Kong's climate? → Marble comes from limestone by heat and pressure. Limestone is carbonate and soluble, so rainwater (weakly acidic from dissolved CO₂) dissolves it along joints → karst. Granite is insoluble; it only weathers mechanically and chemically in place, giving rounded hills and tors.
10. Name the four landforms karst produces, and state the HK region where they occur. → Solution cavity, cave, sinkhole, karst topography, in the Yuen Long – Tuen Mun marble belt in the north-west New Territories.
11. A student says "Yuen Long is flat, so it is safe to build on." Correct them, naming the process. → The flatness is river sediment deposited over the older marble surface. The soluble carbonate bedrock has been dissolved along joints (solution weathering), leaving karst cavities and sinkholes underground. The flatness is recent and hides the hazard, so foundations can fail suddenly and the ground subsides.
12. Name two Hong Kong sites where marble cavity was found, and the two foundation types the Housing Department used there. → Marble cavity: Yuen Long (Wang Fu Court, Long Ching Estate), and also Ma On Shan and Tung Chung. Foundations: Buoyancy Raft Foundation (support on the soil stratum) and Shaft-Grouted Barrette (perimeter grouting increases pile–soil friction).
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

chunks.text:
The exam distinguishes four physical/chemical processes that all "break rock down". Naming the wrong one costs the process mark even when the landform is right.

| Term | Cause | Scale | Rock | HK example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sheeting | pressure release | large | granite | Po Toi Island, Cheung Chau |
| Exfoliation | thermal expansion / contraction | small — boulders | tuff | Pineapple Bun Rock, Sharp Island |
| Block disintegration | joint-controlled breakdown | medium | granite | Bread Rock, Castle Peak |
| Spheroidal weathering | hydrolysis on corners | rounded boulders | granite | Amah Rock, Lion Rock |

- Sheeting is pressure release; exfoliation is thermal. They are different processes at different scales. Exfoliation is characteristically found in tuff, not granite — Pineapple Bun Rock at Sharp Island (Sai Kung) is the classic HK example.
- Sheeting joints form parallel to the land surface after the overburden is eroded and the rock unloads.
chunks.heading: Weathering and mass-movement types — do not confuse these

chunks.text:
![Scar and scree below a slope](figures/EP1_proc_p08_2.png)

Mass wasting — slumping of slope material leaves a scar on the slope above, and the debris accumulates as scree at the foot.

- Scar = the bare, stripped surface left where the failed mass detached. It marks the head of the failure.
- Scree = the angular, sorted-by-size debris cone at the foot. Its grain size decreases downslope because larger fragments travel further.
- Trigger in Hong Kong = intense rainfall saturating the slope, on weathered granite or tuff that has lost its strength.
- Human consequence = debris blocks roads and channels; the bare scar itself is also a bare, erodible surface.

| Stage | Feature | Where it sits |
|---|---|---|
| Detachment | Scar (head scarp) | upslope |
| Transport | Mass movement (slump, rotational slip) | slope body |
| Deposition | Scree / talus cone | foot of slope |
chunks.heading: Mass movement — scar and scree

chunks.text: A fault valley attracts settlement because the crushed rock is easy to cut through and the line is already a line of weakness. But it is still fractured, water-bearing rock. These two real projects show the cost.
chunks.heading: What living on a fault zone actually costs — two HK projects

chunks.text:
- 4.7 km total, of which 3.9 km is tunnel; Yau Ma Tei Interchange → Kai Tak Development Area
- Crosses 7 fault zones and 7 MTR lines
- What the fault zones cause: complex and unstable ground during excavation, risk of collapse, groundwater in the fault gouge, ground movement affecting existing structures, and higher cost from special engineering
- Mitigation: BIM, automatic canopy installation, AI cameras for worker safety
chunks.heading: Central Kowloon Route (CKR)

chunks.text:
- Route: Tai Hang → Cyberport, western Hong Kong Island
- Crosses 8 major faults, plus subsidiary faults, shear zones and rock-type contact zones
- Groundwater inflow up to 150 L/min
- Q-value falls to 0.03 at shear zones — very poor rock quality, requiring extra support
- Fault gouge reduces friction and must be pumped

Exam use: "A fault valley is flat, so why is it not automatically good for building?" → the rock in the fault zone is crushed and fractured, giving weak foundations, groundwater seepage and instability, so it constrains development as well as attracting it.
chunks.heading: Hong Kong West Drainage Tunnel

chunks.text: Marble is the only metamorphic rock that matters for the Hong Kong EP1 syllabus. It is the answer to "solution weathering", and the region to name is the Yuen Long – Tuen Mun marble belt in the north-west New Territories.
chunks.heading: Metamorphic rock — where it is in Hong Kong, and what it does

chunks.text:
[code block omitted]

- Parent rock: limestone — a sedimentary rock made of carbonate
- Process: heat and pressure during metamorphism recrystallise the carbonate
- Result: marble — still carbonate, still soluble, but harder, denser and recrystallised
- Rock cycle in one chain: magma cools → igneous; sediment accumulates and lithifies → sedimentary; heat & pressure → metamorphic (marble from limestone, slate from mudstone)
chunks.heading: The rock cycle link — where marble comes from

chunks.text:
| Property | Granite | Tuff | Marble |
|---|---|---|---|
| Origin | intrusive igneous | extrusive igneous | metamorphic (from limestone) |
| Solubility | insoluble | insoluble | soluble in weak acid |
| Structure | coarse, jointed | fine, resistant | recrystallised, foliated, fissile |
| Main HK landform | rounded hills, tors | rugged peaks, hexagonal columns | karst: sinkholes, caves, solution cavities |
| Main HK problem | deep weathering, landslip | steep slopes, lack of flat land | unstable ground, subsidence |
chunks.heading: Why marble is different from granite and tuff

chunks.text:
1. Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air and the soil → forms weak carbonic acid
2. The acidic water reacts with the carbonate in marble → the rock dissolves
3. Dissolution works along joints and bedding planes, widening them
4. With time the joints become solution cavities, caves and sinkholes
5. The result is karst topography

Exam line: solution weathering = acidic water dissolving soluble rock such as limestone or marble. It is chemical, not physical, and it requires a soluble carbonate rock.
chunks.heading: Solution weathering — the mechanism, step by step

chunks.text:
| Landform | Description |
|---|---|
| Solution cavity | Enlarged joint or bedding plane underground |
| Cave | Cavity large enough to enter |
| Sinkhole | Surface collapse into a cavity |
| Karst topography | The whole landscape of pits, caves and absent surface drainage |
chunks.heading: The landforms karst produces

chunks.text:
- Where: north-west New Territories — Yuen Long, Tuen Mun, extending towards Kam Tin and Sheung Shui
- Rock: metamorphosed carbonate bedrock (marble), in places buried under thick superficial deposits
- Process: solution weathering → karst cavities
- Resulting relief: the belt lies in low-lying, flat land with a low river course — because the Yuen Long River deposited sediment over the old limestone surface
- The trap for students: Yuen Long looks flat and looks ideal for building. It is not — flatness is the result of recent river deposition over karst, so the flatness hides the cavities underneath

Consequences for urban development:
- Unstable ground and risk of sudden ground collapse where cavities are roofed by thin material
- Land subsidence as marble weathers and cavities enlarge
- Poor foundation bearing → need for special ground treatment before piling
- Foundation works are controlled — the area is designated Area Number 2 of the Scheduled Areas under the Buildings Department / CEDD guidance (CEDD GCO Publication 2/90), requiring ground investigation before construction
chunks.heading: Yuen Long – Tuen Mun marble belt — the HK case

chunks.text:
Exam use: "Yuen Long has flat land — why can't you build easily everywhere?"
→ The flat land is river sediment deposited over marble. Beneath it the soluble carbonate rock has been dissolved along joints, producing karst cavities and sinkholes, so the foundation is unstable and prone to collapse and subsidence. The flatness is recent and hides the hazard.
chunks.heading: Yuen Long – Tuen Mun marble belt — the HK case

chunks.text:
The Hong Kong Housing Department confirms marble cavity is found in Yuen Long, Ma On Shan and the Tung Chung reclamation area, formed as the marble is dissolved by groundwater over several hundred thousand years. Cavities can only resist very small additional loads, which puts heavy constraints on design and construction.

| Project | Problem found | Foundation solution |
|---|---|---|
| Wang Fu Court, Yuen Long | Very large marble cavity ~60 m below ground level; rock stratum >175 m deep at some points — ordinary pile foundations could not spread the load | Buoyancy Raft Foundation — BIM modelled the geological profile and produced a 3-D print-out, then a raft supports the building on the soil stratum instead of transferring load to rock |
| Long Ching Estate, Yuen Long | Marble cavity at relatively deep level — common pile types ineffective | Shaft-Grouted Barrette — grouting around the perimeter of the pile thickens the soil, increasing pile–soil friction to support taller buildings |

Exam use: the engineering answer completes the geological one. Marble cavity is not merely a hazard — it is a hazard that changes what can be built and how, requiring ground investigation first and then special foundations. See 2.3 Metamorphic Rocks.
chunks.heading: Real HK sites — marble cavity and how it was solved

chunks.text:
| Rock | Parent rock | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Marble | limestone | recrystallised carbonate, soluble — the HK case |
| Slate | mudstone | foliated, splits into thin flat sheets, very fissile |
| Schist | various | strongly foliated, visible mica flakes |
| Gneiss | various | banded, coarse-grained |
| Quartzite | sandstone | very hard, recrystallised quartz |

Slate from mudstone is the other pair students must be able to state in the rock-cycle chain.

chunks.text:

| Structure | Horizontal bedding → resistant caprock over a weaker layer |

chunks.text:
| Rock / feature        | Characteristic                       | Process                                    | Landform / example                                       | Human consequence                       |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Granite               | Coarse, jointed                      | Spheroidal weathering + erosion            | Tors, corestones — Amah Rock, Lion Rock                  | Rockfall, steep slopes                  |
| Granite               | Coarse, jointed                      | Sheet + gully erosion                      | Badlands — Castle Peak                                   | Erosion, dust, slope repair             |
| Granite               | Massive batholith                    | Denudation                                 | Rounded hills — Kowloon / Central                        | Limited flat land                       |
| Tuff                  | Fine, resistant                      | Extrusive volcanism + denudation           | High rugged peaks — Tai Mo Shan 957 m, Sunset Peak 869 m | Lack of flat land                       |
| Tuff                  | Jointed on cooling                   | Columnar jointing                          | Hexagonal columns — High Island                          | Reservoir basin, scenic area            |
| Dyke (mafic)          | More resistant than granite          | Intrusive volcanism + differential erosion | Headland / bay contrast — Tsing Yi, Silvermine Bay       | Coastal scenery, limited flat land      |
| Sedimentary (breccia) | Layered, bedding joints              | Wave erosion                               | Sea arch, wave-cut platform — Tung Lung Chau, Bluff Head | Flat platform for development           |
| Metamorphic (marble)  | Fissile, recrystallised, soluble | Weathering + dissolution + mass movement   | Karst, slabby slopes — Yuen Long, Sheung Shui            | Sinkholes, weak foundations, subsidence |
| Sedimentary (caprock) | Horizontal bedding                   | Differential erosion                       | Table-top hills — Ma On Shan                             | Buildable summit, cut slopes needed     |
| Mass movement         | Weathered, waterlogged slope         | Slumping / rotational slip                 | Scar (upslope) + scree cone (foot)                       | Debris blocks roads and channels        |
| Fault zone            | Crushed, fractured                   | Faulting (NE–SW)                           | Linear valley — Shing Mun, Tolo Channel                  | Settlement corridor + tunnel risk       |

chunks.heading: EP1 Dynamic Earth - Glossary

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Intrusive igneous rock | Formed from magma cooling underground (e.g., granite) |
| Extrusive igneous rock | Formed from lava cooling on surface (e.g., tuff, volcanic ash) |
| Sedimentary rock | Formed from deposition of sediments in layers, then compaction and cementation (e.g., sandstone) |
| Granite | Coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock in HK |
| Tuff | Fine-grained extrusive igneous rock (volcanic ash compacted) |
chunks.heading: 1. Types of Rock in Hong Kong

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Weathering | Breakdown of rocks in situ (no transport) |
| Physical weathering | Breakdown by mechanical forces (e.g., frost wedging, thermal expansion) |
| Chemical weathering | Breakdown by chemical reactions (e.g., oxidation, hydrolysis) |
| Biological weathering | Breakdown by organisms (e.g., roots, lichens) |
| Hydrolysis | Chemical reaction with water breaking down minerals |
| Oxidation | Reaction with oxygen causing rusting |
| Frost wedging | Water freezes in cracks, expands and splits rock |
| Salt crystallisation (salt weathering) | Physical weathering. Sea spray → salt enters pores → evaporation → crystals grow → pressure → grains break out. Common on exposed coastal granite (Cheung Chau, Lamma) |
| Honeycomb weathering | The FORM produced by salt crystallisation on coastal granite — a pitted, cavernous surface of small cavities. Not a process |
| Spheroidal weathering | The FORM produced by chemical weathering on jointed granite — rounded block, corestone at centre |
chunks.heading: 2. Weathering

chunks.text:
Form vs Process — the most common Paper 2 mistake
| Question asks for | Answer |
|---|---|
| the process | the agent: salt crystallisation, thermal expansion, hydrolysis, solution |
| the form / feature | the appearance: honeycomb, spheroidal, block disintegration, granular disintegration |
HKEAA 2024 Paper 2 Section D Q1(c)(i) asked "What is the physical weathering process shown?" — most candidates wrongly answered "honeycomb weathering". Expected: salt crystallisation.
Exception: honeycomb-like cavities in carbonate rock (Tung Chung / Tolo Harbour marble clasts) are chemical (solution / karst). Check the rock type.
chunks.heading: 2. Weathering

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Erosion | Removal of weathered materials by agents (water, wind, ice) |
| Transportation | Movement of eroded materials |
| Deposition | Settling of transported materials |
chunks.heading: 3. Erosion

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Spheroidal weathering | Rounding of rock corners due to chemical weathering |
| Corestone | Rounded boulder formed by spheroidal weathering |
| Tor | Exposed rock outcrop with rounded boulders |
| Grus | Sandy residual material from weathered granite |
chunks.heading: 4. Spheroidal Weathering & Landforms

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Landslide | Downward movement of rock/soil on slope |
| Shear stress | Force trying to cause sliding down slope |
| Shear strength | Resistance to sliding |
| Slope stability | Balance between shear stress and shear strength |
| Trigger | Event that initiates landslide (e.g., heavy rain) |
chunks.heading: 5. Landslide Causes

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Pore water pressure | Pressure of water in soil pores |
| Effective stress | Stress between soil particles (reduced by water) |
| Lubricating effect | Water reduces friction between particles |
| Surface of rupture | Curved surface where sliding occurs |
| Saturated soil | Soil with all pores filled with water |
| Antecedent rainfall | Rainfall before landslide that saturates soil |
chunks.heading: 6. Role of Water

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Retaining wall | Concrete wall supporting slope |
| Shotcrete | Sprayed concrete on slope surface |
| Rock bolt/anchor | Steel bolt securing loose rock |
| Drainage | Channels/drains to remove water |
| Slope flattening | Reducing slope angle |
| Vegetation | Plants with roots to bind soil |
| Terracing | Creating steps on slope |
| Rockfall mesh | Steel mesh to catch falling rocks |
chunks.heading: 7. Landslide Prevention Measures

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Bedding plane | Surface separating two sedimentary layers, formed when deposition conditions change |
| Stratification | Layering visible in sedimentary rocks |
| Compaction | Burial squeezes sediment: water squeezed out, grains packed tighter |
| Cementation | Minerals precipitate in pore spaces and glue the grains together |
| Lithification | The full process turning sediment into rock: deposition → compaction → cementation |
| Fossil | Remains/traces of organisms preserved in sedimentary rock (not found in igneous) |
chunks.heading: 8. Sedimentary structures

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Fault | Fracture in rock with movement of the two sides along it |
| Fault zone | Band of fractured, crushed rock along a fault — a plane of weakness (groundwater often flows here) |
| Joint | Crack in rock with NO movement along it |
| Plane of weakness | Any fracture along which weathering, erosion or sliding works faster |
| Horst | Block uplifted between two normal faults |
| Graben | Block dropped down between two normal faults |
| NE–SW trend | Dominant direction of Hong Kong's major faults — valleys and gorges often follow it |
chunks.heading: 9. Faults & structures

chunks.text:
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Geopark | Area protecting geological heritage, used for education and sustainable tourism |
| Core zone | Most protected area — visitor access kept minimal, sightseeing from the water |
| Special zone | Limited basic facilities — suited to education and training visits |
| Integrated zone | Concentrates visitors with full facilities, protecting the more sensitive areas |
| Carrying capacity | Maximum number of visitors an area can take without degrading its values |
| Geotourism | Tourism based on geological landscapes, managed so the resource lasts |

chunks.text:
- Complex ground conditions → unstable tunnel excavation
- Risk of collapse → dangerous working environment

| Granular disintegration | Weathering of mineral bonds | Small | Granite | Sandy soils |
| Block disintegration | Joint-controlled breakdown | Medium | Granite | Angular block fragments |
| Spheroidal weathering | Alternating hydrolysis on corners | Rounded boulders | Granite | Rounded tors (Amah Rock, Lion Rock) |

chunks.text:

- Exfoliation commonly found in tuff, NOT granite

chunks.text: Practical manual for running fieldwork/independent enquiry studies. Exam angle: this is what Section B fieldwork-based questions and EP write-ups assume you can do.
chunks.heading: Qualitative Research Manual — with urban geography examples

chunks.text:
Qualitative research collects non-numerical data to explain why and how — meanings, perceptions, experiences, decisions, meanings of place. Quantitative counts and measures (questionnaire tallies, velocity, counts).

| Use qualitative when… | Use quantitative when… |
|---|---|
| The question is about perception, identity, experience ("how do stall holders see the market's decline?") | The question is about frequency, amount, relationship ("how many customers per hour?") |
| You don't know the answer categories in advance (exploratory) | You have fixed categories to test |
| Small-N, in-depth, context matters | Large-N, generalisation matters |
| You need participants' own words as evidence | You need statistics, averages, graphs |

Real geography questions mix both: count shoppers by hour (quant) and ask five shopkeepers why they open when they do (qual). Mixing = triangulation.
chunks.heading: 1. What qualitative research is, and when to use it

chunks.text:
1. Research question — one sentence, answerable in the time available. Test: does it contain where (a real place), who (a group), and what you will find out? Bad: "study urban decay in HK." Good: "How do elderly residents in To Kwa Wan experience the area's physical decay, and which changes do they want first?"
2. Design — choose the method(s) that match the question; state why (examiners mark justification, not method quantity).
3. Sampling — who you talk to and why they represent the group (§4).
4. Instruments — interview schedule, observation proforma, consent form (§6).
5. Fieldwork — collect, record, keep a field diary; pilot first (§6).
6. Analysis — code, categorise, find themes; quote real participants (§7).
7. Write-up — aim → method → what was found (with quotes) → limitations → improvement (§8–9).
chunks.heading: 2. The seven-stage workflow

chunks.text:
One-to-one, open questions with a follow-up list. Best for: in-depth personal experience.
- Urban example: interview 6–8 hawker stall holders at Graham Street Market — "How has your customer base changed since the mall opened?" Follow-ups: rent, age of customers, plans to retire.
- Tip: ask about the past before the present (people remember easier), and never ask leading questions ("Don't you think the redevelopment ruined it?" → "How has the redevelopment affected you?").
chunks.heading: 3.1 Semi-structured interviews — the workhorse

chunks.text:
Group talk surfaces disagreement and shared norms. Best for: contested community issues.
- Urban example: two focus groups of public housing estate residents (Choi Hung Estate) — one young, one elderly — on whether the estate's ageing facilities matter more than rent.
chunks.heading: 3.2 Focus groups — 4–8 people, one discussion

chunks.text:
Watch behaviour rather than asking. Record with a time-sampling proforma (behaviour tallies every 10 min) or field notes of what happened.
- Urban example: Tsim Sha Tsui Promenade — map how different users occupy space (tourists, elderly exercise groups, vendors) over 2-hour windows; note seating conflicts.
- Urban example: urban heat & walkability — walk the same 1 km route at 3 pm, record shade, wind, pedestrian counts, and where people pause.
chunks.heading: 3.3 Observation — structured or participant

chunks.text:
Interview while moving through the site, or show photos and ask. Best for: place memory and attachment.
- Urban example: walk with a long-term resident of Sai Ying Pun past the old dried-seafood shops; "what was here before?" Photos trigger recall no office interview gets.
chunks.heading: 3.4 Walking interviews / photo-elicitation

chunks.text:
Participants draw or annotate a map: perceptions of safety, noise, favourite places.
- Urban example: ask residents of Sham Shui Po to mark where they feel safe/unsafe after dark — the map is the data; compare with crime or lighting records.
chunks.heading: 3.5 Participatory / mental mapping

chunks.text:
Analyse texts: consultation papers, newspapers, ads, government reports. Count frames ("revitalisation" vs "gentrification") and who is quoted.
- Urban example: compare media framing of the Lantau Tomorrow reclamation across two newspapers; or read the North Metropolis consultation docs for whose voices appear and whose are absent.
chunks.heading: 3.6 Documentary & media analysis

chunks.text: One bounded place, multiple methods, deep description. Most DSE/EP qualitative projects are single case studies with 2 methods (e.g. interviews + observation) — that is the sweet spot for the mark scheme.
chunks.heading: 3.7 Case study (the umbrella, not a method)

chunks.text:
- Purposive (most common): deliberately choose information-rich cases — "owners of stalls operating >20 years" (not "whoever is free").
- Maximum variation: sample across contrasts (hawker vs mall retailer; young vs elderly resident).
- Snowball: each participant refers the next — good for hard-to-reach groups (street sleepers, informal vendors).
- Typical case / extreme case: one ordinary example, or the most striking one.
- Sample sizes (guidance, not rules): interviews 8–15 until saturation (new interviews stop yielding new themes); focus groups 2–3 groups of 4–8; observation sessions ≥ 4 time-slots (different days/hours).
- Always justify in writing: "10 interviews were chosen until no new themes emerged (saturation)."
chunks.heading: 4. Sampling: who and why

chunks.text:
1. Informed consent — purpose, what you'll record, how it's stored, right to withdraw; written form; minors require parental/guardian consent (schools and the EP process have their own forms).
2. Anonymity — pseudonyms + no faces in photos; handle personal data under the PDPO (collection purpose stated, data kept secure, deleted after the project). Raw transcripts with names = a fail.
3. Permission — stall owners via the market's association; estates via the management office (gatekeepers) — a shopkeeper refusing is data too ("3 of 12 declined, citing time pressure").
4. Do no harm / no filming in private premises; never photograph children; note your own safety (traffic, heat, lone fieldwork → tell someone your route).
5. Reflexivity — one line on how you (a student outsider, a shop owner's relative) may have shaped answers. Examiners value this.
chunks.heading: 5. Ethics — the part that fails projects

chunks.text:
1. Warm-up: How long have you run this stall? How did you start?
2. Experience: Walk me through a typical day — has it changed over the years?
3. Change: What do you think caused those changes?
4. Meaning: What would be lost if the market closed?
5. Evaluation: What one change would help most?
6. Close: Anything I should have asked?

Rules: funnel order (general → specific), 8–12 questions max, pilot on one person and rewrite anything that gets a blank stare.
chunks.heading: Interview schedule (semi-structured) — urban example

chunks.text: Rows = 10-min intervals; columns = categories (e.g. resting / selling / photographing / passing through / arguing over space), plus a notes column for surprises. Fix your categories before you start.
chunks.heading: Observation proforma (time-sampling)

chunks.text: "You're taking part in a geography study about this street. It takes 10 minutes, it's recorded/anonymised, you can stop at any time, nothing you say affects anything. Signature?"
chunks.heading: Consent script (spoken + written)

chunks.text:
Thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke's six phases) — the default method:
1. Familiarise: read the transcript, jot initial ideas.
2. Code: label interesting bits — `["rent up 40%"] → rent_pressure`.
3. Theme: cluster codes into candidate themes — `rent_pressure + customer_loss → economic unsustainability`.
4. Review: do themes fit the data and answer the research question?
5. Define & name: `theme = "Held on by loyalty, not profit"`.
6. Write: theme → claim → quote(s) as evidence.

Coding table (worked, urban geography):

| Raw quote | Code | Sub-theme | Theme |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Rent went up 40% in three years" | rent rise | costs | Unsustainable economics |
| "Customers are all tourists now, nobody cooks" | customer change | market shift | Loss of local function |
| "I'll close when my lease ends; my son won't do it" | no successor | ageing trader | Fading culture |
| "We stay for the neighbours, we're like family" | social ties | community value | Intangible worth |

Counts add rigour without becoming quantitative: "6 of 9 interviewees mentioned rent first" is fine — with the quotes behind it.
chunks.heading: 7. Analysis — how raw words become findings

chunks.text: Optional alternatives: content analysis (frequency of words/frames in documents), discourse analysis (how language constructs a position — e.g. who is "stakeholder" and who is "obstacle" in a consultation doc), grounded theory (build theory from data — only for MSc-level depth).
chunks.heading: 7. Analysis — how raw words become findings

chunks.text:
1. Title/aim — the research question.
2. Context — 2–3 lines of why this place matters (data: population, change statistic).
3. Method & sampling — what you chose and why it fits the question; sample table (n, ages, roles).
4. Ethics — consent, anonymity, permissions (one short paragraph).
5. Findings — organised by theme, not by interviewee; each theme = claim + quote + your interpretation.
6. Limitations — small sample, recall bias, your own positionality, short observation window.
7. Improvement — one methodological change (longer observation; add a questionnaire for breadth; stratify sampling).

Sentence stems that earn marks:
- "The data suggest that… (n = 6/9), for example one trader explained, '…'"
- "This supports/challenges the concept of … because …"
- "The second method corroborated this: observations at the site showed…"
chunks.heading: 8. Writing up — the structure and the sentences that score

chunks.text:
- Triangulation — at least two methods or two data sources (interview + observation; residents + official docs).
- Member checking — read your themes back to one or two participants ("is this fair?").
- Prolonged/repeated contact — visit at different times, not one afternoon.
- Audit trail — keep consent forms, transcripts, coding sheets, dated field notes.
- Reflexivity — state your standpoint and how it may bias data.
- Thick description — enough context for a reader to judge transferability.
chunks.heading: 9. Quality criteria (what makes qualitative *credible*)

chunks.text:
- Interviewing only friends/family → purposive sample + justify.
- One method → add a second (triangulation).
- Reporting a transcript dump → themes first, quotes as evidence.
- Leading questions → pilot and rewrite.
- No ethics/consent section → automatic ceiling on marks.
- Counting only → "4 people said X" with no words, no meaning → misses the point of qualitative.
- Findings that don't answer the research question → re-align themes to the question before writing.
chunks.heading: 10. Common mistakes (and the fix)

chunks.text:
A. "Who is Central Market renewal for?" — Case study, semi-structured interviews (8 visitors, 4 tenants) + non-participant observation (3 × 2-hour weekday/Sunday slots). Findings: theme access vs audience — visitors valued "air-conditioning and shade", tenants valued "cheap rent", neither mentioned the heritage signage; observation confirmed the arcade's footfall concentrated at 12–2 pm on weekdays. Conclusion: renewal serves commuters, not the original market network. Limitations: no management interview; 3 sessions only. Improvement: add management perspective + a Sunday evening slot.

B. "Perceived safety after dark in Chungking Mansions' surroundings" — participatory mapping (n = 15) + walking interviews (n = 6) + media frame analysis (30 news items). Finding: visitors and workers draw different night-maps — visitors mark exits and lit main roads; long-term workers mark shortcuts, food stalls and greetings as "safe". Media frames emphasise crime; on-the-ground accounts emphasise navigability. Triangulation of three methods makes the claim robust.
chunks.heading: 11. Two fully-worked mini-examples (urban geography)

chunks.text:
- [ ] Research question names a real place, a real group, and a findable answer
- [ ] Method(s) justified against the question; ≥2 methods or sources
- [ ] Sampling described with numbers and a reason (saturation/variation)
- [ ] Consent, anonymity, PDPO/ethics covered; pilot completed
- [ ] Findings organised by theme with real quotes
- [ ] Limitations honest + one concrete improvement
- [ ] Reflexivity line included
chunks.heading: 12. Quick check before you hand it in

docs.title: M1 Conventional Signs & Grid Reference (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/Map and GIS/Concepts/M1 Conventional Signs and Grid Reference (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Every map question opens with "read it off the map first". A wrong grid reference or an unread symbol costs the easy marks that fund the harder explanation later. Paper 1 Section B and the fieldwork-based questions both assume you can locate and name.
chunks.heading: M1 — Conventional Signs and Grid Reference

chunks.text:
- Built structures: buildings (solid black), roads (double line, width = real width), footpaths (dashed), bridges, piers, railways (cross-ticked)
- Vegetation: plantation (regular dots), secondary growth (irregular), scrub, mangrove — pattern, not colour, carries the meaning
- Water: rivers (line, widening downstream), streams, tanks, seasonal watercourses (dashed), coast, mangrove edge
- Boundaries: administrative (dot-dash), contour (thin brown), grid (blue, thin)
- Relief: contours with index contours (thicker, labelled), rock/cliff hachures, quarry, burial ground
- Signs change with scale: at 1:20,000 a building is a shape; at 1:5,000 it may be a named block. Never assume a sign means the same thing on two maps of different scale.

The move that scores: name the feature AND say what it tells you. "Bridge" scores nothing; "bridge with a single span at 650 740 — the river is narrow and confined there, so the crossing is cheap" scores.
chunks.heading: 1. Conventional signs — read them in context

chunks.text:
- 4-figure: find the square, give eastings first (left-to-right), then northings (bottom-top) → `6473` = column 64, row 73 (each digit is a grid line, so the answer locates a square)
- 6-figure: divide each square into ten parts with your eye or the ruler → `647308` = column 64 + 7/10, row 73 + 8/10 (locates a point)
- Common errors that lose marks
  - northing before easting (the classic)
  - giving grid lines when the question wants the square, or vice versa
  - misreading the grid numbers — they only print on the edge; count from the labelled line, not from the paper's edge
- Always give all six figures unless the question says otherwise — a four-figure answer to a six-figure question is a mark lost.
chunks.heading: 2. Grid reference — eastings first, always

chunks.text:
- Grid north (grid lines) ≠ true north (north arrow) ≠ magnetic north (compass) — on HK sheets the difference is small but the question loves asking which is which.
- Bearing: measure from north, clockwise, 000°–360°. Report to the nearest degree or 10° as asked.
chunks.heading: 3. Direction

chunks.text:
1. Exact grid reference (eastings first, right number of figures)
2. Feature named in the map's own language (its conventional sign)
3. What that position/feature implies (direction, distance, relationship)
chunks.heading: Answer structure (3 marks)

chunks.text: - Eastings/northings swapped · 4-figure when 6 asked · naming the sign without interpreting it · describing colour instead of pattern
chunks.heading: Marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Give a 6-figure reference for a point 7/10 across square 6148.
2. Why does a bridge sign tell you more than a river sign about crossing cost?
3. Which is north: grid, true, or magnetic — and where would you find each?
4. A question asks for the direction of a hill from a pier: which north do you use?
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

docs.title: M2 Scale and Map Measurement (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/Map and GIS/Concepts/M2 Scale and Map Measurement (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Distance, direction and area questions are the marks you either take in seconds or give away through a unit slip. The 2027 framework explicitly allows local topographic maps at 1:20,000 and 1:5,000 — scale fluency on those two numbers is assumed.
chunks.heading: M2 — Scale and Map Measurement

chunks.text:
| Form | Example | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| Statement | "1 cm represents 200 m" | plain language |
| Representative fraction (RF) | 1:20,000 | same unit both sides — 1 cm on paper = 20,000 cm = 200 m on ground |
| Linear/bar scale | a printed ruler | read distance off it directly |

Conversions to know cold: 1 km = 100,000 cm · 1 m = 100 cm · 1:20,000 → 1 cm = 200 m = 0.2 km · 1:5,000 → 1 cm = 50 m.
chunks.heading: 1. The three ways scale is written

chunks.text:
- Straight line: measure with a ruler, convert with the RF.
- Curved/irregular (river, road, path): three methods —
  1. String laid along the curve, then straighten and measure
  2. Strip of paper marked at start and finish, matching the curve
  3. Count small squares on graph paper
- Along a route (road + footpath): measure each segment, add first, convert last — converting each piece and rounding early accumulates error.
- Real distance ≠ straight-line distance: a question about walking time needs the route distance and the slope, not the map's straight line.
chunks.heading: 2. Distance

chunks.text:
- Use the grid lines for bearings; measure from north, clockwise.
- Report as three figures: `045°`, `270°`. If asked for the compass point, convert (`045°` = NE).
- "In which direction does the river flow?" — follow the gradient, i.e. from closely spaced contours to widely spaced, and check which way it reaches the sea.
chunks.heading: 3. Direction

chunks.text:
- Count grid squares: each 1 cm² grid at 1:20,000 = 200 m × 200 m = 0.04 km² (4 ha); at 1:5,000 each 1 cm² = 50 m × 50 m = 0.0025 km².
- Estimate partial squares: usually count any half or more as one, ignore the rest — state that you did it.
- Convert only at the end: area scales with the square of the linear scale factor (1:20,000 → 1:10,000 doubles lengths but quadruples area per map cm²).
chunks.heading: 4. Area

chunks.text: `gradient = vertical difference ÷ horizontal distance × 100%` (or as 1 in N). Take the horizontal distance measured on the ground, not along the slope.
chunks.heading: 5. Slope / gradient

chunks.text:
1. Method stated (how you measured: ruler, string, squares)
2. Map distance with units → conversion step shown → ground answer with units
3. Sense check: does 1.4 km match what the map looks like? (Graders reward a plausible answer with working; a unit-slip answer with no check is the classic lost mark.)
chunks.heading: Answer structure (3–4 marks)

chunks.text: - cm ↔ m ↔ km slips · dividing by the scale instead of multiplying · squaring the wrong way for area · using route distance where straight-line was asked (or vice versa)
chunks.heading: Marks lost

chunks.text:
1. A path measures 6.3 cm on 1:20,000. Ground distance?
2. Why does 1:5,000 show four times the area per cm² compared with 1:10,000?
3. A road is 9.8 cm of curve. Describe two ways to measure it without a flexible ruler.
4. Gradient falls 120 m over 600 m horizontal — express it two ways.
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

docs.title: M3 Contours and Landform Profiles (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/Map and GIS/Concepts/M3 Contours and Landform Profiles (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Contours are how the paper asks about relief without a photo. Every landform answer ("why is this slope unstable", "where would a village site") reduces to reading spacing, shape and elevation.
chunks.heading: M3 — Contours and Landform Profiles

chunks.text:
- A contour joins points of equal height above mean sea level.
- Contour interval is fixed per map (state it before answering) — index contours are thicker and labelled.
- Spacing = gradient: close together = steep; far apart = gentle.
- Shape = landform: contours form characteristic patterns.
chunks.heading: 1. The basics

chunks.text:
| Pattern | Landform |
|---|---|
| Concentric closed loops, heights rising inward | hill / peak |
| Closed loops, heights falling inward | depression (with hachures) |
| V shape pointing upstream when crossing a valley | river valley (the V-rule) |
| V shape pointing downhill | ridge |
| Two peaks with a contour saddle between | saddle / col |
| Contours nearly touching on a slope | cliff / very steep slope |
| Smooth, widely spaced, broad | gentle slope / plain |
| Interlocking spurs | alternating ridges — the river winds around them |
| Waterfall | steep drop where a hard rock band crosses the channel (contours bunch, then a break) |
chunks.heading: 2. Patterns you must recognise

chunks.text:
1. Draw the baseline along the transect line, label the start and end points.
2. Mark a vertical scale (e.g. 1 cm = 20 m) — exaggerate if needed, but say you did and by how much.
3. Drop each contour crossing onto the profile at its height; connect smoothly.
4. Label the landforms (ridge, valley, footslope) and annotate steep/gentle sections.
chunks.heading: 3. Reading a profile (cross-section)

chunks.text: `gradient = (height difference) ÷ (horizontal distance)`. Two traps: using the slope length instead of horizontal, and mixing units (convert both to metres first).
chunks.heading: 4. Gradient calculation

chunks.text:
1. Read it: "contours are 50 m apart here versus 200 m apart there" (quote numbers)
2. Name it: steep slope / valley floor / ridge — with the landform term
3. Explain why: rock resistance, river erosion at the valley floor, weathering on the cliff
4. Link to consequence: drainage, slope stability, route choice, settlement — the geography, not just the shape
chunks.heading: Answer structure (4–5 marks)

chunks.text: - Describing without numbers ("steep" with no contour spacing) · forgetting the V-rule direction · drawing a profile without a vertical scale · using slope length for gradient
chunks.heading: Marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Where does a river cross contours in a V, which way does the V point?
2. Two slopes both rise 200 m; one uses 2 cm, the other 8 cm of map — compare gradients.
3. What does a saddle between two peaks suggest for a footpath route?
4. Draw the profile of a transect and label the steepest quarter.
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

docs.title: M4 Map and Fieldwork Data Handling (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/Map and GIS/Concepts/M4 Map and Fieldwork Data Handling (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Section B (fieldwork-based, 15%) and Section C (data/skill-based, 30%) both pay you for the same two moves: pick the right presentation, then read evidence out of it. The command word is usually "describe" (the pattern) then "explain" (the reason).
chunks.heading: M4 — Map and Fieldwork Data Handling

chunks.text:
| Data type | Best choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Comparison of categories (land use in 4 zones) | bar chart (or pie if parts of one whole) | shows size of each category |
| Change over time (temperature through a day) | line graph | shows trend and rate |
| Relationship between two variables (slope vs velocity) | scatter diagram | shows correlation, outliers |
| Distribution along a transect (velocity across a river) | bar or line on the transect | keeps position |
| Percentages of one whole (land use %) | pie or stacked bar | composition |
| Small data set, exact values needed (table of readings) | table (+ median/quartiles) | precision |
| Field notes/photos of a feature | annotated sketch or photo with labels | context |

Rule: the graph must answer the question the marks ask. A pie chart for time series, or a bar chart for correlation, loses the mark before you write anything.
chunks.heading: 1. Choosing the presentation — match it to the data

chunks.text:
- Title states what and where ("Velocity at cross-section A, Ng Tung River, 12 Oct 2026")
- Axis labels with units; scale starts at zero for bar charts (not for line graphs of temperature — say why)
- Even, readable scale intervals; bars same width with equal gaps (histograms: no gaps)
- Points plotted accurately; scatter: plot then draw the line of best fit (not through every point)
- Area graphs: draw the profile, then shade between line and axis
chunks.heading: 2. Drawing it — the checklist graders use

chunks.text:
- Describe (the pattern): give the trend with numbers — "velocity peaks at 0.9 m/s at the centre, falling to 0.2 m/s at the banks", "the curve rises steeply to 14:00 then levels".
- Explain (the reason): channel width, bed roughness, gradient, shading, cloud cover — one cause per data feature.
- Compare: use the words higher/lower, steeper/flatter, earlier/later, more variable, each with a figure for both cases.
- Reliability (a standard 4-marker): repeat readings and average, same method at each site, instrument calibration, enough sample points, timing of the survey — then say how it could be improved.
chunks.heading: 3. Reading it — describe then explain

chunks.text:
- Random (river pebbles, vegetation quadrats) — avoids bias; use numbered grid or random numbers.
- Systematic (transect across a beach) — needed when there is a gradient to detect.
- Targeted/stratified (by land-use zone) — ensures each category is represented.
- Sample size: more = more reliable, but state the practical limits; always say how you reduced bias.
chunks.heading: 4. Sampling in the field

chunks.text:
1. Name the presentation and why it fits the data type
2. Describe the pattern with figures (trend, peak, range, comparison)
3. Explain with the mechanism (physical or human)
4. If asked: reliability + one improvement
chunks.heading: Answer structure (3–5 marks)

chunks.text: - Graph without units or title · describing without numbers · explaining before describing · choosing pie for time data · percentages with no base stated
chunks.heading: Marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Which presentation for discharge measured at 5 points along a transect, and why not a pie?
2. A scatter shows a weak negative correlation — write the sentence that earns the mark.
3. Two sampling strategies for pebble size on a beach: which, and why?
4. "Explain the limitations of your data" — give two real ones.
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

docs.title: M5 GIS Concepts (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/Map and GIS/Concepts/M5 GIS Concepts (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
GIS appears wherever the paper asks "how can technology help" — data collection, analysis, presentation, decision-making. The examiner wants the vocabulary of spatial analysis (layers, overlay, buffer) used to explain a real decision, not a definition of the acronym.
chunks.heading: M5 — GIS Concepts

chunks.text: A system for capturing, storing, checking, analysing and displaying data that are tagged to a location. Key idea: everything has coordinates, so anything can be layered, compared and queried.
chunks.heading: 1. What GIS is

chunks.text:
- Hardware — computers, GPS receivers, scanners, servers
- Software — the GIS itself (ArcGIS, QGIS, free web GIS)
- Data — the heart of it: spatial (where) + attribute (what)
- People — those who build, operate and — critically — act on the analysis
chunks.heading: 2. The four components

chunks.text:
| | Vector | Raster |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | points, lines, polygons | a grid of cells (pixels) |
| Best for | boundaries, roads, buildings, sampling points | continuous surfaces: elevation, temperature, land cover, satellite imagery |
| Precision | exact coordinates | limited by cell size (resolution) |
| Storage | smaller for shapes | larger; grows with resolution |

Attribute data ride along: click a polygon → its area, land use, owner, population. Layers are the same area cut by theme (roads, contours, zoning) — stacked, they can be combined.
chunks.heading: 3. Data models: vector vs raster

chunks.text:
1. Overlay — stack two layers to find where they coincide (flood zone × housing → buildings at risk)
2. Buffer — a set distance around a feature (500 m around a school → noise-insensitive zone; 100 m from a river → no-build strip)
3. Proximity / nearest — which is nearest to what (nearest hospital to each estate)
4. Network/route — shortest or fastest path along a connected network (bus route, evacuation path)
5. Query / reclassify — ask the database a question ("which parcels are >15° slope and inside the green belt?") and reclassify cells to rank suitability

Add spatial statistics (density, clustering, correlation) when the question is about patterns.
chunks.heading: 4. Spatial analysis — the five operations that earn marks

chunks.text:
- Input: field survey with GPS, remote sensing (satellite/air photos), existing maps digitised, census/records, LiDAR, crowdsourced data
- Output: maps, 3-D views, charts, reports for decision-makers
- Error enters at input (positional accuracy, outdated records) and at classification — garbage in, garbage out.
chunks.heading: 5. Data in, answers out

chunks.text:
1. Name the operation precisely (buffer, overlay, proximity)
2. Apply it to this case with numbers ("a 100 m buffer from the river")
3. State what the combination shows (which areas/people affected)
4. Judgement: advantage over paper maps (fast, repeatable, can combine layers) plus one limitation (cost, expertise, data currency, hidden bias)
chunks.heading: Answer structure (4–5 marks)

chunks.text: - Defining GIS instead of using it · saying "computers help" without the operation's name · listing advantages with no limitation · forgetting that layer quality limits the answer
chunks.heading: Marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Siting a new clinic: name two analysis operations and the layers you would combine.
2. Raster or vector for (a) a land-use map, (b) a temperature surface, (c) bus stops?
3. What does a 30 m resolution DEM let you see that a 1 km one does not?
4. Give one way GIS output can mislead a decision-maker.
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

docs.title: M6 GIS and Remote Sensing in Hong Kong (F6 Revision)
docs.path: DSE Geography/Map and GIS/Concepts/M6 GIS and Remote Sensing in Hong Kong (F6 Revision).md

chunks.text:
Why examiners test this
Hong Kong examples turn an abstract "GIS is useful" into evidence. The paper rewards a named system, a named decision, and a limitation — all three in the same answer.
chunks.heading: M6 — GIS and Remote Sensing in Hong Kong

chunks.text:
- Definition: collecting information about an object or area without physical contact, from aircraft or satellites.
- Four resolutions to quote
  - Spatial: pixel size (30 m Landsat vs sub-metre aerial) — what you can distinguish
  - Temporal: revisit time (hours to weeks) — what you can monitor
  - Spectral: bands beyond visible (near-infrared detects healthy vegetation, thermal detects heat islands)
  - Radiometric: sensitivity to brightness difference
- Analysing it: visual interpretation (tone, texture, shape, pattern, shadow) or classification (computer groups pixels into land-cover classes).
- Advantages: coverage, repeat, speed, safe access (typhoon aftermath, fire). Limits: cloud, cost of high resolution, needs ground truth, detail ≠ meaning.
chunks.heading: 1. Remote sensing — the data feeder

chunks.text:
- CSDI (Common Spatial Data Infrastructure) — the government's shared platform: hundreds of datasets from all departments, open API, one map (data.gov.hk / portal.csdi.gov.hk). Siting, planning and research all draw on it.
- Planning Department — Base Data Analysis System / land-use records; Geographic Information Atlas; MyMapHK / Geodatamap for public enquiries
- Survey and Mapping Office — topographic mapping (the 1:20,000 / 1:5,000 sheets)
- LCSD / AFCD / Drainage Services Department — hillside safety, country-park mapping, drainage and flood-prone area mapping
- Students meet GIS directly through the GIS competition work — problem identification → data layers → analysis → recommendation (see the worksheets in the vault's `GIS/` folder).
chunks.heading: 2. GIS in Hong Kong — named systems

chunks.text:
| Need | Layers combined | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Slope risk | geology, slope gradient, rainfall, land use, population | Landslide-prone areas → slope maintenance priority |
| Urban heat island | land cover, temperature (thermal remote sensing), building density | Planting, cool roofs, open-space siting |
| Typhoon / flood response | rainfall, drainage network, low-lying terrain, photos | Drainage works, evacuation routes |
| Brownfield / rural planning | land-use change, ownership, access, slope | Suite A/B/C planning, Belt & Road? no — land-use zoning |
| Conservation | habitat maps, walking distances, development pressure | Site of Special Scientific Interest boundaries |
chunks.heading: 3. Hong Kong applications worth memorising

chunks.text:
1. System/technique named: "using GIS overlay analysis of slope and rainfall layers from CSDI"
2. Process: capture (field GPS, satellite, records) → store as layers → analyse (buffer/overlay/query) → present (map)
3. Decision it supports with a Hong Kong example (where, what changed)
4. Limitation (cost, staff skills, data currency, errors at input, technology dependence)
chunks.heading: 4. Exam answer shape

chunks.text: - "GIS uses computers" with no operation name · Hong Kong example without a place · remote sensing described as photography only · advantages with no limitation · confusing resolution with accuracy
chunks.heading: Marks lost

chunks.text:
1. Which resolution matters for detecting a new hillside failure after rain — and why?
2. Name two CSDI datasets you would combine to site a new clinic.
3. Why is ground truth needed after a land-cover classification?
4. Give one reason a GIS map of flood risk could be misleading.
chunks.heading: Quick self-check

Creditable observations (crop-verified):
1. Tin Shui Wai: farmland / fish ponds / early works (1993) → dense urban grid (2026) — unmistakable at 30 m.
2. Lau Fau Shan village expanded (built index 3.7 → 12.6 in its zone).
3. Pak Nai pond belt persists (water 26.5 → 26.2) — a valid "no change" observation.

Not creditable / excluded from any key:
- Water colour, tide line, sediment/turbidity (Dec vs Mar; whole-frame water drop is largely tide/season).
- Veg/season differences (Dec dry vs Mar spring).
- The alleged linear feature in the 2026 bay: vision QA contradicted itself across five passes (dark↔light, phantom "Shenzhen Bay Bridge" — no such structure exists); possibly aquaculture rafts or a turbidity front. Identity unconfirmed → never credit answers about it.

  5. Fish and aquatic organisms die

chunks.heading: Paper Structure

chunks.text:

chunks.heading: Factors causing high birth rates in Africa (Q1):

chunks.text:

- Death rate: Number of deaths per 1000 population per year
- Natural increase: Birth rate - Death rate

   - Low rainfall
   - Short growing season
chunks.heading: Reasons for sparse population in West China (Q6):

chunks.text:
1. Improve transport networks in rural areas
   - Connect remote areas to cities
   - Facilitate migration and trade

   - Reduce shortage

1. Provide low-interest loans

1. Eutrophication

docs.path: F3 Geography/F3 Kahoot drill - landslides forces HK relief map reading (parallel).md

chunks.text:
Build rule (your standing): no stems / places / numbers / photos from the actual V1 paper. The 25 items below test the same four topic blocks (landslide concept, shear stress vs strength, management, HK relief + map reading) using fresh wording. Suitable for any F3 cohort.
For the teacher: all distractors carry a teaching note — read the "why this distractor" line in the answer key before running the game.
Kahoot import: each question is ≤ 80 characters (Kahoot's hard limit on the question text). 4 options, answer positions are deliberately rotated.
chunks.heading: F3 First Term Test 2026-27 — Kahoot drill (parallel, not from paper)

chunks.text:
Q1. (concepts)
Which of the following is always required for a slope to fail as a landslide?
	- A) Heavy rain lasting at least 24 hours
	- B) An earthquake within 100 km
	- C) Shear stress greater than shear strength  ✅
	- D) Human activity somewhere on the slope

Q2. (concepts)
A "natural hazard" becomes a "disaster" when:
- A) The hazard occurs at night
- B) The harm to people, property or economy actually happens  ✅
- C) The government issues a warning
- D) The slope is steeper than 30°

Q3. (HK context)
Which two natural hazards have actually caused deaths in Hong Kong in the past 20 years?
- A) Typhoons and floods  ✅
- B) Earthquakes and landslides
- C) Volcanic eruptions and droughts
- D) Tsunamis and locust plagues

Q4. (concepts)
Compared to a "natural hazard", a "natural disaster" places greater weight on:
- A) The cause being a natural event
- B) The severity of the trigger event
- C) Whether harm to people or property actually occurs  ✅
- D) Whether the event was forecast

Q5. (concepts)
"Elements at risk" from a landslide include all of the following EXCEPT:
- A) Houses on the slope
- B) Roads and pavements below
- C) Crops on adjacent farmland
- D) The shear strength of the rock at depth  ✅
chunks.heading: Game 1 — Concepts (Q1–5)

chunks.text:
Q6. (forces)
Adding water to a slope during prolonged rain decreases the slope's:
- A) Shear stress
- B) Shear strength  ✅
- C) Gradient
- D) Weight

Q7. (forces)
A retaining wall primarily acts on a slope by:
- A) Lowering the water table inside the slope
- B) Adding to the slope's shear strength so the mass resists movement  ✅
- C) Making the gradient gentler
- D) Warning residents of pending failure

Q8. (forces)
Steepening a cut slope (e.g. for a new road) increases the risk of failure because:
- A) It lowers the water table
- B) It increases the down-slope pull on the slope materials, raising shear stress  ✅
- C) It removes vegetation
- D) It cools the rock surface

Q9. (forces)
Which combination of changes most increases the chance of failure?
- A) ↑ stress and ↑ strength
- B) ↓ stress and ↓ strength
- C) ↑ stress and ↓ strength  ✅
- D) No change in either force

Q10. (forces)
A drainage channel on a slope face reduces failure risk by:
- A) Holding the soil back like a wall
- B) Removing rainwater before it can add weight and reduce friction  ✅
- C) Smoothing the slope face
- D) Cooling the rock surface
chunks.heading: Game 2 — Shear stress vs strength (Q6–10)

chunks.text:
Q11. (management)
Which of the following is a preventive engineering measure?
- A) Soil nails with shotcrete cover  ✅
- B) Helicopter rescue of trapped residents
- C) Distribution of emergency shelters
- D) Insurance payouts to affected families

Q12. (management)
The HKO Landslip Warning Signal is best described as:
- A) Remedial — it is issued only after a slide has occurred
- B) Preventive — it cuts exposure to risk before a slide happens  ✅
- C) Engineering — it is built into the slope
- D) Remunerative — it pays for damages

Q13. (management)
A "flexible (debris-flow) barrier" is built at:
- A) The top of a hill, to catch rainfall
- B) The slope toe or in a gully below, to catch moving debris  ✅
- C) Inside the building foundation
- D) The river mouth

Q14. (management)
A retaining wall and a surface drainage channel are different because the wall:
- A) Holds back soil and rock; the channel drains off excess water  ✅
- B) Drains off excess water; the channel holds back soil
- C) Both drain water but in different directions
- D) Both hold back soil but at different heights

Q15. (management)
Clearing loose rock debris from a slope face after a failure is best classified as:
- A) Preventive engineering
- B) Preventive non-structural
- C) Remedial  ✅
- D) Forecasting
chunks.heading: Game 3 — Management: preventive vs remedial (Q11–16)

chunks.text:
Q16. (management)
Restricting building development on slopes steeper than a stated gradient is an example of:
- A) Engineering prevention
- B) Non-structural prevention (planning)  ✅
- C) Remedial action
- D) Insurance
chunks.heading: Game 3 — Management: preventive vs remedial (Q11–16)

chunks.text:
Q17. (HK relief)
The tallest natural peak in Hong Kong is:
- A) Victoria Peak
- B) Lantau Peak
- C) Sunset Peak
- D) Tai Mo Shan  ✅

Q18. (HK relief)
Most of Hong Kong's natural lowlands (river plains and coastal flats) are found in:
- A) Hong Kong Island
- B) Kowloon
- C) The northern and central New Territories  ✅
- D) Lantau Island

Q19. (HK relief)
The sides of Victoria Harbour are not considered natural lowlands because:
- A) The slopes are too steep
- B) Most of the lowland has been reclaimed from the sea  ✅
- C) They are above 500 m
- D) They are made of granite

Q20. (map reading — gradient)
A slope rises 80 m over a horizontal distance of 1.6 km. What is the gradient, expressed as 1 : n?
- A) 1 : 20
- B) 1 : 20,000  ✅
- C) 1 : 80,000
- D) 1 : 200

Q21. (map reading — vertical exaggeration)
A map cross-section is drawn with horizontal scale 1 : 20,000 and vertical scale 1 cm = 50 m. What is the vertical exaggeration?

VE= v. scale/ h. scale
=  1: 5000 / 1:20000
= 1:5000 x 20000/1
= 4

- A) 0.4×
- B) 2×
- C) 10×  ✅
- D) 50×

The point 25 metres east and 80 metres north of grid square 813427 lies at:

- A) Title only
- B) Title and axes only

- D) Title and one contour

Q24. (map reading — intervisibility)
Two hilltops A (300 m) and B (250 m) are 4 km apart. A point on the line between them reaches 280 m. Are A and B intervisible?
- A) Yes — both points are above the line

Use this game after the standard 25-Q Kahoot. The questions assume students already know the basic concepts; here they have to apply, compare, justify, and calculate under time pressure. Each item is calibrated to the 70–90% mark band — easy marks have been cut, distractors are close, and several items require two-step reasoning.

Two corrections to apply before running (caught at the QA pass): see the foot-of-file notes.
chunks.heading: F3 First Term Test 2026-27 — Hard-mode Kahoot drill (parallel, not from paper)

chunks.text:
Q1. (paired concept — pick the better answer)
Which pair of statements is both correct?
- A) A hazard is a natural event and a disaster is a natural event.
- B) A hazard may cause harm and a disaster is harm that has occurred.  ✅
- C) A hazard always kills someone and a disaster is a forecast.
- D) A hazard is human-caused and a disaster is natural.

Q2. (classification trap)
The HKO announces a Typhoon Signal No. 8 in advance of a tropical cyclone reaching Hong Kong. Is this announcement a "natural hazard", a "disaster", or "neither"?
- A) A natural hazard — the signal itself is dangerous.
- B) A disaster — it warns of harm.
- C) Neither — the signal is a forecast response, not a hazard or disaster.  ✅
- D) Both — the signal is a hazard and a disaster at once.

Q3. (definition in context — pick the strict textbook definition)
Which of the following is the most precise definition of a landslide?
- A) When soil moves a long way.
- B) When a slope collapses and material moves down-slope under gravity.  ✅
- C) When any rock falls anywhere.
- D) When rain soaks into the ground.
chunks.heading: Game 1 — Concepts at exam depth (Q1–5)

chunks.text:
Q4. (paired facts)
Which combination is both correct for Hong Kong?
- A) Natural terrain covers about 30% of HK and ~100 landslides a year on natural terrain.
- B) Natural terrain covers about 60% of HK and ~300 landslides a year on natural terrain.  ✅
- C) Natural terrain covers about 80% of HK and ~3,000 landslides a year on natural terrain.
- D) Natural terrain covers about 95% of HK and landslides are not a major hazard.

Q5. (multi-step concept)
A slope has shear stress = 120 kPa and shear strength = 95 kPa. Which statement is correct?
- A) The slope is stable — both forces are below 200 kPa.
- B) The slope is stable — stress is below strength.
- C) The slope is unstable — stress exceeds strength by 25 kPa.  ✅
- D) The slope is unstable — strength exceeds stress by 25 kPa.
chunks.heading: Game 1 — Concepts at exam depth (Q1–5)

chunks.text:
Q6. (two-cause problem)
Heavy prolonged rain affects a slope in two ways. Which pair captures both?
- A) ↑ gradient and ↓ weight.
- B) ↑ cohesion and ↑ friction.
- C) ↑ stress (water weight) and ↓ strength (water in pores loosens grains).  ✅
- D) ↑ strength and ↓ stress.

Q7. (quantitative: stress vs strength with management)
A slope has stress 80 kPa, strength 60 kPa. A retaining wall is built. The wall adds 30 kPa of effective strength. After the wall, the slope is:
- A) Still unstable — 80 > 60 + 30 is false, so unstable.
- B) Stable — 80 < (60 + 30) = 90.  ✅
- C) Unstable — walls never work.
- D) Cannot tell — the values must be in the same units.

Q8. (cause-into-force language — the essay skill)
"Weathered granite with open joints" affects a slope by:
- A) ↑ stress from the joints themselves.
- B) ↓ strength because the joints allow water in and reduce cohesion.  ✅
- C) ↑ strength because the joints bind the rock.
- D) No effect — only rain matters.

Q9. (vegetation removal — two reasons)
Removing vegetation from a slope increases landslide risk because:
- A) Roots no longer bind the soil and throughfall replaces interception, so more water enters the slope.  ✅
- B) The colour of bare soil absorbs more heat.
- C) The slope looks ugly to people.
- D) Vegetation removal always reduces stress.
chunks.heading: Game 2 — Forces in non-routine scenarios (Q6–10)

chunks.text:
Q10. (unusual cause — man-made slope failure)
Many older Hong Kong slopes fail because they were built "below standard" — too steep, no drainage, weak fill. This means:
- A) ↑ stress (steep gradient) and ↓ strength (weak fill, water can get in).  ✅
- B) ↓ stress and ↑ strength.
- C) The slopes were built to international standard.
- D) Standard is irrelevant if it rains.
chunks.heading: Game 2 — Forces in non-routine scenarios (Q6–10)

chunks.text:
Q11. (sort into the right bucket — pick the odd one out)
Which is the only engineering-preventive measure in the list?
- A) Soil nails with shotcrete cover.  ✅
- B) Distribution of emergency shelters.
- C) Helicopter rescue teams.
- D) Insurance payouts.

Q12. (sort into the right bucket — pick the only non-structural preventive measure)
- A) Soil nails.
- B) Retaining wall.
- C) GEO inspection and maintenance programme.  ✅
- D) Rock debris clearing after a slide.

Q13. (force changed — pick the right match)
Soil nails with shotcrete cover on a cut slope:
- A) ↓ stress by removing water.
- B) ↑ strength by binding surface material and stopping water ingress.  ✅
- C) ↑ stress by adding mass to the slope.
- D) ↓ gradient by re-profiling.

Q14. (force changed — drainage)
A surface drainage channel on a cut slope primarily:
- A) ↑ stress and ↑ strength.
- B) ↓ stress only.
- C) ↑ strength only.
- D) ↓ stress (removes water weight) and ↑ strength (less water in pores, cohesion/friction intact).  ✅

Q15. (force changed — flexible barrier)
A flexible (debris-flow) barrier at a slope toe primarily works by:
- A) Adding shear strength to the slope.
- B) Lowering the water table.
- C) Catching the debris that comes down — so it reduces exposure rather than acting on the slope forces.  ✅
- D) Re-profiling the slope.
chunks.heading: Game 3 — Management: trickier classifications (Q11–16)

chunks.text:
Q16. (combined-strategy judgment)
A slope is being managed with: soil nails, drainage channels, regrading the slope gentler, restricting further development on similar slopes, and the HKO warning signal. Which is most likely the judgement a top-mark essay would draw?
- A) Soil nails alone are sufficient.
- B) The HKO warning alone is sufficient.
- C) A combination is most effective because each measure acts on a different force (stress, strength, exposure).  ✅
- D) Restricting development is irrelevant.
chunks.heading: Game 3 — Management: trickier classifications (Q11–16)

Q17. (HK relief — peak list)
Hong Kong's three tallest natural peaks, in order from highest to lowest, are:
- A) Tai Mo Shan · Lantau Peak · Sunset Peak.  ✅
- B) Lantau Peak · Tai Mo Shan · Victoria Peak.
- C) Victoria Peak · Sunset Peak · Tai Mo Shan.
- D) Tai Mo Shan · Victoria Peak · Lantau Peak.
