The northern New Territories has more natural lowland than Hong Kong Island because:
- A) The underlying rock is harder.
- B) The northern NT has wide river plains and narrow coastal flats, while HK Island is mostly hilly.  ✅
- C) The northern NT is closer to the sea.
- D) It rains more in the north.

Q19. (reclaimed vs natural lowland — paired answer)
Which pair of statements is both correct?
- A) HK Island is mostly lowland and Kowloon's harbour sides are mostly natural lowland.
- B) HK Island is mostly hilly and most of the harbour sides have been reclaimed.  ✅
- C) HK Island is mostly reclaimed and the NT has no natural lowland.
- D) HK Island is mostly hilly and the harbour sides are mostly natural lowland.

On a fully annotated cross-section worth 5 marks, the marks are awarded for:
- A) Title and shape only.
- B) Title, shape, and one label.
- C) Title (1), vertical scale (1), correct shape (3).  ✅

Q24. (map reading — intervisibility calculation)
A (300 m) and B (200 m) are 6 km apart. The line of sight between them passes over a 280 m ridge 4 km from A. Are A and B intervisible?
- A) Yes — both points are above the ridge.
- B) Yes — the ridge is below A.
- C) No — the ridge (280 m) is above the line of sight at that point (≈ 233 m), so it blocks the view.  ✅
- D) Cannot tell — the data is incomplete.

Q25. (map reading — scale conversion with a step in km)
On a 1 : 25,000 map, the road from grid ref 615493 to 655513 measures 12.8 cm. What is the ground distance?

chunks.heading: Game 4 — HK relief + harder map reading (Q17–25)

chunks.text:
Q21 (instructor's note): I drafted the answer as B (2×) but the correct VE is 5×. A 1:50,000 map means 1 cm = 500 m; vertical scale 1 cm = 100 m; so 500 ÷ 100 = 5×. Replace option B with "5×" and keep A/C/D as the wrong distractors. The same "didn't recalculate every option" slip that hit the first Kahoot — apologies.
Q20 (instructor's note): the unit conversion is correct in the answer key, but a student reading the option "1 : 10" could be tempted to think that's right (the simple division 2,000 ÷ 200 = 10). The right form is the unitless ratio 1 : 10,000. If you want to remove that trap, replace option A with "1 : 10 m" (a wrong unit) and keep C as the answer.

chunks.text:
OB1-Hard. (12 marks — map reading + numerical application)
A 1 : 25,000 map extract shows contours every 25 m. A proposed road runs from grid reference 615493 to 655513. Measured on the map, the road is 12.8 cm long.
(a) State the scale in sentence form. (1)
(b) Convert the road length to ground distance, showing workings. (2)
(c) The road rises from 50 m to 280 m. Calculate the average gradient as 1 : n. (2)
(d) Calculate the vertical exaggeration if a cross-section is drawn with vertical scale 1 cm = 50 m. (2)
(e) A student says: "this road is too steep for normal traffic." Suggest a non-engineering change that would reduce the gradient along the same route, and explain why. (2)
(f) Identify one force affected by your change in (e) and explain the mechanism. (3)

OB2-Hard. (6-mark essay, parallel to Section D — command-word traps)
"Using the language of shear stress and shear strength, suggest and explain three engineering measures that could be applied to a single cut slope in Hong Kong to reduce the risk of failure. For each measure, name the force it changes, and describe the mechanism by which it does so. Conclude with a judgement: are these measures best used together, or is one of them sufficient on its own?" (6 marks)
chunks.heading: Two open question-bank items (harder, parallel to OB1/OB2 in the standard game)

chunks.text:
Mark scheme:
- Frame (1): defines stress > strength as failure condition.
- Three measures × (1 mark each) = 3: each correctly names force (e.g. soil nails → ↑ strength) and gives a one-sentence mechanism.
- Conclusion (1): combination best; explains why (different levers).
- Judgement (1): explicit statement of which measure is most effective for this slope, with reason.

chunks.heading: Part 1 — Map reading skills (15 marks + 6 MCQs)

chunks.text:
0 · Natural hazards — the concept (definition · types · distribution):

What is a natural hazard?

| Term | Meaning (say it this way) |
|---|---|
| Natural hazard | a natural event — not caused by people — that may harm people, buildings, crops or the economy |
| Disaster | what the hazard becomes when the harm actually happens: people hurt, things destroyed |
| Elements at risk | whatever could be damaged: people, houses, roads, crops, shops |

Same event, two outcomes: heavy rain hitting empty hillsides = hazard only · heavy rain above crowded, badly built housing = disaster.

Types of natural hazards — four types (as in the textbook):

| Type | What happens | Members |
|---|---|---|
| Geological | the ground itself gives way or moves | landslide · debris flow · subsidence |
| Tectonic | the Earth's crust shakes or erupts | earthquake · volcano · tsunami |
| Meteorological | extreme weather — wind, rain, stormy sea | typhoon · flood · storm surge · drought |
| Biological | living things cause the harm | epidemic / spreading disease · locust plagues |

Hong Kong's own set: typhoons (meteorological), floods (meteorological), landslides (geological) — which is why the rest of this pack drills landslides.

Distribution — where hazards happen, and why:
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
| Hazard                  | Common here                                                                                     | Why                                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Earthquakes & volcanoes | Pacific "Ring of Fire" (Japan, W. Pacific margin, W. USA, Chile) · Mediterranean–Himalayan belt | they sit along plate boundaries, where plates collide or pull apart |
| Typhoons                | tropical oceans — especially the NW Pacific (SE Asia, S China coast)                        | warm tropical seas spin small storms into typhoons                      |
| Floods & landslides     | monsoon Asia (S China, India) · steep slopes anywhere, incl. HK                                 | heavy seasonal rain saturates the ground until it gives way             |

One-line rule for students: hazards cluster where their causes are — plate boundaries, warm seas, heavy rain on steep ground.

Taught as one causal chain, not two lists:

stress vs strength → balance tips → causes → management = deliberately tipping it back

a · The two forces (definitions cold — the DBQ sets its causal vocabulary in these words):
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
|            | Shear stress                                                          | Shear strength                                                      |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| What it is | the pull of the slope's own materials downslope                       | the slope's resistance to that pull                                 |
| Comes from | slope gradient · weight of soil, water, buildings on the slope            | cohesion (grains sticking together) · friction (grains rubbing) |
| The rule   | failure when stress > strength — this one line opens the 6-mark essay | management = raise strength, lower stress, or both at once              |

b · Causes in that language (the DBQ's causal vocabulary — every cause translated into forces):
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
| Cause | Mechanism (what physically happens) | Balance effect |
|---|---|---|
| Heavy / prolonged rain | water fills pore spaces → adds weight; lubricates grains → loosens them | ↑ stress AND ↓ strength (↓ cohesion, ↓ friction) |
| Weathered granite | decomposed rock + open joints lose cohesion | ↓ strength |
| Steep or cut slope | steeper gradient → larger downslope component of the weight | ↑ stress |
| Vegetation removal | roots no longer bind soil; throughfall replaces interception → more water into the slope | ↓ strength |
| Poor maintenance | blocked drains / seepage → water ingress at the slope face | ↑ stress AND ↓ strength |

The measure table (fixes the essay gap — every row names the force it changes):
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
| Strategy | Force it changes | Where used | Type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Soil nails / shotcrete | ↑ strength (bonds surface, stops water ingress) | strengthened slopes | preventive (engineering) |
| Retaining wall | ↑ strength (holds back soil & rock) | rural / cut slopes | preventive (engineering) |
| Drainage + surface channels, weep holes | ↓ stress (removes water weight) and ↑ strength (friction/cohesion intact) | urban slopes / slope face | preventive (engineering) |
| Flexible (debris-flow) barrier | stops downslope impact | slope toe / gully | preventive (engineering) |
| Regrading / terracing | ↓ gradient ⇒ ↓ stress (flattens the slope the weight acts on) | cut slopes, road alignments | preventive (engineering) |
| Planting & turfing the slope face | ↑ strength (roots bind the surface) + intercepts rain before it enters the soil | restored cuts, slope faces | preventive (engineering) |
| Restrict development on steep slopes, risk assessment | ↓ gradient/weight ⇒ ↓ stress | planning | preventive (non-structural) |
| GEO / Lands Dept inspection & maintenance | keeps strength from deteriorating | territory-wide | preventive (non-structural) |
| HKO landslide warning + education | reduce exposure ⇒ minimises damage | territory-wide | preventive (non-structural) |
| Clearing rock debris, rescue teams, shelters, insurance | after failure ⇒ minimise losses | affected area | remedial |
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
Sorting exercise — three buckets; the test question is when does it act?

| Bucket | Test question | Members |
|---|---|---|
| Engineering preventive | built before failure, physically stops movement? | soil nails · shotcrete · retaining wall · drainage / channels / weep holes · flexible barrier · regrading · turfing |
| Non-structural preventive | rules & upkeep only — nothing built? | restrict steep-slope development · risk assessment · GEO / Lands Dept inspection & maintenance · HKO warning + education |
| Remedial | only after failure, to limit losses? | clearing rock debris · rescue teams · shelters · insurance |

Case block — 18 June 1972 Mid-Levels (Po Shan):

| | |
|---|---|
| Trigger | 652.3 mm of rain in 3 days |
| Destruction | Kotewall Court (12 storeys) destroyed |
| Losses | 67 deaths / 19 injured — worst in HK history |
| Why it failed | weathered granite + steep slope + below-standard man-made slopes |
| Use in the paper | evidence phrases students can quote in (b)(ii)/(iii) |

Modern statistics (read the cause, not the coincidence):
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
| Trend | Correct reading (✔) | Trap reading (✘) |
|---|---|---|
| Summer (May–Sept) concentration | failures cluster in the wet season — intense rain is the trigger | "rain alone causes landslides" (strength & gradient must be there too) |
| Deaths falling decade by decade | because of GEO inspection, better slope standards and the warning signal | "fewer deaths = less rainfall" |
| Where the damage lands | mainly roads and pavements now — disruption, not fatalities | "landslides are no longer serious" |

Four misconception items drilled explicitly:

| ❌ Not this                       | ✅ Because                                                               |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| a retaining wall is remedial     | it is preventive — built before failure to hold soil back         |
| the landslip warning is remedial | it is preventive — cuts exposure before failure happens           |
| "fewer deaths = less rainfall"   | deaths fell because of inspection, standards and the warning signal |
| surface channel = wall           | surface channel drains water away; wall holds back soil & rock  |

6-mark essay plan — one line per step, 6 steps for 6 marks:
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
| Line | Write | Why it earns |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Define: a slope fails when shear stress > shear strength | sets the frame in force language |
| 2 | Strategy 1 — name the force it changes (e.g. drainage ⇒ ↓ stress) | "each naming the force" = where the marks are |
| 3 | Strategy 2 — name its force (e.g. soil nails ⇒ ↑ strength) | same rule |
| 4 | Strategy 3 — name its force (e.g. restrict steep-slope development ⇒ ↓ stress) | same rule |
| 5 | Minimising damage: warning, evacuation, shelters, insurance | covers the remedial side |
| 6 | Short judgement: most effective = a combination | closes with a judgement |
chunks.heading: Part 2 — Landslide management (19-mark DBQ + 6-mark essay)

chunks.text:
- Identify — name only, no reason.
- Describe — what the pattern/data does; give the figure.
- Explain — why, with mechanism + evidence.
- Calculate … show your workings — formula, substitution, answer with unit/ratio.
- Support with evidence — quote a number/figure from the source.
- Suggest — any reasonable idea is creditable.
- Evaluate — weigh up and reach a judgement.
- Rule for students: "describe" answers lose marks when the verb is "explain".
chunks.heading: Task words (what each demands)

chunks.text:
| Command word                                     | What it demands (say it this way)                                      | Answer starter                                                                | Marks     |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------- |
| State / Name / List / Identify               | one fact — no reason needed                                            | just the word or phrase                                                       | 1         |
| Define                                       | one-sentence meaning with the key words in it                          | "A landslide is …"                                                          | 1         |
| From Figure/Table … , how much …? (read off) | quote the value with its unit, "about" if read between marks       | "About 35 km"                                                                 | 1         |
| Describe (pattern / trend / figure / table)  | WHAT it does: direction, start & end values, steepest bit — no why | "It rises steadily from 20 to 60, steepest after 1990"                        | 2–3       |
| Describe how … changes with … (graph)        | the trend plus where it changes direction                          | "Increases to a peak in 1995, then falls"                                     | 2–3       |
| Explain / Why / Give reasons                 | WHY: mechanism, then link back to the data                             | "… because …, as shown by …"                                              | 2–3       |
| Compare (and contrast)                       | both places, same criterion, difference/similarity words               | "While A …, B …"                                                              | 2–3       |
| What is the relationship between X and Y?    | direction (positive/negative) + strength + one data point              | "As X increases, Y also increases — a strong positive relationship (20 → 60)" | 2         |
| Calculate … (show your workings)             | formula → substitution → answer with unit                          | "45 ÷ 1.5 = 30 km/h"                                                          | 1–2       |
| Suggest / Give possible reasons              | any plausible idea — creditable if reasonable                      | "Possibly …"                                                                  | 1–2       |
| Support with evidence / Use the data         | every point carries a number quoted from the source                    | "… (Table 1: 62%)"                                                            | per point |
chunks.heading: DBQ question words (Section C — what the 19 marks are asking for)

chunks.text:
Five rules that cost marks when broken:
1. Describe = what, Explain = why — the most common lost marks.
2. Every "support with evidence" point quotes a number or names the figure it came from.
3. No workings = no mark: formula, substitution, answer + unit, in that order.
4. Values read off a chart get "about / approximately" — never false precision.
5. The command word sets the depth: state (1 mark) → describe (2–3) → explain (2–3) → evaluate/judgement (top of the range).
chunks.heading: DBQ question words (Section C — what the 19 marks are asking for)

docs.title: F3 Geography - Living with Natural Hazards

chunks.text: Landslides are the collapse of slopes. They occur when a mass of soils and rock moves down a slope rapidly due to gravity.
chunks.heading: Definition:

chunks.text:
- In Hong Kong, natural terrain covers about 60% of total land area
- Each year, about 300 landslides occur on natural terrain
- Some landslides occur on man-made slopes in built-up areas
chunks.heading: Key Facts:

chunks.text:
| English | Chinese |
|---------|---------|
| Landslide | 山泥傾瀉 |
| Gravity | 重力 |
| Natural terrain | 天然山坡 |
| Man-made slope | 人造斜坡 |
| Built-up area | 建成區 |
chunks.heading: Key Terms:

chunks.text:
| Effect | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| Injuries & Deaths | People can be hurt or killed |
| Building damage | Buildings may be buried or knocked down |
| Infrastructure damage | Water pipes, gas pipes, power lines damaged |
| Service disruption | Supply of water, gas, electricity cut off |
| Traffic disruption | Roads blocked, traffic stopped |

chunks.text:

chunks.heading: Case Studies in Hong Kong:

chunks.text:
DSE Terminology:

| English | Chinese |
|---------|---------|
| Shear stress | 剪切力 |
| Shear strength | 抗剪切力 |

Stable slope: Shear strength > Shear stress

Unstable slope: Shear stress > Shear strength
chunks.heading: Slope Stability Concept:

chunks.text:
Factors that push slope materials down:

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Steep slope gradient | Larger gradient = greater shear stress |
| Weight of materials | Heavier materials = greater tendency to fall |
| Rainwater | Adds weight to slope |
chunks.heading: Shear Stress (剪切力) / Driving Force (驅動力):

chunks.text:
Factors that resist movement:

| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Cohesion (內聚力) | Force that causes soil grains to stick together |
| Friction (摩擦力) | Resistance between soil grains |
| Vegetation roots | Hold soil together |

When shear strength decreases → slope becomes unstable
chunks.heading: Shear Strength (抗剪切力) / Resisting Force (抗力):

chunks.text:
- Most landslides occur in wet summer months
- Heavy rainfall:
  - Adds weight to slope materials
  - Reduces cohesion (water separates soil particles)
  - Reduces friction
  - Result: Resisting force decreases → landslide
chunks.heading: 1. Heavy Rainfall

chunks.text:
- Weathering = wearing away/breakdown of rocks
- Caused by: rain, temperature changes, natural processes
- Result: Hard rocks become weak → easily broken → landslide
chunks.heading: 2. Strong Weathering

chunks.text:
HK_Relief_Distribution

- Hong Kong has many steep slopes (>30°)
- Steeper slopes = greater shear stress (driving force)
- More likely to collapse
chunks.heading: 3. Steep Slopes

chunks.text:
| Factor | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| Deforestation | Removes stabilizing roots |
| Slope excavation | Undercuts slope |
| Construction | Adds weight to slope |
| Poor drainage | Water accumulates |
chunks.heading: B. Human Factors

chunks.text:
| Fact | Data |
|------|------|
| Natural terrain in HK | 60% of land area |
| Annual landslides (natural) | ~300 per year |
| Wettest months | May-August |
| Most landslides | Wet summer months |
chunks.heading: 5. Key Data

chunks.text:
1. What is a landslide? → Mass of soil/rock moves down slope due to gravity
2. Effects? → Injuries, deaths, building damage, infrastructure damage, traffic disruption
3. Why slopes collapse? → Shear stress > Shear strength (or Driving force > Resisting force)
4. Causes in HK? → Heavy rainfall, weathering, steep slopes
chunks.heading: How to answer:

chunks.text:
- Rain adds weight → increases driving force
- Rain reduces cohesion & friction → decreases resisting force
- Therefore: Heavy rain = More landslides
chunks.heading: Remember:

chunks.heading: 9. Vocabulary

chunks.text:
House rule (your standing): at F.3 / DSE level, describe weathered granite products using regolith or deep weathered profile / weathered mantle — not grus. The term grus is granular-weathered granite sand; it is geomorphology / A-level / university vocabulary and rarely used in secondary-school DSE materials or exam mark schemes.

| Use this (DSE) | Not this (avoid) | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Regolith (風化層 / 風化剖面) | grus | Regolith = the entire loose, decomposed layer above fresh bedrock. Includes clay, silt, sand, organic matter. This is the textbook term in HK DSE Geography. |
| Deep weathered profile (深厚風化層) or weathered mantle (風化表層) | grus | Emphasises the thickness of weathering (HK granites weather 30–60 m deep in places). The thickness is what matters for slope stability. |
| Chemical weathering (化學風化) — produces clay minerals + soluble ions from feldspar | grus | The process (chemical breakdown) and its result (clay-rich regolith) are what students need to know. The grain-size outcome "grus" is a specific texture, not the headline idea. |

HKDSE-style answer sentence (model):

"Hot and wet climate promotes chemical weathering of granite, producing a thick regolith (deep weathered profile) that supplies loose material for landslides."
chunks.heading: Weathering vocabulary — HKDSE-friendly terms (house style)

chunks.text:
If a textbook or mark scheme uses the word "grus" (rare, but possible in some extension readings), explain it as "granular weathered granite sand — a type of regolith" rather than teaching it as a standalone term.

docs.title: Understanding the Relief of Hong Kong

chunks.text: Hong Kong's terrain is hilly and mountainous with steep slopes. There are limited lowlands mainly in coastal plains and reclaimed land.
chunks.heading: 1. Overall Relief Features

chunks.text:
| Feature | Data |
|---------|------|
| Natural terrain | ~60% of land area |
| Developable land | ~25% of land area |
| Steep slopes (>15°) | Too steep for development |
| Country parks | ~40% of remaining land |
chunks.heading: Key Statistics:

chunks.text: Reading the map: colour = height (pale green = lowlands 0–50 m · dark brown = highlands 700 m+) · ▲ = peak + official height · ● = town · thin lines = contours 100/300/500/700 m, with pale 800/900 m lines inside the dark summit block (closed rings = a rounded top, not a plateau). Compare the green north with the brown centre — that contrast is the distribution pattern.
chunks.heading: 2. Distribution of Relief

chunks.text:
| Region | Features |

| New Territories | Most mountainous, highest peaks |
| Hong Kong Island | Steep peaks (Victoria Peak: 552m) |

chunks.heading: A. Geological Factors (地質因素)

chunks.text:
| Process | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| Volcanic eruptions | Formed mountain ranges and peaks |
| Weathering | Breaks down rocks, creates valleys |
| Erosion | Removes weathered material, shapes landscape |
| Mass movement | Creates slopes and valleys |
chunks.heading: B. Geological Processes

chunks.text:
1. Hard rocks (volcanic, granite) resist erosion → remain as hills/mountains
2. Limited sediment deposition → few flat plains formed
3. Steep original terrain → remains steep after erosion
chunks.heading: C. Why Most Areas Are Hilly/Mountainous

chunks.text:
1. Limited sedimentary deposition - Not much river flood plain formation
2. Steep coastal slopes - Quick drop to sea depth
3. Limited alluvial plains - Few large rivers
chunks.heading: D. Why Lowlands Are Limited

chunks.text: Reading the profile (NW → SE, 24 km): Yuen Long plain (~10 m) → steep climb to Tai Mo Shan 957 m → down through the Kowloon hills → Victoria Harbour at sea level. One line shows the whole pattern below: low north-west → mountainous centre → low coast. Vertical scale exaggerated ≈ ×6.
chunks.heading: 5. Distribution Pattern

chunks.text:

- Lower elevation
- More flat land
- River plains (e.g., Yuen Long)

Southern & Eastern Areas:
- Higher elevation
- Steep slopes
- Mountainous terrain

Kowloon & HK Island:
- Urban areas on reclaimed land
- Hills in background

chunks.heading: Gradient in Ratio:

chunks.text:
1. Draw a line across the area on the map (Section line A-B)

2. Mark contour crossings where the line crosses each contour

3. Create vertical scale:
   - Determine height range (e.g., 0m to 500m)
   - Choose appropriate vertical scale

4. Plot points:
   - At each crossing, mark the height
   - Use a ruler to project vertically

5. Join points:
   - Connect with smooth curve (not straight lines)

6. Add labels:
   - Label heights on y-axis
   - Add title and orientation
chunks.heading: Steps:

chunks.text:
- Steep slopes = steep line on cross-section
- Gentle slopes = gentle line
- Valley = dips down
- Ridge = peaks up
chunks.heading: Tips:

chunks.text:
Title (1) · correct vertical scale (1) · correct shape (3) — a section with no title or no vertical scale loses marks before the shape is even looked at. Always:
1. Title the section (e.g. "Cross-section of M–N")
2. State the vertical scale as instructed (e.g. 1 cm = 100 m)
3. Plot every contour crossing, then join with a smooth curve
4. Label the height axis and the end points

chunks.heading: Mark split for a 5-mark cross-section

chunks.text:
Draw a straight line between the two points on your finished cross-section. If any higher ground rises above that line, the two points cannot see each other (not intervisible). Always answer with the line drawn and a because-clause.

chunks.heading: 5b. Intervisibility (1 mark)

chunks.text: Vertical exaggeration shows vertical scale larger than horizontal scale to make relief more visible.
chunks.heading: What is VE?

chunks.text:
- Horizontal scale: 1:10,000 (1 cm = 100 m)
- Vertical scale: 1:1,000 (1 cm = 10 m)
- VE = 10,000 ÷ 1,000 = 10 times
chunks.heading: Example A (from your notes)

chunks.text:
- VE = 20,000 ÷ 10,000 = 2 times
- (Vertical scale 1 cm = 100 m means 1:10,000 — convert first!)

VE is always ≥ 1; never divide vertically by horizontally.
chunks.heading: Example B (map at 1:20,000, vertical scale 1 cm = 100 m)

chunks.text:
- Makes subtle relief features more visible
- Shows地形 more clearly
- Common in geography exams
